items.body:
## Overview

Implements adaptive mtp with a new option `--spec-type draft-mtp-adaptive`

Suggested configuration to use is: `--spec-type draft-mtp-adaptive --spec-draft-n-max 12`

The algorithm is a counting based state machine with a climb counter and a weighted drop-pressure accumulator. The depth climbs one step after a number consecutive verifies that accepted every drafted token; any miss adds (N - acceptance) to the drop pressure and the depth drops one step once it exceeds a certain amount. High depths fall quickly (a total miss adds N), low depths hold, and at the floor no pressure accumulates at all.  The specific climb difficulty and drop pressure values were empirically determined over a wide range of tests.

`--spec-draft-n-max` bounds the upper adaptive range and both the floor and the cold-start depth default to 3.  The default floor of 3 may be adjusted  with `--spec-draft-n-min-adpative`, although in testing 3 seems to be the best value to choose here.

As higher depths are reached the barrier to climb higher is reduced.  This allows for predictive runs to quickly ascend after they've "proven" themselves.

## Testing and Performance Results

Model: Qwen3.8-27B Q8_0 on 2x Radeon AI PRO R9700 (gfx1201, ROCm).
Configs: plain `draft-mtp` with `--spec-draft-n-max 2` and `3`, and `draft-mtp-adaptive`
with `--spec-draft-n-max 12` (controller starts at the configured `--spec-draft-n-min-adaptive`
floor of 2 or 3 and adjusts on its own). Temperature 0.6, top-k 20, top-p 0.95, min-p 0.001,
8 threads, ctx 8192, 2 seeds per cell.

Tasks (realistic output lengths):
- prose / hard prose: "write a 1000-word essay ...", capped at 1600 tokens (the model
  generated the full 1600 in every run)
- coding: a mid-file C++ benchmark program (merge sort vs heap sort vs std::sort) to
  complete, ~750-800 tokens of generated continuation



### Throughput

| spec config | prompt | tokens/s (mean) | tokens/s (range) | draft accept | mean draft len | depth reached |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| fixed depth 2 | coding | 67.2 | 67.2-67.3 | 92.2% | 2.0 | - |
| fixed depth 3 | coding | 78.8 | 78.5-79.0 | 86.8% | 3.0 | - |
| adaptive (n_max 12, floor 2) | coding | **86.4** | 86.2-86.5 | 58.4% | 8.0 | 2 -> 10..11 |
| adaptive (n_max 12, floor 3) | coding | 85.3 | 83.7-86.9 | 59.3% | 7.5 | 3 -> 9..12 |
| fixed depth 2 | prose | 53.3 | 51.3-55.3 | 62.1% | 2.0 | - |
| fixed depth 3 | prose | **56.4** | 52.5-60.3 | 52.2% | 3.0 | - |
| adaptive (n_max 12, floor 2) | prose | 54.4 | 50.4-58.3 | 54.8% | 2.8 | 2 -> 3..4 |
| adaptive (n_max 12, floor 3) | prose | 54.8 | 51.2-58.5 | 51.4% | 3.2 | 3 -> 4..5 |
| fixed depth 2 | hard prose | 51.2 | 51.1-51.2 | 57.8% | 2.0 | - |
| fixed depth 3 | hard prose | **52.6** | 52.6-52.6 | 46.7% | 3.0 | - |
| adaptive (n_max 12, floor 2) | hard prose | 51.0 | 50.8-51.1 | 51.8% | 2.6 | 2 -> 3 |
| adaptive (n_max 12, floor 3) | hard prose | 51.3 | 51.1-51.4 | 46.7% | 3.1 | 3 -> 4 |

Console logs for the above runs 
[prfinal-console-all.txt](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/31147070/prfinal-console-all.txt)

### Demonstration of content replay speedups

It's difficult to fully capture and show the moments where the model is recalling content from memory, or regenerating code where predictions really spike.  

The following shows the console log from the coding output from a long Web coding session prompt.  When the Qwen3.8-27B model is recalling code generated from its thought process, we can see it spiking well above 100 t/s.  This demonstrates the capability of the adaptive MTP to take full advantage of such opportunities.   This system typically sustains around 30-35t/s for non-MTP generation, so the following hopefully demonstrates the capacity for amazing speed gains.

## Overview
This is really just a gate change.  
Decode with quantized KV (q4_0/q8_0) was falling into the VEC kernel. On BMG the TILE kernel wins decode across the board: measured +42% to +169% on Qwen3.6-35B, Gemma 4 26B and Gemma 4 12B at 32K and 118K context, zero regressions. Also confirmed by a Discord report on a 2-bit model (+50%/+68%).

## Additional information
~~Adds "GGML_SYCL_FA_DECODE_KERNEL=0/1/2"~~
~~0: Default. Quantized KV decode uses TILE, F16 unchanged~~
~~1: Force VEC for all decode~~
~~2: Force TILE for all decode~~
This is gated for BMG only.

## Requirements
No additional libraries needed.

## Testing
Tested on 4 models (Qwen 27B, Qwen 35B, Gemma 26B, Gemma 12B)
All TILE > VEC, min +41.9% max +168.7%.

items.title: SYCL: TILE for quantized KV decode

items.body:
## Summary

On Intel Arc Pro B70 (Battlemage G31, 32 GB, 608 GB/s), token-generation
speed collapses with context depth far beyond what KV-cache bandwidth can
explain. The excess cost is a near-constant **~21-25 ns per KV position per
full-attention layer per token**, and it is invariant across:

- **backend**: Vulkan (Mesa 26.1.6 ANV) and SYCL (oneAPI 2025.3, L0 V2) pay the same tax;
- **model/geometry**: hybrid Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (2 KV heads × hs256), Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B (4 × hs128), Gemma 4 26B-A4B / 12B (8 × hs512) — KV row width 1 KiB vs 8 KiB makes no difference;
- **build**: b8183 and b10235 behave identically at depth;
- **quantization**: Q2_K vs Q4_K_M identical depth deltas.

Byte-independence rules out DRAM bandwidth. The signature fits
memory-latency-bound attention matvecs: too few outstanding loads to cover
GDDR6 latency. Supporting evidence: GPU holds max clock at its power cap
while useful traffic is a fraction of peak; running 4 concurrent streams
scales aggregate throughput ~2.4× (parallel streams supply the MLP a single
stream lacks); the same llama.cpp code on an AMD Strix Halo iGPU with less
than half the bandwidth holds the sibling model flat to 65k
(https://lilting.ch/en/articles/qwen35-ctx-kv-cache-vulkan-optimization).

## Environment

- GPU: Intel Arc Pro B70 32 GB (PCI 8086:e223), PCIe passthrough to a Linux VM (6 vCPU, 16 GB RAM). d0 results match published bare-metal numbers, and all depth effects are on-card, so virtualization is not a factor.
- Host driver: xe, kernel 6.17; Vulkan: Mesa 26.1.6 (kisak), KHR_coopmat active; SYCL: oneAPI 2025.3 image, compute runtime 26.18.
- llama.cpp b10235 (also tested b8183), Vulkan and SYCL builds, `-ngl 999 -ub 512 -fa 0 -n 256 -p 0 -r 1 -d <depth>`.

## Data (tg256, t/s)

| model | backend | d0 | d32k | d65k | d127k |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Q4_K_M (hybrid, 10 attn layers) | Vulkan | 70.7 | 58.4 | 32.2 | 20.7 |
| Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Q2_K | Vulkan | 72.0 | 60.2 | 33.4 | 21.2 |
| Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Q2_K | SYCL | 81.5 | 52.9 | 38.5 | 22.8 |
| Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B Q4 (48 attn layers) | Vulkan b10235 | 87.1 | 37.6 | ~11-13 | |
| Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B Q4 | Vulkan b8183 | 103.7 | 35.8 | | |
| Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B Q4 | SYCL | 105.9 | 20.5 | 11.2 | |
| Gemma 4 26B-A4B Q4 | Vulkan | 69.2 | 57.8 | 30.9 | |
| Gemma 4 12B Q4 | Vulkan | 48.4 | 31.7 (d32k) | 22.5 | |
| Gemma 4 12B Q4 | SYCL | 51.8 | 34.8 (d32k) | 25.3 | |

Per-token excess over each model's own d0 baseline, divided by
(n_kv × full-attention layers), lands at 21-25 ns for every row above
(Gemma global-layer counts estimated from sliding_window_pattern).

Physics reference: Qwen3.6's KV is only 20 KiB/token (10 attn layers × 2 KV
heads × 256 × 2 × f16; 30 of 40 layers are DeltaNet with fixed state), i.e.
2.6 GB at 127k — ~5 ms/token at realistic bandwidth. Measured excess: ~33 ms.

## Control: same card, same model, different kernels — no depth tax

Intel's own stack (intel/llm-scaler-vllm 0.21.0-b2, vLLM v0.21.1 XPU, same
B70, same Qwen3.6-35B-A3B as GPTQ-Int4) decodes **flat to 127k**:

| depth | llama.cpp Vulkan b10235 (Q4_K_M) | vLLM XPU (GPTQ-Int4) |
|---|---|---|
| ~0 | 70.7 | 18.8-22.4 |
| 32k | 58.4 | 22.6 |
| 65k | 32.2 | 18.3-22.5 |
| 127k | 20.7 | 16.2-21.8 |

vLLM XPU's baseline is ~3.5× lower (eager GPTQ-MoE kernels), but its depth
cost is ~zero — demonstrating the Xe2 hardware itself can serve 127k
context with no per-position penalty. The tax measured above is specific to
ggml's decode-attention kernels.

## Additional findings from the same investigation

1. **Silent CPU fallback** (gdb-verified): with fa off, when the prefill
   score tensor (n_kv × n_ubatch × n_heads × 4B) exceeds free VRAM, the
   scheduler reroutes the matmul to the CPU backend with no warning —
   ~100× slowdown that presents as a hang. A log line when an op planned
   for GPU falls back would save users days. Likely the mechanism behind
   #18808's "almost stops".
2. **`-ctk q8_0` with fa off** also silently falls back to CPU on Vulkan.
3. **SYCL cannot load models whose weight buffer exceeds ~16.5 GiB**
   (`ggml_backend_sycl_buffer_type_alloc_buffer: can't allocate ... on
   device`, 29 GiB free): the SYCL backend allocates weights as one buffer
   and get_max_size does not reflect the device's real single-allocation
   ceiling; the Vulkan backend chunks. Qwen3.6-35B Q4_K_M (19.6 GiB)
   cannot run on SYCL on a 32 GB card. UR_L0_ENABLE_RELAXED_ALLOCATION_LIMITS,
   NEOReadDebugKeys/AllowUnrestrictedSize, legacy L0 adapter: no effect.
4. **b8183 → b10235 regressed MoE decode d0 ~19% on Vulkan**
   (Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B: 103.7 → 87.1 tg256).
5. fa=on is uniformly slower than fa=off on Xe2 for tg at every depth
   (Qwen3.6: 68.5/32.1/20.8/12.5 vs 70.7/58.4/32.2/20.7), q8_0 KV does not
   close the gap.

## Ask

The per-position constant suggests the decode-path attention matvec kernels
(both backends) issue too few concurrent loads on Intel to hide memory
latency at large n_kv. Happy to run diagnostics/patches on this hardware —
single-owner box, can bisect or profile on request.

items.body:
## Overview

Draft SM120 CUTLASS MoE prefill path, disabled by default. It currently supports:

- GPT-OSS MXFP4 with fused W13
- Qwen3.6-35B-A3B NVFP4

It repacks expert weights, reuses one routing schedule and input quantization per layer, then runs grouped W13/W2 with CUDA epilogues. Unsupported cases fall back to the existing CUDA path.

This branch also contains earlier CUDA and Attention experiments and is not intended to merge as one patch. Useful pieces can be split out separately.

## Additional information

Measured on one RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition with batch 8192, 25 CPU threads and FlashAttention.

### GPT-OSS-120B MXFP4 prefill

| Path | Best ubatch | pp8192 |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Existing llama.cpp | 2048 | 11,738.58 tok/s |
| Strict native CUDA | 8192 | 17,708 tok/s |
| Optimized CUTLASS | 8192 | 25,713.80 tok/s |
| Same-machine vLLM | 8192 | 36,819 tok/s |

CUTLASS is 2.19x faster than current llama.cpp and reaches 69.8% of same-machine vLLM.

### Qwen3.6-35B-A3B NVFP4 prefill

| Prompt | Native eager | CUTLASS eager | Speedup |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 512 | 9,819.79 tok/s | 12,998.69 tok/s | 1.324x |
| 2048 | 11,362.81 tok/s | 15,309.67 tok/s | 1.347x |
| 8192 | 10,065.18 tok/s | 13,548.77 tok/s | 1.346x |

CUDA Graphs reach 13,551.11 tok/s at pp8192, close to eager CUTLASS.

| Component | Native | CUTLASS |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Steady CUDA kernel time | 1,291.861 ms | 863.054 ms |
| MoE GEMM | 282.364 ms | 63.213 ms |
| Expert scheduling | 61.069 ms | 1.108 ms |
| Activation quantization | 45.941 ms | 27.656 ms |
| Attention | 76.195 ms | 75.589 ms |

The first CUTLASS use adds a 74.715 ms weight transform, excluded above.

### Decode

| Path | Decode |
| --- | ---: |
| Native MMVQ | 201.868 tok/s |
| CUTLASS | 170.207 tok/s |

Nsys reports 5.882 ms/token for MMVQ and 6.634 ms/token for CUTLASS. All 36 expert layers used CUTLASS, so MMVQ remains better for single-token decode.

```text
supported SM120 W4A4 prefill -> CUTLASS
single-token decode          -> MMVQ
everything else              -> existing llama.cpp path
```

Correctness passed 6/6 Qwen eager cases, 6/6 CUDA Graph cases, and all six GPT decode cases. Full-model Qwen logits validation is still pending.

Enable with `GGML_CUDA_CUTLASS_MOE=ON`. Current CUTLASS revision: `b46b16d003484063bca4ed365e44095c4c6ed633`.

- [Full results](https://github.com/leonardHONG/llama.cpp/blob/feat/blackwell-moe-prefill-experiments/scripts/blackwell-moe-prefill/RESULTS.md)
- [Build and experiment commands](https://github.com/leonardHONG/llama.cpp/blob/feat/blackwell-moe-prefill-experiments/scripts/blackwell-moe-prefill/README.md)
- [GPT-OSS decode notes](https://github.com/leonardHONG/llama.cpp/blob/feat/blackwell-moe-prefill-experiments/scripts/blackwell-moe-prefill/gpt_oss_mxfp4_decode.md)
- [Qwen NVFP4 prefill notes](https://github.com/leonardHONG/llama.cpp/blob/feat/blackwell-moe-prefill-experiments/scripts/blackwell-moe-prefill/qwen_nvfp4_prefill.md)



## CUTLASS integration

CUTLASS does not provide a single runtime API like cuBLAS. The kernel shape, layout, data types, and GPU architecture are fixed at compile time.

For this path, CUTLASS only provides the SM120 block-scaled W4A4 GEMM.

| Part | Where it is handled |
| --- | --- |
| SM120 W4A4 GEMM | CUTLASS |
| GGUF weight conversion | llama.cpp repack code |
| Activation quantization | llama.cpp CUDA code |
| Kernel selection and fallback | llama.cpp CUDA backend |
| MoE token grouping | llama.cpp CUDA code |
| SwiGLU and expert reduction | llama.cpp CUDA code |

GGUF stores quantized values and block scales together. CUTLASS expects separate value and scale tensors in its own layout, so the GGUF weights cannot be passed to the kernel directly. They are repacked on first use and cached.

For dense models the flow is basically:

```
GGUF weight -> repack -> activation quantization -> CUTLASS GEMM -> output scale
```

Dense and MoE use the same repack/cache code and the same GEMM launcher.

## MoE-specific work

For MoE, each token selects several experts and each expert receives a different number of rows. CUTLASS runs the grouped W13 and W2 GEMMs, but it does not build the groups.

I group the routed rows by expert and reuse that grouping for W13 and W2:

```
routing
  -> group rows by expert
  -> expand and quantize
  -> CUTLASS grouped W13
  -> scale, bias, SwiGLU, and A2 quantization
  -> CUTLASS grouped W2
  -> scale, bias, routing weight, and expert reduction
```

The W13 post-processing produces the quantized input for W2. The W2 post-processing combines the selected expert outputs back into one row per token. These two stages and the expert scheduling are the parts that remain MoE-specific.

These are custom CUDA kernels rather than CUTLASS epilogues. They fuse the scale, bias, activation, or routing reduction so another intermediate tensor is not materialized between stages.

Once the tensors are in the layout CUTLASS expects, the actual GEMM launch is fairly small. Most of the code is the glue around it: repacking GGUF weights, quantizing activations, caching converted weights, choosing the kernel, and handling graph and fallback cases.


## Requirements

-  I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)
-  AI usage disclosure: Yes, paired with Codex

items.body:
## Overview

DFlash2 adds two more modules compared to DFlash, grouped dynamic depthwise convolution and candidate selector. 

The formula is for reference. `out[i,c] = Σ_t (base[t,c] + δ[i,t,g(c)]) · x[i−t,c]`. `base` is the static kernel, `δ` is the dynamic part predicted from the input.`x` is divided into groups `g(c)` and `δ` is shared across a group. Another one is `edge(p→c) = ⟨A[p] ⊙ project(h), B[c]⟩ + unary[c]`. `A`/`B` are the codebooks for the predecessor and the candidate. This position's hidden is projected by `project(h)`to the same rank to multiply `A`. And `unary[c]` is the draft's own score for `c`.  

DFlash2 is enabled when the checkpoint is DFlash2; no need to use extra flag.

We evaled `Qwen3.8-27B` at `Q4_K_M`on Apple M5 Pro 64 GB. And the test data is first 8 problems of GSM8K.
Concurrency is set to 1 and temperature is 1.0, top-p 0.95, top-k 20. We use default `xhigh` reasoning and set
2,048 maximum new tokens.

| Method | Draft quant | Block | Decode TPS | Decode speedup | Acceptance | Normal stops |
|--------|------|--:|------:|------:|-----:|---|
| Autoregressive | — | — | 10.42 | 1.00× | — | 8/8 |
| DFlash2 | BF16 | 8 | 19.31 | 1.85× | 4.92 | 8/8 |
| DFlash2 | Q8_0 | 8 | 18.43 | 1.77× | 5.08 | 8/8 |
| DFlash2 | Q4_K_M | 8 | 18.89 | 1.81× | 5.03 | 8/8 |

# Vulkan/MTP performance bug triggered by ubatch=256 + f16 KV cache at large context

## Summary
With MTP speculative decoding enabled and `--ubatch-size 256` combined with `--cache-type-k/v f16`, prompt processing collapses to ~36 t/s and generation to ~9.5 t/s at context >= ~50k. Every other combination of ubatch/cache-type in the 2x2 matrix below is healthy. Reproduced on upstream master commit `b062ba7` with embedded MTP.

## Environment
- GPU: AMD Radeon AI PRO R9700 (32 GB), Vulkan backend
- OS: Windows 11, AMD driver 32.0.31035.1003
- Model: qwen35 dense 27B, Q5_K_P quantization (~18.8 GiB)
- MTP mode: embedded (`--spec-type draft-mtp`); an external MTP draft also reproduces on a separate build

## Repro command (llama-server)
```
llama-server.exe -m <path-to-model>/model.gguf --spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 3 -c 50000 -dev <vulkan-device> -ngl 999 -sm none -b 4096 -ub 256 -t 4 -fa on -ctk f16 -ctv f16 --no-mmap
```
Request: prompt `[4131]*4096`, `n_predict 512`, temp 0, `ignore_eos`, seed 42.

## 2x2 matrix at ctx=50000, MTP (n-max 3)
| ubatch | KV cache  | PP (t/s) | TG (t/s) | Result  |
| ------ | --------- | -------- | -------- | ------- |
| 256    | f16/f16   | ~36      | ~9.5     | BROKEN  |
| 1024   | f16/f16   | ~641     | ~50      | healthy |
| 256    | q8_0/q8_0 | ~594     | ~53      | healthy |
| 1024   | q8_0/q8_0 | ~630     | ~60      | healthy |

## Key observations
- Bug is specific to ubatch=256 + f16/f16 KV + MTP + large context.
- Healthy at ctx=16384 with the same ub256/f16/f16 + MTP (TG ~64), broken by ~50k.
- Without MTP, ub256/f16/f16 at 50k is healthy (~660 PP) - MTP is required to trigger.
- The transition is deterministic and abrupt; in prior testing with the failing configuration, performance flipped between healthy and broken around the ~47.6k context boundary.
- Ordinary Vulkan operation without MTP is healthy at 50k-100k context.
- Reproduces on upstream master commit `b062ba7` with embedded MTP, independent of any external draft/fork.

## Workaround
Use `--ubatch-size 1024` (either KV cache type) with MTP at large context; or use `--cache-type-k/v q8_0` with ubatch=256. Both avoid the collapse.

## Expected behavior
ubatch=256 + f16/f16 KV with MTP should perform comparably to the other matrix cells at large context (~50-60 t/s), not collapse to ~9.5 t/s.

### Name and Version


version: 9197 (0443f8906) 
built with MSVC 19.44.35227.0 for Windows AMD64
main branch with #23174 merged

### Operating systems

Windows

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

llama-cli

### Command line

```shell
.\llama-cli.exe `
  -m ".gguf" `
  --ctx-size 16384 `
  --n-gpu-layers auto `
  --flash-attn on `
  --jinja `
  --reasoning auto `
  -ctk q4_1 `
  -ctv q5_1 `
  -ctkd iq4_nl `
  -ctvd iq4_nl `
  -ctxcp 16 `
  -cpent 8192 `
  -cram 4096 `
  --batch-size 4096 `
  --ubatch-size 512 `
  --spec-type draft-mtp `
  --spec-draft-n-max 2 `
  --spec-draft-p-min 0.75 `
  -dev SYCL0 `
  -p "Explain in detail how speculative decoding works. Write at least 500 words." `
  -n 512 `
  -lv 3
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

I am seeing excessive memory usage and a severe performance regression when using the SYCL backend together with `draft-mtp` speculative decoding.

This is not limited to a large 9B model. I can also reproduce a major slowdown with a smaller 2B MTP model when both SYCL and MTP are enabled. This suggests that the issue may not simply be caused by insufficient VRAM capacity, but may be related to CPU fallback/offload, host-device transfer overhead, or SYCL-side memory planning/allocation behavior around MTP / `GATED_DELTA_NET`.

I tested both PR #23174 and PR #23187, and both showed similar high memory usage / slowdown behavior on my setup.

draft-mtp is definitely active. The runtime output includes:
```
prompt eval time =    1340.41 ms /    28 tokens (   47.87 ms per token,    20.89 tokens per second)
       eval time =    9975.30 ms /   512 tokens (   19.48 ms per token,    51.33 tokens per second)
      total time =   11315.70 ms /   540 tokens
draft acceptance rate = 0.48456 (251 accepted / 518 generated)
statistics draft-mtp: #calls(b,g,a) = 1 259 259, #gen drafts = 259, #acc drafts = 158, #gen tokens = 518, #acc tokens = 251
```
So the problem is not that MTP is failing to activate.

However, when using SYCL together with MTP, memory usage becomes much higher than expected and performance can degrade severely. This also happens with the smaller 2B MTP model.

In some cases the GPU may still appear to have enough VRAM available, but performance still drops significantly. This makes me suspect that something may be falling back or being offloaded to CPU, or that there is expensive host-device synchronization / transfer happening in the MTP path.

With the same model, prompt, and runtime parameters, Vulkan does not show the same level of memory growth or performance degradation.

When using SYCL with draft-mtp, memory usage should scale predictably with:

- context size
- batch / ubatch size
- KV cache type
- draft length
- MTP temporary tensors
- GATED_DELTA_NET intermediate tensors

For a 2B model, enabling MTP on SYCL should not cause a severe slowdown if there is enough GPU memory available, unless CPU fallback/offload is expected.

If CPU fallback/offload is currently expected for some MTP / GATED_DELTA_NET cases on SYCL, it would be helpful to document that clearly, because the resulting performance behavior can be surprising.

I am not sure yet whether this is primarily a SYCL backend issue, an MTP speculative decoding issue, a GATED_DELTA_NET K > 1 issue, a CPU fallback/offload issue, or a memory planner / temporary buffer lifetime issue. However, since both PR #23174 and PR #23187 show similar behavior on my setup, and even the 2B MTP model is affected(Resulting in significant delays for the first token and a decrease in token throughput), I think this is worth tracking as an upstream SYCL + MTP issue rather than as a model-size-specific problem.

### Name and Version

./llama-server --version
version: 746 (da296d6)
built with GNU 15.3.0 for Linux x86_64





### Operating systems

Linux

### GGML backends

HIP

### Hardware

CPU :  1th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i5-11400F
GPU: AMD Radeon RX 6800

### Models

https://huggingface.co/GianniDPC/Qwen3.6-27B-IQ4_XS-pure-with-MTP-GGUF
qwen3.6-27b-IQ4_XS-pure-with-MTP-IQ4.gguf


### Problem description & steps to reproduce

 When enabling Native MTP (--spec-type draft-mtp) while using --fit-target , the MTP draft context is created with proposed max 262144 ctx reported by QWEN3.6 27B, instead of the fit-reduced context size. With 16GB GPU using an adequate small GGUF + reduced ctx like ~50K this eat some ~30k of the supposed available ctx. The issue is clearly visible launching the exact llama-serve script with Vulkan:

| Backend | MTP | Final `n_ctx` | Context [MiB] | Compute [MiB] | Context loss vs. no-MTP |
|---------|-----|--------------|---------------|---------------|------------------------|
|  ROCm    | ✅  | 19,456       | 544           | 37            | 72,448                 |
| ROCm    | ❌  | 91,904       | 245           | 37            | —                      |
| Vulkan  | ✅  | 69,120       | 544           | 38            | 40,960                 |
| Vulkan  | ❌  | 110,080      | 245           | 34            | —                      |

The "right amount" of ctx left available available with ROCm + MTP should be: ~55.8K tokens not 19,4k (~2.9x improvement on this test case). This is a huge difference for a 16GB GPU user, makes or brakes usability of such quant size.

That should be because:
 - CUDA/HIP (get_alloc_size) calls ggml_cuda_flash_attn_ext_get_alloc_size(), which accounts for F16 K/V copies proportional to  n_ctx. So flash attention workspace is counted upfront during fit, and over-allocating it directly reduces available context.

 - Vulkan (get_alloc_size) just returns ggml_nbytes(tensor) — the raw tensor size. Flash attention temp buffers are pre-allocated on-demand during execution, not during the fit phase. So the over-sized n_ctx doesn't inflate the memory estimate the same way.

## Result:
Compute memory and --fit-target margin are the same yet llama.cpp's  HIP is overestimating required GPU memory by roughly 800 MiB when I use MTP.


## How to reproduce

Launch llama-serve with and without --spec-type draft-mtp , I've posted next in "Relevant log output" such memory allocation reports of the same script ROCm vs vulkan from my RX 6800 RDNA2 GPU.

        --cache-type-k-draft q4_0 --cache-type-v-draft q4_0 \
        --spec-ngram-mod-n-match 24 --spec-ngram-mod-n-min 8 --spec-ngram-mod-n-max 32 \
        --ctx-checkpoints 128 --cache-ram 6000 -np 1 -ngl 99 -lv 4 --no-warmup \

## Summary

With speculative decoding enabled (`temp 0`, fixed seed, otherwise identical settings), greedy output diverges from the identical non-speculative run. The divergence is **deterministic** (reruns are byte-identical) and is classified as **CUDA numerical divergence under batched speculative verification**, not a logic bug: the plain `draft-simple` path — which exercises batched verification with none of the DFlash2 code — reproduces it on one workload, while the DFlash2 path amplifies it (diverges on both workloads tested, and earlier).

Outputs remain coherent; this is a bit-exactness concern only, and speculative acceptance is unaffected. No fix is claimed here — this is a documentation/confirmation request.

## Environment

- llama.cpp at PR #27342 head: `5ecbe1ac17ec0484c5b44af0bd580cdc9c428ed4` (local build, MSVC 19.44, CUDA 12.4, sm_86)
- OS: Windows 11 x86_64
- GPU: NVIDIA RTX 3090 Ti 24 GB
- Target: `empero-ai/Qwen3.8-27B-Ridge-GGUF` `Qwen3.8-27B-Ridge-3.7bpw.gguf` (IQ2_M)
- Draft: `incoai/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2-GGUF` `Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2-Q4_K_M.gguf` (1,143,006,752 bytes; SHA-256 `18a380efc9b7ed8d88677fc895f5c11ae170653434ee378f7348f715c14d0594`)

## Repro (llama-cli, 6 runs)

Baseline (`--spec-type none`):

```
llama-cli -m <target> -ngl 999 --flash-attn on -c 8192 \
  --cache-type-k q4_0 --cache-type-v q4_0 -b 256 -ub 128 -t 8 \
  --temp 0 -s 42 --no-display-prompt -no-cnv -st \
  -n 256 -f prompt_short.txt < nul
```

Speculative variants add:

```
  -md <draft> --spec-draft-ngl 999 --spec-draft-n-max 7 --spec-draft-p-min 0 \
  --spec-type draft-simple        # or draft-dflash
```

Run the same with `-n 512 -f prompt_coding.txt`. Note: `--draft-model` is **not** a valid flag in this build; use `-md` (cli) / `--spec-draft-model` (server).

## Results (token-level, same-vocab `llama-tokenize`)

| workload | none vs draft-simple | none vs draft-dflash |
|---|---|---|
| short (n=256) | diverge at gen-token ~109 | diverge at gen-token ~49 |
| coding (n=512) | **identical 512/512** | diverge at gen-token ~372 |

Stripped-output MD5 (static banner/prompt-echo removed; generation content only):

| run | short | coding |
|---|---|---|
| none | `db0b78ede21fcb32543217e5cbfd437f` (1330 B) | `1d69d9619a1bde9249dac21e6fccaf99` (2482 B) |
| draft-simple | `c55e97dec9b537272f72dc578e1f00dc` (1346 B) | `1d69d9619a1bde9249dac21e6fccaf99` (2482 B) — **= none** |
| draft-dflash | `25dfca084f4cec36bc8f71f5eaa8da24` (1401 B) | `24d531f596c8aa41c1119ea01bd824d7` (2459 B) |

Reruns are byte-identical (determinism confirmed).

Example near-tie flips (short workload): `" storage of information."` vs `", recall, forgetting"`; `". Too many"` vs `"syllables. Too"`. Coding workload: digit flip `"1, 2"` vs `"8, 4"` in generated code.

## Analysis

- Batched verification alone (`draft-simple`, no DFlash hooks) perturbs CUDA target logits at near-ties: it diverges on the short workload yet is byte-identical on coding → **near-tie dependent, not systematic**.
- `draft-dflash` diverges on both workloads and earlier: DFlash2's extraction graph (`llama_set_embeddings_layer_inp` graph-output marking) amplifies the numeric shift but is **not the sole cause** (proven by the `draft-simple` divergence).
- Deterministic across reruns → consistent with CUDA fp-non-associativity in the batched verification decode (e.g. n_max=7 draft batch in one flash-attn batch vs sequential target decode) and/or graph-extraction side effects.
- Supporting data point: z-lab's Metal validation of DFlash2 achieved byte-identical greedy output (see z-lab/llama.cpp-fork#1), suggesting a platform-numeric component.

## Questions

1. Is bit-exact greedy output expected to be preserved under batched speculative verification on CUDA? (MTP presumably shows the same class of divergence.)
2. Is there a supported way to force the sequential target-decode path during verification, for bit-exact comparisons?
3. If this is accepted as generic numerics, it may be worth a short note in PR #27342 so downstream users don't mistake it for output corruption.

Cross-links: PR #27342 (DFlash2), companion issue [mtmd vision position-gap](#27408), z-lab/llama.cpp-fork#1 (Metal byte-identical validation).
items.title: spec: greedy output diverges from non-speculative baseline under batched verification on CUDA (deterministic numerics; draft-simple alone reproduces, DFlash2 amplifies)

# Token corruption (wrong-alphabet characters) with two concurrent long generations; identical solo run is clean

## Summary

When **two slots decode concurrently for an extended period** (10+ minutes each),
generated Hungarian text contains systematic token-level corruption: characters
from the wrong alphabet substituted for visually/byte-adjacent Hungarian letters
(`ø` U+00F8 instead of `ő` U+0151, `ì` U+00EC instead of `í` U+00ED), plus
malformed word endings. An **identical prompt with identical settings run solo
produces zero corrupted characters** even at greater length.

Possibly related: #27296 ("MTP breaks long/short inference?" — state leaking
between sequential requests). Our case adds a CUDA reproduction and a
concurrency dimension.

## Environment

- llama.cpp build 452 (commit `9558fa4`), CUDA backend, built with g++ (host), nvcc CUDA 12.8
- 2× NVIDIA RTX 3090 (no NVLink; PCIe, `nvidia-smi topo` = PHB), driver 570.133.07
- Linux, model fully offloaded (`-ngl 999`)
- Model: `unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF` `Qwen3.8-27B-Q6_K.gguf` (embedded MTP layer,
  `nextn_predict_layers=1`) + `mmproj-F16.gguf`

## Server invocation

```
llama-server -m Qwen3.8-27B-Q6_K.gguf -mm mmproj-F16.gguf \
  --spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 3 \
  --jinja -ngl 999 --ctx-size 458752 --parallel 2 \
  -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0 --cache-reuse 0 --no-context-shift \
  --temp 1.0 --top-p 0.95 --top-k 20 --min-p 0.0
```

MTP draft acceptance during affected runs: `draft acceptance = 0.846, mean len = 3.54`.

## Reproduction

1. Start two long chat-completion requests at the same time (one with
   `reasoning_effort: xhigh`, one with thinking disabled; both generate a
   ~20–38K-token Hungarian landing page over 7–15 minutes on the two slots).
2. Inspect the outputs.

## Observed

The longer (xhigh) stream contains **14 wrong-alphabet characters** and dozens of
malformed words. Samples (verbatim):

> `az ügyvédi irodák szolgalatára késült szerödéselemzø asszisztens: átnìzi a beékezett szerzödéseket`
> (intended: *szolgálatára készült szerződéselemző … átnézi a beérkezett szerződéseket*)

> `JELENTÁS` (intended: *JELENTÉS*), `belsø`, `idø`, `jelentø`, `lévøk`, `kockázasos`, `sülyozásba`, `törlí`

Hungarian has no `ø` or `ì`; these are near-neighbour byte/token substitutions,
i.e. sampling-level noise, not stylistic errors. The concurrently running second
stream showed milder, word-level corruption.

## Control (same settings, solo)

The identical prompt with `reasoning_effort: xhigh`, run **alone** on the same
server: 26K tokens of thinking + partial output, **zero** wrong-alphabet
characters. Severity correlates with **concurrent decode duration**:

| Scenario | Result |
|---|---|
| short parallel pair (~4 min overlap) | clean / near-clean |
| long parallel pair (7–15 min overlap) | corrupted (worst in the longest stream) |
| long solo (18 min) | clean |

## Suspicion

Draft rollback / KV bookkeeping of the embedded-MTP speculative path under
concurrent batched decoding (thousands of reject-rollback events per long run at
~15% rejection). Happy to run instrumented builds or provide the full outputs.

## Summary

Under parallel mixed load (`-np 4 --kv-unified`), `llama-server` on an **integrated HIP GPU** (Strix Halo / gfx1151, 128 GB UMA) returns **complete responses that verbatim belong to a different, earlier request**. A large-prompt request receives, as its entire response, the literal answer text of a short request from an earlier round. We also observed a **chimeric** response fusing tokens of two different requests' expected outputs.

**Bisected to a single commit: c7d87229 "ggml-cuda : restore prop.integrated on HIP builds" (#24233).**

| build | result (validated responses, nonce-checked) |
|---|---|
| 505b1ed1 (parent window start) | clean — 0 violations / 168 |
| 5839ba35 (= parent of c7d87229) | clean — 0 / 36 |
| **c7d87229** | **cross-request replays: 3 hard / 36** |
| e8f19cc0 (window end) | cross-request replays: 7 hard + 1 chimera / 96 |

The same harness against **CPU builds** of both window endpoints shows no build-dependent difference (model-compliance noise only) — consistent with the culprit being the HIP integrated-memory path. This presumably explains why it went unnoticed: discrete GPUs are unaffected; it needs an **integrated** AMD GPU (`prop.integrated == 1`), multiple slots and concurrent mixed traffic.

## Environment

- AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395 (Strix Halo), gfx1151, 128 GB unified memory, ROCm 7.14, Ubuntu 24.04
- Build: `cmake -DGGML_HIP=ON -DAMDGPU_TARGETS=gfx1151 -DGPU_TARGETS=gfx1151 -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=/opt/rocm/llvm/bin/clang -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=/opt/rocm/llvm/bin/clang++` (Release)
- Server: `llama-server -m <model> -ngl 999 -c 65536 -np 4 --kv-unified --jinja --chat-template-kwargs '{"enable_thinking":false}'`
- Model: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B MoE (Q4-class quant). First hit this in production behind LocalAI (same symptom after its vendored-llama.cpp bump crossed this commit); reproducing on vanilla `llama-server` rules the wrapper out.

## Reproduction

Load pattern per round (~30 s, script below): (B) short "repeat exactly this code: <nonce>" request → (C) large-prompt (~10k tokens) request whose system prompt requires echoing a per-request nonce in the first line → (D) burst of 4 concurrent short nonce requests (2 streamed / 2 plain). Every response is validated to contain its **own** nonce and no nonce of an **earlier** request.

On affected builds the round-N large-prompt request receives a literal foreign nonce as its complete response, typically from a round-(N−1) burst request. Verbatim from run logs at e8f19cc0:

```
R4/C got='pd-20260722-115649-3-d1'      (expected: reply echoing pc-...-4-c + a summary)
R5/C got='pd-20260722-115649-4-d2'
R6/C got='pd-20260722-115649-1-d1'
R7/C got='pd-20260722-115649-6-d1'
R8/C got='pd-20260722-115649-7-d1'
R3/C got='<!-- run:pc-20260722-115649-2-d0 -->'   <-- chimera: pc-...-2 stem fused with a -d0 burst suffix
```

In production we additionally observed: a poisoned slot re-serving its stored answer to unrelated requests **20+ minutes later** (the victim's `usage` then reports the foreign request's token counts), and occasional degeneration into repeated single characters (`/////...`).

### SYCL MTP on Intel Arc: correct output but no speed gain over baseline

**Build:** b9292 (master, oneAPI 2025.3.3)
**GPU:** Intel Arc Pro B70 (32656 MiB)
**Model:** Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-uncensored-heretic-Native-MTP-Preserved-Q4_K_M.gguf (MoE, 256 experts, 8 active)

#### Summary

After the recent merges (#23174 GDN K>1, #23142 MoE prefill, #23287 backend sampling), SYCL MTP produces **100% correct output** with **perfect draft acceptance**. This is a major milestone — earlier builds produced garbled text.

However, MTP consistently underperforms the non-MTP baseline:

| Config | Tok/s | Draft Accept | Output |
|--------|-------|-------------|--------|
| No MTP | **73.3** | — | ✅ Clean |
| MTP (draft-mtp, n_max=2) | **57.8** | 26/26 (100%) | ✅ Clean |
| MTP (draft-mtp, n_max=3) | ~48 | ~80% | ✅ Clean |

MTP is **~21% slower** than generating without speculation, despite 100% draft accuracy. This is the opposite of the expected result (typically 1.5-2x speedup on CUDA).

#### What was fixed (since b9159)

- 🟢 **GDN K>1** (#23174 karavayev) — eliminated garbled output entirely
- 🟢 **MoE prefill** (#23142 sanmai) — improved prefill, reduced generation overhead
- 🟢 **Backend sampling** (#23287) — D2H optimization, top-10 logits only
- 🟢 **VRAM leak** (#23461) — MTP resources freed on idle slots

#### What remains

The MTP head forward pass adds significant launch overhead on SYCL. Each MTP step requires:
- 1 main model decode (40 layers, ~8 experts each)
- 1 MTP head decode (1 layer, same expert count)
- 1 verification pass (batched main model decode)

On SYCL/Intel Arc, the per-kernel dispatch cost is 100-500µs vs ~5µs on CUDA. The 100% draft acceptance means the draft tokens are perfect — the bottleneck is purely kernel dispatch overhead, not compute.

#### Comparison with Vulkan

The same b9187 code built with `-DGGML_VULKAN=ON` achieves 53 tok/s with MTP — similar throughput but Vulkan has lower dispatch overhead per kernel.

#### Launch command for reproduction

```bash
source /opt/intel/oneapi/setvars.sh --force && export GGML_SYCL_F16=1 && \
  ~/llama.cpp/build-sycl-mtp-b9292/bin/llama-server \
  --jinja --chat-template-file ~/models/chat_template-v18.jinja \
  -m ~/models/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-uncensored-heretic-Native-MTP-Preserved-Q4_K_M.gguf \
  --spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 2 --spec-draft-n-min 1 \
  -t 24 -ngl 99 -ub 512 -b 4096
```

#### Prior related issues

- #23149 (eval bug, resolved by PR merges)
- #23155 (original bug report, closed as duplicate)
- #23142 (MoE prefill, merged)
- #23174 (GDN K>1, merged)

#### Note

This is not a regression — the output quality and correctness fixes are invaluable. This report is to track that MTP generation speed on SYCL+MoE architectures still needs Intel kernel-level optimization (likely kernel fusion or SYCL graph support for the MTP head pipeline).

## Summary
On the Vulkan backend, Qwen3.5-27B (architecture qwen35, hybrid Gated DeltaNet + full-attention layers) generates garbage / truncated output when the batch size is set to 512. The same model and configuration generate correct, coherent text at batch sizes 1024 and 4096.

## Environment
- OS: Windows 11 (build 26200)
- GPU: AMD Radeon RX 7900 XTX (24 GB), AMD proprietary driver
- Backend: Vulkan
- Software: koboldcpp 1.119 (nocuda build, Vulkan backend) which bundles the llama.cpp Vulkan backend. The underlying kernel issue appears to be in ggml-vulkan.

## Model
- Architecture: qwen35 (Gated DeltaNet / linear-attention hybrid, full_attention_interval = 4, 3x DeltaNet + 1x full-attention per group, ssm state_size 128)
- GGUFs tested: Q4_K_M and Q6_K_M quantizations of Qwen3.5-27B, including a variant carrying the built-in MTP/NextN head
- Context: reproduced at both 32768 and 262144

## Repro steps
1. Load the model with the Vulkan backend.
2. Set batch size to 512 (llama.cpp: -b 512; koboldcpp: batchsize=512), ubatch 512.
3. Send a simple generation request (e.g. 'Write a short poem about the ocean.').
4. Observe output: random token fragments / garbage, or generation stops after 1-2 tokens (e.g. 'The.') with an early EOS.

With batch size 1024 or 4096 the same request produces normal coherent output.

## Notes
- MMQ disabled; Flash Attention on/off both reproduce the issue.
- KV cache f16 and q8_0 both reproduce the issue.
- MTP drafting on/off both reproduce the issue.
- The symptom pattern points at the Gated Delta Net kernel path selection: at small batch the autoregressive (non-chunked) path corrupts the logits, while at larger batch the chunked/fused path works correctly.
- Related: #20610 (Qwen3.5-27B garbage on Vulkan), #21888, #24812, #20515.

## Expected behavior
Output quality should be independent of batch size.

## Overview The Q4_K/Q5_K scale unpack branches on a runtime value to pick between two layouts. nvcc can't fold that, so it predicates it and then repeats the whole thing for every column of the ncols_dst loop instead of doing it once. Swapping the branch for a mask select fixes it: predicated instructions at ncols_dst=8 go from 226 to 34, and the Q4_K kernel at 16 columns from 2256 to 1648. None of the other quant types have this problem, they already unpack unconditionally (Q3_K does the same 6-bit layout with plain shifts). We see perf gains from batch size >=4 on RTX 5090 and >=5 on RTX 4090 (more details in the Performance drop down), however we do not see a gain with DGX Spark, and in fact a small regression at batch sizes 4-6, which is why the change is gated off there. The most probable reason for this can be that the memory bandwidth on DGX Spark is much lower than that of RTX 4090 or 5090, and this means even with this optimization there is no effective time to save, since in the original code the unpack was already running while the kernel waits on the weight loads and so was not adding to the total time.
Performance

## Benchmarks (RTX 5090, sm_120, CUDA 12.9, driver 620.23) Both builds are from the same commit; the only difference is this patch. Batch size below refers to `ne11`, the number of columns the matmul receives in a single forward pass. It can arise in three ways, which are indistinguishable to the kernel: N concurrent requests against a server started with `-np N`, a draft block of `n_max + 1` tokens on a single slot, or `llama-bench -p N` directly. Two rows per model. `decode` is `llama-bench -p N -n 0 -embd 1 -r 40`, a single forward pass of N tokens with nothing generated, which is the decode step at batch N. `end to end` is llama-server tokens/sec, which also includes prefill, sampling and the draft model, and is therefore always lower. `*` marks a quant type this patch does not modify. ### 1. vs batch size Llama-3.1-8B, no draft model; only `-np` changes. Other models Batch pinned at 4, no draft model. | model | metric | Q4_K_M | Q5_K_M | Q6_K * | |---|---|---|---|---| | **Llama-3.1-8B** | decode | **+8.9%** | **+6.6%** | **-0.8%** | | | end to end | +7.4% | +5.5% | +0.3% | | **gemma-4-12B** | decode | **+8.2%** | **+6.3%** | **+0.0%** | | | end to end | +6.8% | +6.0% | +0.1% | | **Qwen3.6-27B** | decode | **+6.2%** | **+5.1%** | **+0.3%** | | | end to end | +8.0% | +4.2% | +0.5% | ### 3. # Server wedge: generation stalls mid-decode; /health OK but /slots hangs; process must be SIGKILLed

## Summary

Under long-running load the server occasionally **stops generating mid-decode**:
`print_timing` lines cease, GPU utilization drops to 0%, the process stays alive,
`/health` still returns `{"status":"ok"}`, but **`/slots` hangs** (no response)
and the client stream goes idle until the client-side timeout. In one instance
the process also **ignored SIGTERM** and required `kill -9`.

Observed **3 times in 2 days across two builds and two different models, with
and without MTP**, so it does not appear specific to a model, speculative
decoding, or a recent regression.

## Environment

- llama.cpp CUDA backend; observed on build 452 (`9558fa4`) and build 561 (`ee4c505`)
- 2× RTX 3090 (PCIe/PHB, no NVLink), driver 570.133.07, CUDA 12.8, Linux
- No `Xid` errors in `dmesg` in any incident (not a GPU fault)

## Incidents

**A)** Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Q8_0 (MoE, **no MTP**), single slot, 32K ctx, long-context
eval task: generation stopped after ~286 tokens (timing lines ceased), client
timed out after 20 min, server log showed `cancel task` then the process kept
spinning (`R` state), ignored SIGTERM, needed SIGKILL. Immediately before the
stall: `slot get_availabl: … selected slot by LCP similarity, f_sim_best = 0.999`.

**B)** Qwen3.8-27B Q6_K (embedded MTP, `--spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 3`),
`--parallel 2`, two concurrent agent workloads: slot 1 decoding normally
(~40 tok/s, `n_decoded = 8337`), then all timing output stops; `/health` OK,
`/slots` hangs, GPU 0%. Restart required. Full journal excerpt (926 lines around
the stall) available on request.

**C)** Same symptom pattern on build 561 during a client 300 s stream-idle
timeout; restart healed it.

## Server invocation (incident B)

```
llama-server -m Qwen3.8-27B-Q6_K.gguf -mm mmproj-F16.gguf \
  --spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 3 \
  --jinja -ngl 999 --ctx-size 458752 --parallel 2 \
  -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0 --cache-reuse 0 --no-context-shift \
  --temp 1.0 --top-p 0.95 --top-k 20 --min-p 0.0
```

(`--cache-reuse 0 --no-context-shift` were added after incident A as a hunch;
incident B shows they do not prevent it.)

## Notes

- `/health` responding while `/slots` hangs suggests the slots endpoint blocks on
  a mutex held by the stuck decode path — a liveness probe on `/slots` (or a
  watchdog around the decode loop) would at least make the state detectable.
- Happy to reproduce with added instrumentation and to share full journals.

# Token corruption (wrong-alphabet characters) with two concurrent long generations; identical solo run is clean

## Summary

When **two slots decode concurrently for an extended period** (10+ minutes each),
generated Hungarian text contains systematic token-level corruption: characters
from the wrong alphabet substituted for visually/byte-adjacent Hungarian letters
(`ø` U+00F8 instead of `ő` U+0151, `ì` U+00EC instead of `í` U+00ED), plus
malformed word endings. An **identical prompt with identical settings run solo
produces zero corrupted characters** even at greater length.

Possibly related: #27296 ("MTP breaks long/short inference?" — state leaking
between sequential requests). Our case adds a CUDA reproduction and a
concurrency dimension.

## Environment

- llama.cpp build 452 (commit `9558fa4`), CUDA backend, built with g++ (host), nvcc CUDA 12.8
- 2× NVIDIA RTX 3090 (no NVLink; PCIe, `nvidia-smi topo` = PHB), driver 570.133.07
- Linux, model fully offloaded (`-ngl 999`)
- Model: `unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF` `Qwen3.8-27B-Q6_K.gguf` (embedded MTP layer,
  `nextn_predict_layers=1`) + `mmproj-F16.gguf`

## Server invocation

```
llama-server -m Qwen3.8-27B-Q6_K.gguf -mm mmproj-F16.gguf \
  --spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 3 \
  --jinja -ngl 999 --ctx-size 458752 --parallel 2 \
  -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0 --cache-reuse 0 --no-context-shift \
  --temp 1.0 --top-p 0.95 --top-k 20 --min-p 0.0
```

MTP draft acceptance during affected runs: `draft acceptance = 0.846, mean len = 3.54`.

## Reproduction

1. Start two long chat-completion requests at the same time (one with
   `reasoning_effort: xhigh`, one with thinking disabled; both generate a
   ~20–38K-token Hungarian landing page over 7–15 minutes on the two slots).
2. Inspect the outputs.

## Observed

The longer (xhigh) stream contains **14 wrong-alphabet characters** and dozens of
malformed words. Samples (verbatim):

> `az ügyvédi irodák szolgalatára késült szerödéselemzø asszisztens: átnìzi a beékezett szerzödéseket`
> (intended: *szolgálatára készült szerződéselemző … átnézi a beérkezett szerződéseket*)

> `JELENTÁS` (intended: *JELENTÉS*), `belsø`, `idø`, `jelentø`, `lévøk`, `kockázasos`, `sülyozásba`, `törlí`

Hungarian has no `ø` or `ì`; these are near-neighbour byte/token substitutions,
i.e. sampling-level noise, not stylistic errors. The concurrently running second
stream showed milder, word-level corruption.

## Control (same settings, solo)

The identical prompt with `reasoning_effort: xhigh`, run **alone** on the same
server: 26K tokens of thinking + partial output, **zero** wrong-alphabet
characters. Severity correlates with **concurrent decode duration**:

| Scenario | Result |
|---|---|
| short parallel pair (~4 min overlap) | clean / near-clean |
| long parallel pair (7–15 min overlap) | corrupted (worst in the longest stream) |
| long solo (18 min) | clean |

## Suspicion

Draft rollback / KV bookkeeping of the embedded-MTP speculative path under
concurrent batched decoding (thousands of reject-rollback events per long run at
~15% rejection). Happy to run instrumented builds or provide the full outputs.
items.title: Token corruption (wrong-alphabet chars) with two concurrent long generations; identical solo run is clean

### Name and Version

```
version: 0.1.0-dev (build 1, commit 9f0d017)
built with GNU 13.3.0 for Linux x86_64
```

Full commit: `9f0d017efb4a388bd5c60a27a575c90f20868e51` (2026-08-17)

### Operating systems

Linux

### GGML backends

CUDA

### Hardware

| | |
|---|---|
| GPU | NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 Laptop GPU (GB203M), 24463 MiB, compute capability 12.0 |
| CPU | Intel Core Ultra 9 275HX |
| Laptop | HP OMEN MAX 16 (board 8D41) |
| Driver | 595.84 |
| CUDA runtime | 13.2 |
| CUDA toolkit used to build | 13.3, V13.3.73 |
| OS | Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS, kernel 7.0.0-29-generic |

Build configuration:

```
CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE          = Release
CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES  = 120
GGML_CUDA                 = ON
GGML_CUDA_GRAPHS          = ON
GGML_CUDA_FA              = ON
GGML_CUDA_FORCE_CUBLAS    = OFF
GGML_CUDA_FORCE_MMQ       = OFF
GGML_SCHED_MAX_COPIES     = 1
```

### Models

Qwen3.8-27B Q4_K_M GGUF (arch `qwen35`, 27.32B params, 15.65 GiB, hybrid attention + SSM, 64 layers, `n_embd_head_k/v = 256`), loaded together with the F16 mmproj for vision.

The hang reproduces with two different Q4_K_M builds of this architecture: the stock unsloth `Qwen3.8-27B-Q4_K_M.gguf` and a third party abliterated build of the same model. So it is not specific to one quantization run or one finetune.

### Problem description and steps to reproduce

Under sustained inference load, the GPU stops servicing a command channel. The NVIDIA kernel driver's Robust Channel watchdog declares the GPU locked after a 7 second notify timeout, raises Xid 8, and `llama-server` aborts inside `ggml_abort` with a CUDA error.

Setting `GGML_CUDA_DISABLE_GRAPHS=1` eliminates the failure completely. Nothing else needs to change.

Command line that reproduces the hang:

```bash
llama-server \
  --model Qwen3.8-27B-Q4_K_M.gguf \
  --mmproj mmproj-F16.gguf \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 \
  -b 2048 -ub 512 -fitt 0 \
  --cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0 \
  --cache-ram 32768 --ctx-checkpoints 32 \
  --threads 12 --threads-batch 12 \
  -ngl 999 --no-mmap --mlock \
  --reasoning-preserve \
  --temp 1.0 --top-p 0.95 --top-k 20 --min-p 0.0 \
  --presence-penalty 0.0 --repeat-penalty 1.0 \
  -np 1 -lv 4
```

The exact same command line prefixed with `GGML_CUDA_DISABLE_GRAPHS=1` does not hang.

Steps:

1. Start `llama-server` with the command above.
2. Drive it with a real coding agent workload (I used OpenCode) so the slot stays busy with long prompts and long generations.
3. Wait. The hang is stochastic, not deterministic. It never happens on the first request.

#### Failure rate

Across 11 observed hangs, time from server start to hang was:

```
min      4 minutes
mean   8.6 minutes
max     15 minutes
```

With `GGML_CUDA_DISABLE_GRAPHS=1` the same workload has run 50 minutes and then 32+ minutes without a single hang, on the same boot, same GPU, same model, same client. Assuming the failure rate is unchanged, the probability of surviving 32 minutes by chance is under 3 percent.

#### A/B evidence, same boot, same hour, same model

| PID | `GGML_CUDA_DISABLE_GRAPHS` | fusion | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4555 | not set | enabled | hang at 16:27:41 |
| 10643 | not set | enabled | hang at 16:37:15 |
| 3568 | `=1` | disabled | 50 minutes clean, stopped manually |
| 40527 | `=1` | **enabled** | 32+ minutes clean and still running |

PID 40527 is the important row. It has kernel fusion enabled and only CUDA graphs disabled, and it is stable. So this is not the fusion path, it is the graph path.

#### Collateral damage

While `llama-server` holds the GPU, the X server hits Xid 8 on its own channel too:

```
NVRM: Xid (PCI:0000:02:00): 8, pid=2434, name=Xorg, channel 0x00000002
```

This is consistent with a single long running or non terminating kernel blocking the GPU for more than the 7 second watchdog window, starving other channels.

#### What I ruled out

- **Power / TGP.** Hangs occur identically at the stock 95 W limit and at the full 175 W (150 W base + 25 W Dynamic Boost). Not a power delivery problem.
- **Thermal.** `HW Thermal Slowdown` counter is 0. Temperatures ranged 67 to 82 C against a 87 C target, 89 C slowdown, 92 C shutdown. No thermal event.
- **Hardware fault.** No Xid 79, no Xid 63/64, no ECC errors. A clean reboot does not prevent the hang, it recurs 16 minutes into a fresh boot.
- **MTP / speculative decoding.** Hangs with and without `--spec-type draft-mtp`.
- **Kernel fusion.** `GGML_CUDA_DISABLE_FUSION=1` is not required. With fusion enabled and only graphs disabled the server is stable.
- **KV cache quantization.** `q8_0` K and V are used in both the hanging and the stable configuration.

### First Bad Commit

Not bisected. Present in `9f0d017`.

This looks distinct from the two existing Blackwell reports:

- #21564 reports Xid 43 (illegal memory access) traced to `flash_attn_stream_k_fixup`.
- #24399 reports a device exception from an out of range shared memory store in `mul_mat_q<Q8_0,128>`.

Both of those are illegal accesses. What I am seeing is a **hang**, not an illegal access: the RC watchdog fires on a 7 second timeout and the hardware exception counters stay at zero. Different failure mode, and the workaround is different as well.

### Relevant log output

#### Kernel log

Every hang is preceded by the watchdog line:

```
kernel: NVRM: krcWatchdog_IMPL: RC watchdog: GPU is probably locked!  Notify Timeout Seconds: 7
kernel: NVRM: Xid (PCI:0000:02:00): 8, pid=4555, name=llama-server, channel 0x00000007
```

Sample sequence over one afternoon:

```
15:05:41  Xid 8  llama-server  channel 0x00000007
15:20:45  Xid 8  llama-server  channel 0x00000007
15:24:35  Xid 8  llama-server  channel 0x00000007
15:28:33  Xid 8  llama-server  channel 0x00000007
15:35:44  Xid 8  llama-server  channel 0x00000007
16:24:12  Xid 8  Xorg          channel 0x00000002
16:27:41  Xid 8  llama-server  channel 0x00000007
16:37:15  Xid 8  llama-server  channel 0x00000005
```

## Overview

I found an issue with quants, that they become very slow on prefill. Later I googled the exact issue. Found out that q_8 is working perfectly fine, but it did not compress enough memory for single gpu to use newest qwen 3.8 model. Tested each quant individually to get results, which were unsatisfactory:

All "after" numbers measured at the same ~9000 token prompt for a fair comparison. Before the fix the small quants collapse and time out at long prompts, so those are at shorter prompts:

| KV | before | after (~9000 tok prompt) |
|----|--------|--------------------------|
| q4_0 | 74 t/s | 1182 t/s |
| q4_1 | ~157 | 1175 |
| q5_0 | slow / timeout | 1167 |
| q5_1 | 125 | 1164 |
| q8_0 | 1159 (already fast) | 1159 |

At equal prompt length all quant KV types now run within ~2% of each other, so the fix makes them all as fast as q8_0.

Than tried reverse engineer to find the problem with opus 4.8. Because it is working on q_8 i decided that the fix will be easy, as AI can find patterns and apply similar patterns for smaller quants. q4_0 was successfull from the start, later I ran into issues with q4_1, q5_0, q5_1. It took several hours to recompile them (they also need GGML_CUDA_FA_ALL_QUANTS=ON to be enabled), but the issue was fixed. After re-testing at the same prompt length all quants run at about the same speed. Still though I think there is room for improvement, but for maximum memory squeeze and performance q4_0 looks like the sweet spot for now. For a little bit better quality use q8_0, or q5_1 which sits between q4_0 and q8_0 in quality.

## Additional information

Fixes #27109. Tested on 2x RTX 3090 with Qwen 3.8 27B, outputs are numerically correct.

llama.cpp prebuild for rtx 3090 lower Quants fast prefill fix (if you don't want to compile): https://github.com/Cybertiron/llama.cpp/releases/tag/b27109-quant-kv-fix

## Requirements

- [x] I have read and agree with the contributing guidelines
- AI usage disclosure: YES - the CUDA kernel code was written with AI (Opus 4.8). I found the problem, directed the debugging and tested/verified everything myself on my own 2x RTX 3090.

## Summary

Under parallel mixed load (`-np 4 --kv-unified`), `llama-server` on an **integrated HIP GPU** (Strix Halo / gfx1151, 128 GB UMA) returns **complete responses that verbatim belong to a different, earlier request**. A large-prompt request receives, as its entire response, the literal answer text of a short request from an earlier round. We also observed a **chimeric** response fusing tokens of two different requests' expected outputs.

**Bisected to a single commit: c7d87229 "ggml-cuda : restore prop.integrated on HIP builds" (#24233).**

| build | result (validated responses, nonce-checked) |
|---|---|
| 505b1ed1 (parent window start) | clean — 0 violations / 168 |
| 5839ba35 (= parent of c7d87229) | clean — 0 / 36 |
| **c7d87229** | **cross-request replays: 3 hard / 36** |
| e8f19cc0 (window end) | cross-request replays: 7 hard + 1 chimera / 96 |

The same harness against **CPU builds** of both window endpoints shows no build-dependent difference (model-compliance noise only) — consistent with the culprit being the HIP integrated-memory path. This presumably explains why it went unnoticed: discrete GPUs are unaffected; it needs an **integrated** AMD GPU (`prop.integrated == 1`), multiple slots and concurrent mixed traffic.

## Environment

- AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395 (Strix Halo), gfx1151, 128 GB unified memory, ROCm 7.14, Ubuntu 24.04
- Build: `cmake -DGGML_HIP=ON -DAMDGPU_TARGETS=gfx1151 -DGPU_TARGETS=gfx1151 -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=/opt/rocm/llvm/bin/clang -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=/opt/rocm/llvm/bin/clang++` (Release)
- Server: `llama-server -m <model> -ngl 999 -c 65536 -np 4 --kv-unified --jinja --chat-template-kwargs '{"enable_thinking":false}'`
- Model: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B MoE (Q4-class quant). First hit this in production behind LocalAI (same symptom after its vendored-llama.cpp bump crossed this commit); reproducing on vanilla `llama-server` rules the wrapper out.

## Reproduction

Load pattern per round (~30 s, script below): (B) short "repeat exactly this code: <nonce>" request → (C) large-prompt (~10k tokens) request whose system prompt requires echoing a per-request nonce in the first line → (D) burst of 4 concurrent short nonce requests (2 streamed / 2 plain). Every response is validated to contain its **own** nonce and no nonce of an **earlier** request.

On affected builds the round-N large-prompt request receives a literal foreign nonce as its complete response, typically from a round-(N−1) burst request. Verbatim from run logs at e8f19cc0:

```
R4/C got='pd-20260722-115649-3-d1'      (expected: reply echoing pc-...-4-c + a summary)
R5/C got='pd-20260722-115649-4-d2'
R6/C got='pd-20260722-115649-1-d1'
R7/C got='pd-20260722-115649-6-d1'
R8/C got='pd-20260722-115649-7-d1'
R3/C got='<!-- run:pc-20260722-115649-2-d0 -->'   <-- chimera: pc-...-2 stem fused with a -d0 burst suffix
```

In production we additionally observed: a poisoned slot re-serving its stored answer to unrelated requests **20+ minutes later** (the victim's `usage` then reports the foreign request's token counts), and occasional degeneration into repeated single characters (`/////...`).

<details><summary>repro-crossover.py (needs httpx)</summary>

```python

Each round: (B) short "repeat exactly: <nonce>" request, (C) large-prompt

(D) burst of 4 concurrent short nonce requests (2 streamed / 2 plain).

items.body:
## Overview

Fixes a regression after #24233, which restored HIP integrated GPU detection. On my AMD APU, this also made the ROCm host-buffer path available for HIP integrated GPUs. With that path enabled, prompt input appears corrupted: chat templates and system prompts can be ignored, and generated output becomes garbage.

This change keeps integrated GPU detection/reporting intact, but disables direct ROCm_Host compute on HIP integrated GPUs. The fix does not disable host-buffer exposure entirely, pinned buffers remain available to preserve functionality, while only the problematic direct compute path is blocked.

## Additional information

Tested locally on gfx1151 / RDNA3.5 APU with ROCm 7.14. The corrupted input/output issue is fixed with this patch.
The issue appeared in external harnesses like Pi and OpenCode. It can also be reproduced in the built-in web UI with a sufficiently large combined first input. For example, gemma-4-26B-A4B with 4676 tokens of context or more outputs `<unused49>` indefinitely. Other models can be way more resilient and their output starts by saying 'Based on the text provided, which appears to be a corrupted or "hallucinated" version of a Wikipedia article'.

## Requirements

- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- AI usage disclosure: YES - I used AI assistance to review and patch the relevant code. I tested and reviewed the final change myself.

items.body:
## Bug: AMD GPU token substitution corruption on Qwen3.6-27B (both Vulkan and ROCm)

### Summary

All models produce consistent character substitution errors in generated text on AMD GPU backends (Vulkan and ROCm). The CPU backend produces correct output. Cloud vLLM with the same model also produces correct output. The corruption is deterministic, reproducible, and not model-specific.

**Version:** b10298 (commit 15586e2d7)

### Symptom

URLs and long token sequences get corrupted with character substitutions. Examples from Qwen3.6-27B:

| Input | GPU output |
|-------|-----------|
| `awesome-zsh-plugins` | `awesome-zh-plugins` |
| `awesome-zsh-plugins` | `awesome-zshell-plugins` |
| `awesome-zsh-plugins` | `awesome-ssh-plugins` |
| `froggeric` | `frogger` |
| `helix-assist` | `helix-Assist` |

Short strings like `zsh-plugins` reproduce correctly in isolation. The corruption only appears in longer sequences, suggesting precision accumulation in attention over longer contexts.

### Reproduction

1. Start llama-server with any GGUF model on AMD GPU (Vulkan or ROCm backend)
2. Send a chat completion asking to repeat a URL:

```bash
curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "code",
    "messages": [
      {"role": "system", "content": "You are a precise assistant. Repeat exactly."},
      {"role": "user", "content": "Repeat this URL exactly:\nhttps://github.com/unixorn/awesome-zsh-plugins/blob/main/README.md"}
    ],
    "max_tokens": 100,
    "temperature": 0.0
  }'
```

3. Observe corrupted URL in the response
4. Run the same request on CPU backend (`--n-gpu-layers 0`) and observe correct output

### Environment

- **GPU 0:** AMD Radeon RX 7900 XTX (Navi 31, RDNA3, discrete)
- **GPU 1:** AMD Ryzen 9 9950X integrated GPU (RAPHAEL_MENDOCINO)
- **Vulkan driver:** Mesa RADV 26.1.6, Vulkan API 1.4.354
- **ROCm:** latest (via `ghcr.io/ggml-org/llama.cpp:server-rocm`)
- **Kernel:** 6.17.9
- **llama.cpp version:** b10298 (commit 15586e2d7)
- **Containers:** `ghcr.io/ggml-org/llama.cpp:server-vulkan` and `ghcr.io/ggml-org/llama.cpp:server-rocm`

### Exclusion testing

Every variable tested produces identical corruption on GPU. Only the CPU backend is correct.

| Variable | Values tested | Result |
|----------|--------------|--------|
| Model quants | Q4_K_XL, Q4_K_M, UD-Q4_K_XL, UD-Q5_K_XL | All corrupted |
| GPU backend | Vulkan (RADV), ROCm (HIP) | Both corrupted |
| KV cache type | q8_0, f16 | Both corrupted |
| GPU count | Both GPUs, single GPU (`GGML_VULKAN_DEVICE=0`) | Both corrupted |
| Speculative decoding | On (draft-mtp), off | Both corrupted |
| Thinking/reasoning | Enabled, disabled | Both corrupted |
| Chat template | Custom template, raw completion | Both corrupted |
| Temperature | 0.0 (greedy) | Still corrupted |
| **CPU backend** | `--n-gpu-layers 0` | **Correct** |

Forcing a single GPU via `GGML_VULKAN_DEVICE=0` rules out multi-GPU issues like #26197.

### Not model-specific: Gemma 4 also corrupts

Tested Gemma 4 31B (`gemma-4-31B-it-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf`) on the same Vulkan backend. It also corrupts URLs, but with a different pattern — inserting spaces instead of substituting characters:

| Input | Gemma 4 output |
|-------|---------------|
| `awesome-zsh-plugins` | `awesome zsh-plugins` |
| `helix-assist` | `helix assist` |
| `froggeric` | `froggereric` |
| `Qwen-Fixed-Chat-Templates` | `Qwen-Fixed-Chat- Templates` |

The corruption pattern differs by model (Qwen3.6 substitutes characters, Gemma 4 inserts spaces) but both produce incorrect output on AMD GPU.

### Not a model issue: cloud vLLM is correct

The same Qwen3.6-27B model running on cloud vLLM (different quant, different inference engine) reproduces all test URLs perfectly. This confirms the corruption is specific to llama.cpp on AMD GPU.

### Conclusion

This is a general AMD GPU compute issue in llama.cpp, not model-specific, not quant-specific, not backend-specific. It affects all models on the RX 7900 XTX. Both GPU backends (Vulkan and ROCm) produce identical corruption patterns, suggesting a shared AMD code path issue.

Potentially related issues:
- #26197 (multiple AMD GPUs lead to gibberish output) — ruled out by single-GPU test
- #20029 (Vulkan garbage output on AMD)
- #25612 (split-mode garbled output)

items.body:
### Name and Version

Built from `505b1ed1` (2026-07-15). The relevant code is **unchanged in current master** (`86d86ed`, 2026-07-17): the assert at `ggml/src/ggml-cpu/repack.cpp:4282` and `ggml_repack_get_optimal_repack_type()` are as described below.

### Operating systems

macOS (Apple Silicon, arm64 / NEON)

### GGML backends

CPU (Metal build, but run with `-ngl 0`)

### Hardware

Apple Silicon, 128 GB unified memory

### Models

`bullerwins/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-GGUF` — `DeepSeek-V4-Flash.Q8_0.gguf` (arch `deepseek4`; attention in Q8_0, routed experts in MXFP4).

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

On **Apple Silicon (arm64/NEON), CPU only (`-ngl 0`)**, `deepseek4` (DeepSeek-V4-Flash) produces **garbled output** — an endless run of `=` — instead of text. This is **not** the CUDA/ROCm expert issue in #25582 / #25436, and not fixed by the rejected assert change in #25412. It is the **CPU online-repack path silently corrupting `blk.N.attn_output_a` / `blk.N.attn_output_b`** (the MLA low-rank output projection).

```
./llama-cli -m DeepSeek-V4-Flash.Q8_0.gguf -ngl 0 -cnv -st -p "What is the capital of France? Answer briefly."
# -> [Start thinking] ==================================================  (garbage)
```

**Bisection** (each variant is a one-line change to `ggml_repack_get_optimal_repack_type()` returning `nullptr` for the named tensors, then a full rebuild + rerun):

| repack disabled for… | output |
|---|---|
| nothing (stock) | garbled (also hits the `:4282` assert on the 3D expert stacks) |
| 3D tensors only (`ggml_n_dims != 2`) | **still garbled** |
| the DSA `indexer` tensors | still garbled |
| `attn_kv` | still garbled |
| `attn_q_a` / `attn_q_b` | still garbled |
| **`attn_output_a` / `attn_output_b`** | **correct** ("Paris") |
| everything | correct |

So the culprit is exactly `attn_output_a/_b` — 86 of 494 tensors. Excluding *only* those from repack yields coherent output.

**Controls (both pass with fully stock repack on the same machine):**
- `gemma4-31b` Q4_K_M (dense) — correct.
- `Agents-A1` Q8_0 (`qwen35moe`, 256 routed experts) — correct.

So this is **`deepseek4`-specific**, not a general MoE or 3D-tensor repack problem — a 256-expert MoE and a dense model both repack fine.

### Root cause (analysis)

`ggml_repack_get_optimal_repack_type()` selects a repack `tensor_traits` purely by tensor **type** (q4_0/q4_K/q5_K/q6_K/q2_K/q8_0/iq4_nl/mxfp4) and `ne[1] % 8`; it **never checks `ggml_n_dims`** and does not exclude the MLA output-projection tensors. `extra_buffer_type::supports_op` *claims* `MUL_MAT_ID` for 3D `src0` (`repack.cpp:4795`), but the compute path `forward_mul_mat` asserts 2D (`repack.cpp:4282`). For `attn_output_a/_b` specifically, repacking reorders the weight in memory and the result read back is wrong — silently, when the assert is avoided.

Note: changing the assert to `>= 2` (as in the rejected #25412) is not a fix — it turns the crash into silent garbage, which is what the "3D tensors only" row above shows.

I'm happy to test a proper patch. The mechanism for why `attn_output_a/_b` in particular is affected (while `attn_q_a/_b`, same type, is not) I have not pinned down — likely how those tensors are consumed in the `deepseek4` MLA graph after repack reorders them.

### Relevant log output

```
/ggml/src/ggml-cpu/repack.cpp:4282: GGML_ASSERT(ggml_n_dims(op->src[0]) == 2) failed
  ...forward_mul_mat_id... (stock repack, before any workaround)
```

items.body:
### Name and Version

```
$ llama-cli --version
version: 9721 (dfsg)
built with gcc for x86_64-linux-gnu
```

(Ubuntu 26.10 `llama.cpp 9721+dfsg-1ubuntu1` package, `libggml0-backend-hip 0.15.2-1` from the `ppa:bullwinkle-team/rocm-with-generics` PPA, ROCm 7.2.4.)

I have also confirmed the underlying pattern still exists on `master` (`ggml/src/ggml-cuda/mmvq.cu` — host `get_device_table_id(int cc)` at ~line 89 and device `get_device_table_id()` at ~line 73 use two different lookups). See "Why #24129 doesn't fully close this" below.

### Operating systems

Linux

### GGML backends

HIP

### Hardware

AMD Ryzen AI 7 350 w/ Radeon 860M (gfx1152, RDNA3.5, Strix Halo family iGPU), integrated 16 GiB VRAM (UMA).

### Models

`unsloth/Qwen3-0.6B-GGUF:Q4_0` (any Q4_0/Q4_1/Q5_0/Q5_1/Q8_0/Q6_K/IQ4_NL model that dispatches through the MMVQ `n=1` path reproduces).

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

MMVQ produces `NaN` outputs for `ncols_dst == 1` (batch=1 decode) whenever the loaded HIP code object was compiled for `--offload-arch=gfx11-generic` and the runtime device is RDNA3.5 (gfx1150/gfx1152/gfx1153 without native code in the fatbin). Symptom in `llama-cli` is coherent-looking prompt processing followed by tokens rendered as `?????...` at plausible generation rates. HSA_OVERRIDE_GFX_VERSION=11.0.0 (native gfx1100) or =11.5.1 (native gfx1151) both hide the bug — they steer HIP to a native code object instead of `gfx11-generic`.

**Minimal repro** (fatbin without a gfx1152 native code object; equivalent to the current Debian/Ubuntu `ggml` build):

```
lxc launch --ephemeral --profile rocm-gpu ubuntu-daily:stonking generics-repro
lxc exec generics-repro -- sudo add-apt-repository ppa:bullwinkle-team/rocm-with-generics -y
lxc exec generics-repro -- sudo apt install -y llama.cpp libggml0-backend-hip

# NaN outputs from MMVQ (all n=1 cases fail):
lxc exec generics-repro -- /usr/libexec/x86_64-linux-gnu/ggml/test-backend-ops test -b ROCm0 -o MUL_MAT -p 'type_a=q4_0'
# ...
# [MUL_MAT] NaN at index 0 (ROCm0=nan CPU=4.080024)   MUL_MAT(type_a=q4_0,type_b=f32,m=16,n=1,k=256,...): FAIL
# every n=1 case fails; every n>=2 case passes

# Garbage tokens from llama-cli:
lxc exec generics-repro -- bash -c "echo 'What is 2+2?' | llama-cli -hf unsloth/Qwen3-0.6B-GGUF:Q4_0 --predict 15 --single-turn"
# > What is 2+2?
# | ???????????????
```

`AMD_LOG_LEVEL=3` on the failing run shows the runtime resolving to the generic code object:

```
Using generic code object for device: amdgcn-amd-amdhsa--gfx1152 co: amdgcn-amd-amdhsa--gfx11-generic
```

### Root cause

`ggml/src/ggml-cuda/mmvq.cu` has two `get_device_table_id()`s and they disagree on `gfx11-generic` + RDNA3.5:

- **Device** (`__device__`, ~line 73), compile-time preprocessor: for `gfx11-generic`, `__GFX11__` is set (so `RDNA3` is defined) but none of `__gfx1150/51/52/53__` are set (so `RDNA3_5` stays undefined) → `RDNA3_0` is defined → returns `MMVQ_PARAMETERS_RDNA3_0`. For Q4_0/Q4_1/Q5_0/Q5_1/Q8_0/IQ4_NL at `ncols_dst == 1`, `calc_nwarps(...)` returns 8 (2 for Q6_K). The kernel is emitted with `__launch_bounds__(8*warp_size, 1)` and sizes `__shared__ float tmp_shared[nwarps-1][...][warp_size]` for an 8-way inter-warp reduction.
- **Host** (`__host__`, ~line 89), runtime `cc`: on gfx1152 `cc = GGML_CUDA_CC_OFFSET_AMD + 0x1152`, so `GGML_CUDA_CC_IS_RDNA3_5(cc)` is true → returns `MMVQ_PARAMETERS_RDNA2` → `calc_nwarps(...)` returns 1 → launches `block_dims = (warp_size, 1, 1)`.

Only warp 0 executes, so the `if (threadIdx.y > 0) tmp_shared[threadIdx.y-1][...] = ...` writes never happen. The reduction loop `for (int l = 0; l < nwarps-1; ++l) tmp[j][i] += tmp_shared[l][...];` runs with `nwarps == 8` (compile-time), reading uninitialized LDS for `l = 0..6` → NaN, then propagates through the rest of the graph and shows up as `?????` at the sampler.

Confirmed by the test-backend-ops bisection: every `MUL_MAT(type_a=q4_0, n=1, ...)` case fails with `NaN at index 0`; every `n>=2` case passes. That's exactly the `if (ncols_dst == 1)` boundary in `calc_nwarps` where the RDNA3_0 branch would return 8 vs. falling through to 1.

Trivial FP32 kernels compiled the same way (`--offload-arch=gfx11-generic`) and run on the same gfx1152 produce correct results, so this is not a general clang miscompile of the generic target — it's specifically a host/device disagreement on the MMVQ tuning table.

### Why PR #24129 doesn't fully close this

[#24129](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/24129) (merged) added `__gfx1152__` / `__gfx1153__` to the `RDNA3_5` macro in `hip.h`. That is the right fix for the case where the fatbin **does** ship a native gfx1152 code object — the runtime loads native gfx1152, the device compile sees `__gfx1152__` → `RDNA3_5` → returns `MMVQ_PARAMETERS_RDNA2`, matches the host. Great.

But if a build has `--offload-arch=gfx11-generic` in its target list without a native gfx1152, the runtime falls through to the generic code object, and `__gfx11_generic__` (which *is* set for the generic target — confirmed with `hipcc --offload-arch=gfx11-generic -E -dM`) is not part of the `RDNA3_5` macro. So on that same hardware the mismatch is unchanged. This is the situation in the Debian/Ubuntu `ggml` build (whose target list, via `rocm-target-arch` from `pkg-rocm-tools`, currently emits `gfx11-generic gfx1100 gfx1101 gfx1151 …` without gfx1152/1153) and, from what I can tell, in the TheRock build path that [#25436](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/issues/25436) (DeepSeek V4 garbled on Strix Halo, still open) and possibly [#24962](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/issues/24962) are hitting.

More generally, the host/device pattern is inherently fragile: any future target/generic pair where the two lookups disagree will silently reintroduce this. The specific instance was fixed but the root shape wasn't.

### Proposed fix

Derive `nwarps` from the compiled kernel instead of recomputing it on the host: refactor `calc_launch_params` to be templat

items.body:
## Overview

<!-- Describe what this PR does and why. Be concise but complete -->

This PR adds support for MTP (Multi Token Prediction) heads. I tested this on Qwen3.6 27B and Qwen3.6 35BA3B but in principle it should work for any MTP model. I've posted the detailed results below, but typically I see a steady-state acceptance of around 75% with 3 draft tokens, which is more than >2x speed-up over baseline. The design decisions I took to get to this stage are as follows:

- The MTP model is a separate model which loads from the same GGUF, the idea is that MTP should automatically start and we shouldn't need to distribute the MTP gguf separately but also it has it's own context/kv-cache etc. 
- I saw a problem in #18039 where the hidden features weren't propagated correctly across multiple ubatches, so this PR adds a separate "hook" for the MTP to consume after each `ubatch`
- The MTP speculative class is fairly trivial (although it does depend on #22400, but could work without it)

> [!TIP]
> MTP is compatible with Vision input and Tensor/Pipeline Parallelism

> [!NOTE]
> Prompt processing (PP) speed typically takes a negative hit when MTP is enabled mainly due to Device-To-Host (D2H) embedding transfers. It's something to be optimized in the future.

> [!NOTE]
> Parallel decoding with MTP is supported, but not fully optimized yet.
