items.body:
This PR adds **DSpark** speculative decoding, layered on the merged **DFlash** drafter. DSpark (DeepSeek + PKU, 2026 — *"Confidence-Scheduled Speculative Decoding with Semi-Autoregressive Generation"*, the DeepSpec repo) is DFlash plus a small **semi-autoregressive Markov head**: where DFlash takes an independent argmax at each block position (every position marginalizes over all possible predecessors, so acceptance decays along the block), DSpark adds a low-rank, previous-token-conditioned logit bias and samples the block left-to-right, so each draft conditions on the one actually sampled before it. This lifts accepted length at near-zero extra draft cost.

DSpark **reuses the entire DFlash machinery unchanged** — the encoder/decoder graph, target-layer feature extraction (`llama_set_embeddings_layer_inp` / `_nextn`), KV-cache injection, and the verify/accept path. The only additions are:

- a new draft architecture **`dspark`** (`llama_model_dspark : llama_model_dflash`) that reuses the DFlash graph and additionally loads the Markov head (`markov_w1`, `markov_w2`) and an optional confidence head; it shares the target's token-embeddings / lm_head (same as DFlash);
- a new speculative type **`draft-dspark`** (`common_speculative_impl_draft_dspark : common_speculative_impl_draft_dflash`) that reuses `process()` (extraction + injection) and overrides only `draft()`: the block is anchor-first (position 0 already predicts the first draft token) and sampled with the Markov bias `bias(prev) = markov_w2 · markov_w1[prev]`, computed on-device (`llama_dspark_markov_bias`);
- a `Qwen3DSparkModel` converter.

**Greedy decoding is lossless**: the Markov bias only changes *which* tokens are proposed; every draft is still verified against the target, so the output is identical to non-speculative greedy.

The confidence head is converted/loaded but **not used at inference** in this PR (phase 1); the draft-quality win from the Markov head is self-contained and is what the numbers below measure.

## How to run

Complete example from scratch (Qwen3-8B). Drafts for other sizes are on the same org: `deepseek-ai/dspark_qwen3_{4b,8b,14b}_block7`.

**1. Get the models** — target + its DSpark draft:
```bash
huggingface-cli download Qwen/Qwen3-8B --local-dir Qwen3-8B
huggingface-cli download deepseek-ai/dspark_qwen3_8b_block7 --local-dir dspark_qwen3_8b
```

**2. Convert to GGUF** — the draft ships no tokenizer and reuses the target's, so pass `--target-model-dir`:
```bash
python convert_hf_to_gguf.py Qwen3-8B --outtype bf16 --outfile Qwen3-8B.gguf
python convert_hf_to_gguf.py dspark_qwen3_8b --outtype bf16 \
    --target-model-dir Qwen3-8B --outfile Qwen3-8B-DSpark.gguf
```
You may quantize the *target* (e.g. `llama-quantize Qwen3-8B.gguf Qwen3-8B-Q4_K_M.gguf Q4_K_M`); keep the draft bf16 — it's tiny, and acceptance is unaffected by target quant.

**3. Build** with CUDA:
```bash
cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=ON && cmake --build build --config Release -j
```

**4. Run** — the only DSpark-specific flags are `-md <draft>` and `--spec-type draft-dspark`
(`--spec-draft-n-max` = draft tokens per step; the released checkpoints use block size 7):
```bash
./build/bin/llama-server -m Qwen3-8B.gguf -md Qwen3-8B-DSpark.gguf \
    --spec-type draft-dspark --spec-draft-n-max 7 \
    --temp 0 --top-k 1 -np 1 -c 4096 -ngl 99 -fa on --jinja
```

**5. Send a request** (the server logs `draft acceptance = ...` per request):
```bash
curl http://localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{
  "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Explain the Pythagorean theorem."}],
  "temperature": 0, "max_tokens": 256
}'
```

`llama-cli` works the same way (`-m ... -md ... --spec-type draft-dspark`). Note: `draft-dspark` needs the target's hidden states (KV-cache injection), so use `llama-server` / `llama-cli` — the `speculative-simple` example does not drive that path.

## Performance

### SpeedBench (llama.cpp's own `tools/server/bench/speed-bench`)

Qwen3-8B (bf16), matched `--spec-draft-n-max 7`, `qualitative` split (11 categories), greedy. Baseline is the same server with no draft model. DSpark reaches **1.88× overall decode speedup** vs baseline (DFlash is 1.55×), and beats the merged DFlash on **every one of the 11 categories** (overall **1.21×**).

DSpark vs baseline:

## This has been closed with plans to organize and re-open
I have redesigned about half of the entire system in ways that fix all major issues exposed by this pr. I have not decided yet if ill push here or make a new clean pr with a new commit history after applying the final changes one by one. I still have some work but this is just a heads up that I am aware of the issues and im fixing them
## Overview

I want to make this as short as possible. I made a CUDA only for now feature where it tracks a heat map of all expert usage and the hottest experts are cached on GPU and computed there, while cold experts are computed on the CPU. off by default can be set by "--expert-hot-s N" (or -ehs for short), autofit from free VRAM using the native auto fit functions sizing based on how many experts would be offset to the cpu "--expert-hot-s -1", or off (0, default). But if you want to test you an use --ecf to force it on

Also adds: hysteresis gate + dwell on slot swaps, per-expert scale handling, a CUDA-only backend guard (Vulkan/CPU are rejected with a warning as I have not managed to get non cuda gpus to work fully and honestly can't figure it out and it does nothing on a cpu install, but still left a force activate argument), and auto-activation of --cmoe when manual slots are selected as the GPU will act as caching not slots.

Measured on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Q2_M / Q5_K_P with 8 GB VRAM: ~1.7-2.1x
steady-state decode speedup over stock (56 vs 33 tok/s, 36 vs 17 tok/s) using autofit.

## Additional information

Known limitations:
- Tier only engages at n_tokens == 1 (single-token decode); multi-slotbatches fall back to stock mul_mat_id.
- Verified on separate gate/up expert tensors (Qwen-style). Gemma 4 seemed broken as it resulted in incoherent output and initially i theorized it was because of `gate_up_exps` models breaking my implementation. but aparently the model i tried to run had stopped working on the latest upstream too, even tho it works fine on the one from a few days ago. So does not seem like my issue. I am almost certain it works properly, but i would appreciate a correction
- CUDA-only by design; the guard logs a warning and skips the tier on other back-ends unless forcefully activated.
- Due to differences in how experts are processed on the CPU vs the GPU, even at temp 0 when different experts are cached, the output may slightly vary. I have run extended tests and confirmed this is not silent corruption and happens on the original llama too if you change "--n-cpu-moe"
- Not intended for multiple GPUs. Aparently it CAN work but I have no way of testing and developing it currently.

## Requirements

- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master CONTRIBUTING.md)
- AI usage disclosure: Yes. On most the steps I got stuck I brainstormed with AI on how to resolve each problem, although all final code was written or verified by me (Although note i am not heavily experienced). Ai also caught and corrected a few of the smaller bugs in my code or changes the defaults/names of variables when i could not be bothered to do it manually.

Some numbers have been updated to reflect the minor optimization I commited. The full optimization numbers are better, but I wont put them here till its ready as thats misleading

Original llama.cpp vs my pull request
| Model | Size | S | Stock (tok/s) | Request (tok/s) | Ratio | Coherent after 128k tokens? |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |

*It caues some CPU overhead, recommended to not run with -t at your max logical threads or if cpu usage is max during normal generation. Results on different hardware may vary

### Summary

With DSpark speculative decoding (`--spec-type draft-dspark`) on DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731, llama-server reliably aborts with a CUDA error after roughly **2,000–2,600 decoded tokens** in a single response. Three crashes over two days, all with the same signature; short responses never crash. Reproduced on **b10242 and b10257**.

### Error

```
/home/mp/llama.cpp/ggml/src/ggml-cuda/ggml-cuda.cu:106: CUDA error
E CUDA error: an unsupported value or parameter was passed to the function
E   current device: 0, in function ggml_cuda_mul_mat_cublas_impl at /home/mp/llama.cpp/ggml/src/ggml-cuda/ggml-cuda.cu:1541
E   cublasSgemm_v2(ctx.cublas_handle(), CUBLAS_OP_T, CUBLAS_OP_N, ne01, ne11, ne10, (const float *) alpha, (const float *) src0_ptr, s01, (const float *) src1_ptr, s11, (const float *) beta, (float *) dst_ptr, ne0)
```

Last server log line before the abort (crash #3):

```
I slot print_timing: id  0 | task 7 | n_decoded =   2518, tg =  20.42 t/s, tg_3s =  21.22 t/s
```

### Pattern

| Crash | Build | Prompt tokens | Decoded before abort | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| #1 | b10242 | ~11k | ~2,5–3k (est., 16.6 t/s × ~3 min) | long reasoning response |
| #2 | b10242 | ~4k | ~2–2.5k (est.) | long reasoning response |
| #3 | b10257 | ~4k | **2,518** (from `print_timing`) | long reasoning response |

- Only long, reasoning-heavy generations crash; code-heavy answers of a few hundred tokens are fine.
- An FP32 GEMM (`cublasSgemm_v2`) in the decode path looks unusual — suspicion: the DSpark markov head or the DeepSeek sparse-attention indexer produces a degenerate shape (a dim/stride of 0 or an ld below the cuBLAS minimum) once the sequence crosses some threshold.
- For comparison: Qwen MTP profiles (`--spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 3`, same machine, same multi-GPU setup) have never shown this crash. We are currently testing whether `--spec-draft-n-max 3` instead of 5 avoids it on DSpark, too.

### Setup

- Model: `DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731` UD-Q4_K_XL (unsloth GGUF, 5 split files) + `dspark-DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-Q8_0.gguf` sidecar
- GPUs: 2× Quadro RTX 8000 (48 GB) + 3× Tesla V100-PCIE-32GB, pinned via `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=<uuid list>` (RTX first)
- Driver 580.173.02, CUDA runtime 13.0, built with nvcc 12.0, `CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=70;75`, Linux x86_64
- Command (crash #3, `${PORT}` filled in by llama-swap):

```
llama-server --port ${PORT} \
  --model .../DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-UD-Q4_K_XL-00001-of-00005.gguf \
  -ngl 99 -c 137728 -sm layer --tensor-split 12,12,6,8,5 -fit off \
  -b 2048 -ub 2048 --flash-attn on -np 1 -t 4 --mlock --direct-io \
  --jinja --reasoning-format deepseek --no-context-shift \
  --temp 1.0 --top-k 40 --top-p 1.0 --min-p 0.05 --repeat-penalty 1.0 \
  --model-draft .../dspark/dspark-DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-Q8_0.gguf \
  --spec-type draft-dspark --spec-draft-n-max 5 --gpu-layers-draft 99 \
  --device-draft CUDA4 --cache-reuse 256
```

(K/V cache f16; the draft sidecar is pinned to the device holding the main model's output layer — other placements abort at load with `pre-allocated tensor (output.weight) in a buffer (CUDA4) that cannot run the operation`.)

Happy to provide full logs, GDB backtraces or test patches — the crash is reproducible within minutes by asking for a long reasoning answer.

items.body:
## Overview

`llama-speculative-simple` creates the draft context without `ctx_other` and never null-checks the result. For drafters that borrow tensors from the target model (DFlash models without their own token embeddings or output head, such as the deepseek-ai dspark checkpoints), `llama_init_from_model` returns null, and the unchecked `ctx_dft` reaches `llama_decode`, which crashes.

This PR makes the following changes:

- Passes the target context as `ctx_other` when creating the draft context.
- Exits with a clear error message if the draft context still cannot be created.
- Warns, for DFlash drafters, that this example does not stage target-model features, so draft acceptance will be much lower than through `llama-server`, which uses the full framework path.

## Additional information

The crash can be reproduced with:

```
llama-speculative-simple -m Qwen3-8B-bf16.gguf -md dspark_qwen3_8b_block7.gguf \
  --spec-type draft-dspark -ngl 99 -ngld 99 -fa on --temp 0 -n 128 -p "..."
```

The failure occurs at prompt evaluation. The "dflash requires ctx_other" message emitted during context creation is easy to miss, because the same message also appears benignly during memory fitting.

The feature-staging gap itself is described in the companion issue #26884. I am happy to work on full DFlash support in this example if there is interest.

## Requirements

- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- AI usage disclosure: YES. Claude Code was used to help develop and test the fix and to format this description to the PR template. I reviewed every line and take full responsibility for the changes.
items.title: speculative-simple : pass ctx_other to the draft context and fail gracefully

items.body:
Two related problems when using dflash-family drafters with `llama-speculative-simple`:

1. The draft context was created without `ctx_other` and not null-checked, which crashes on drafters that borrow the target's token embeddings / output head (e.g. the deepseek-ai dspark checkpoints). Fixed by #26883.

2. Even with `ctx_other` wired, the example evals the prompt with plain `llama_decode` on both contexts, so the dflash encoder never receives the target-layer features for the prompt. The drafter then drafts without its conditioning input and acceptance drops to single digits, where the same model pair through llama-server reaches its normal 40-50%. This failure is silent, so it is easy to mistake for a drafter or quantization problem (it cost us a while).

If speculative-simple is meant to stay a minimal example for classic drafters, the warning added in #26883 may be enough. Otherwise the prompt pass needs to go through the framework's speculative path so target-layer extraction is armed before the target prompt eval and the encoder is fed before the first draft.

items.body:
## Summary

On Intel Arc Pro B70 (Battlemage G31, 32 GB, 608 GB/s), token-generation
speed collapses with context depth far beyond what KV-cache bandwidth can
explain. The excess cost is a near-constant **~21-25 ns per KV position per
full-attention layer per token**, and it is invariant across:

- **backend**: Vulkan (Mesa 26.1.6 ANV) and SYCL (oneAPI 2025.3, L0 V2) pay the same tax;
- **model/geometry**: hybrid Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (2 KV heads × hs256), Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B (4 × hs128), Gemma 4 26B-A4B / 12B (8 × hs512) — KV row width 1 KiB vs 8 KiB makes no difference;
- **build**: b8183 and b10235 behave identically at depth;
- **quantization**: Q2_K vs Q4_K_M identical depth deltas.

Byte-independence rules out DRAM bandwidth. The signature fits
memory-latency-bound attention matvecs: too few outstanding loads to cover
GDDR6 latency. Supporting evidence: GPU holds max clock at its power cap
while useful traffic is a fraction of peak; running 4 concurrent streams
scales aggregate throughput ~2.4× (parallel streams supply the MLP a single
stream lacks); the same llama.cpp code on an AMD Strix Halo iGPU with less
than half the bandwidth holds the sibling model flat to 65k
(https://lilting.ch/en/articles/qwen35-ctx-kv-cache-vulkan-optimization).

## Environment

- GPU: Intel Arc Pro B70 32 GB (PCI 8086:e223), PCIe passthrough to a Linux VM (6 vCPU, 16 GB RAM). d0 results match published bare-metal numbers, and all depth effects are on-card, so virtualization is not a factor.
- Host driver: xe, kernel 6.17; Vulkan: Mesa 26.1.6 (kisak), KHR_coopmat active; SYCL: oneAPI 2025.3 image, compute runtime 26.18.
- llama.cpp b10235 (also tested b8183), Vulkan and SYCL builds, `-ngl 999 -ub 512 -fa 0 -n 256 -p 0 -r 1 -d <depth>`.

## Data (tg256, t/s)

| model | backend | d0 | d32k | d65k | d127k |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Q4_K_M (hybrid, 10 attn layers) | Vulkan | 70.7 | 58.4 | 32.2 | 20.7 |
| Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Q2_K | Vulkan | 72.0 | 60.2 | 33.4 | 21.2 |
| Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Q2_K | SYCL | 81.5 | 52.9 | 38.5 | 22.8 |
| Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B Q4 (48 attn layers) | Vulkan b10235 | 87.1 | 37.6 | ~11-13 | |
| Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B Q4 | Vulkan b8183 | 103.7 | 35.8 | | |
| Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B Q4 | SYCL | 105.9 | 20.5 | 11.2 | |
| Gemma 4 26B-A4B Q4 | Vulkan | 69.2 | 57.8 | 30.9 | |
| Gemma 4 12B Q4 | Vulkan | 48.4 | 31.7 (d32k) | 22.5 | |
| Gemma 4 12B Q4 | SYCL | 51.8 | 34.8 (d32k) | 25.3 | |

Per-token excess over each model's own d0 baseline, divided by
(n_kv × full-attention layers), lands at 21-25 ns for every row above
(Gemma global-layer counts estimated from sliding_window_pattern).

Physics reference: Qwen3.6's KV is only 20 KiB/token (10 attn layers × 2 KV
heads × 256 × 2 × f16; 30 of 40 layers are DeltaNet with fixed state), i.e.
2.6 GB at 127k — ~5 ms/token at realistic bandwidth. Measured excess: ~33 ms.

## Control: same card, same model, different kernels — no depth tax

Intel's own stack (intel/llm-scaler-vllm 0.21.0-b2, vLLM v0.21.1 XPU, same
B70, same Qwen3.6-35B-A3B as GPTQ-Int4) decodes **flat to 127k**:

| depth | llama.cpp Vulkan b10235 (Q4_K_M) | vLLM XPU (GPTQ-Int4) |
|---|---|---|
| ~0 | 70.7 | 18.8-22.4 |
| 32k | 58.4 | 22.6 |
| 65k | 32.2 | 18.3-22.5 |
| 127k | 20.7 | 16.2-21.8 |

vLLM XPU's baseline is ~3.5× lower (eager GPTQ-MoE kernels), but its depth
cost is ~zero — demonstrating the Xe2 hardware itself can serve 127k
context with no per-position penalty. The tax measured above is specific to
ggml's decode-attention kernels.

## Additional findings from the same investigation

1. **Silent CPU fallback** (gdb-verified): with fa off, when the prefill
   score tensor (n_kv × n_ubatch × n_heads × 4B) exceeds free VRAM, the
   scheduler reroutes the matmul to the CPU backend with no warning —
   ~100× slowdown that presents as a hang. A log line when an op planned
   for GPU falls back would save users days. Likely the mechanism behind
   #18808's "almost stops".
2. **`-ctk q8_0` with fa off** also silently falls back to CPU on Vulkan.
3. **SYCL cannot load models whose weight buffer exceeds ~16.5 GiB**
   (`ggml_backend_sycl_buffer_type_alloc_buffer: can't allocate ... on
   device`, 29 GiB free): the SYCL backend allocates weights as one buffer
   and get_max_size does not reflect the device's real single-allocation
   ceiling; the Vulkan backend chunks. Qwen3.6-35B Q4_K_M (19.6 GiB)
   cannot run on SYCL on a 32 GB card. UR_L0_ENABLE_RELAXED_ALLOCATION_LIMITS,
   NEOReadDebugKeys/AllowUnrestrictedSize, legacy L0 adapter: no effect.
4. **b8183 → b10235 regressed MoE decode d0 ~19% on Vulkan**
   (Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B: 103.7 → 87.1 tg256).
5. fa=on is uniformly slower than fa=off on Xe2 for tg at every depth
   (Qwen3.6: 68.5/32.1/20.8/12.5 vs 70.7/58.4/32.2/20.7), q8_0 KV does not
   close the gap.

## Ask

The per-position constant suggests the decode-path attention matvec kernels
(both backends) issue too few concurrent loads on Intel to hide memory
latency at large n_kv. Happy to run diagnostics/patches on this hardware —
single-owner box, can bisect or profile on request.

### Name and Version

.\build\bin\Release\llama-cli.exe --version                                                                                         
version: 9590 (d2462f8f7)
built with MSVC 19.44.35227.0 for x64

### Operating systems

Windows

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

llama-cli, Other (Please specify in the next section), llama-server

### Command line

```shell
.\build\bin\Release\llama-cli.exe -m gemma-4-12B-it-qat-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf -mm mmproj-F32.gguf -v
# then in chat:
# /video C:\Users\Ben\Videos\test.mp4
# Tell me about this video
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

### Name and Version

version: b9590 (d2462f8f7)
built for Windows x86_64, CUDA backend (RTX 3090)

### Operating systems

Windows

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

llama-cli, mtmd

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Video input on Windows hangs in two different ways depending on where the MP4 MOOV atom is located. Both appear to be in the ffmpeg/ffprobe subprocess pipe handling in `tools/mtmd/mtmd-helper.cpp` (`mtmd_helper_video`). This extends #24394 (silent zero-frame failure on Linux) with Windows repro data — on Windows it hangs rather than failing silently.

**Case 1: MOOV atom at end of file (default ffmpeg output)**

`probe()` succeeds (ffprobe has to read the entire piped input to find the moov, so it fully drains stdin and exits cleanly). The ffmpeg decode step then produces zero frames:

```
0.24.617.771 D start_ffmpeg: launching: ffmpeg -nostdin -i cache:pipe:0 -vf fps=4.000000 -f rawvideo -pix_fmt rgb24 pipe:1 -loglevel error
0.24.622.579 D start_ffmpeg: subprocess_create ret=0 proc_alive=1
0.24.622.583 D start_ffmpeg: starting feeder thread for 1194147-byte buffer
0.24.622.649 D read_next_frame: reading frame 0, expecting 2764800 bytes (720x1280)
0.24.668.259 D read_next_frame: fread returned 0 after 0/2764800 bytes (ferror=0)
0.24.668.268 D add_text: <|turn>system ...
0.24.668.306 D add_text: Video:
0.24.668.319 D add_text: Tell me about this video<turn|>
```

The prompt is assembled with the bare `Video:` text and no frames, and then llama-cli hangs (no generation, no error).

**Case 2: MOOV atom at front (`-movflags +faststart`)**

After remuxing the same file with `ffmpeg -i test.mp4 -c copy -movflags +faststart test_fast.mp4`, the hang moves *earlier*, into `probe()` itself. The log stops here and never prints the probe result line:

```
0.28.766.262 D res  add_waiting_: add task 0 to waiting list. current waiting = 0 (before add)
0.28.766.269 D que    post: new task, id = 0, front = 0
0.28.767.532 D probe: launching: ffprobe -v quiet -show_entries stream=width,height,r_frame_rate,nb_frames,duration -select_streams v:0 -of default=noprint_wrappers=1 pipe:0
(hangs indefinitely)
```

**Isolation: ffprobe itself behaves correctly on the same file**

Running the exact probe command manually with a real pipe (cmd.exe, binary-safe):

```
C:\Users\Ben>cmd /c "type C:\Users\Ben\Videos\test_fast.mp4 | ffprobe -v quiet -show_entries stream=width,height,r_frame_rate,nb_frames,duration -select_streams v:0 -of default=noprint_wrappers=1 pipe:0"
width=720
height=1280
r_frame_rate=30/1
duration=7.050391
nb_frames=211
The process tried to write to a nonexistent pipe.
```

ffprobe prints the metadata and exits promptly. Because the moov is at the front, it stops reading stdin early; the writer (`type`) gets the expected broken-pipe error and terminates. So the deadlock is in how `mtmd_helper_video` handles this early-exit case on Windows: the feeder thread is blocked in `fwrite()` on the child's stdin while the main thread is blocked in `fgets()` on the child's stdout, and neither unblocks when ffprobe stops reading / exits.

**Minor side issue** while debugging: the `probe()` debug line prints `fps_target` and a not-yet-assigned `info.n_frames`, e.g. `probe: 720x1280 fps=4.00 duration=7.02s n_frames=0` for a 30 fps / 211-frame video — `info.n_frames` is assigned on the line *after* the `LOG_DBG`, and `fps` here is the sampling target, not the source fps. Made the logs confusing to interpret.

Test video: 720x1280, H.264, 7.05 s, 30 fps, ~1.2 MB. Happy to provide the file or more verbose logs if useful.

Video input is new in #24269 (b9577); also reproduces after the #24316 refactor.

items.body:
### Summary

The failure is not a single isolated bad completion. It appears in clusters during repeated warm `stream=true` chat completion requests. The most reproducible symptom is an assistant response consisting almost entirely of repeated `?` characters, while the HTTP/SSE stream remains structurally valid and `curl` exits successfully.

I am on 9682 (558e221b7).

This looks possibly related to #20610 and #21888, but my case is not identical:

* Linux + Mesa RADV
* AMD RX590 / Polaris10
* `llama-server`
* streaming chat completions
* warm repeated requests
* clustered failures after many successful requests
* Qwen3.5 model
* `--no-kv-offload` does not eliminate the issue, but changes the output regime significantly

I have seen some very promising results with the hardware when the responses are healthy, the generation is fast, the GPUs are great value and you can fit so many models on it. If we could solve this issue, that would make AI accessible to a whole generation of cards.

Note that in this ticket, I refer and test a lot Qwen but I had a similar experience with Gemma4 producing '<unused49>' tokens. Disabling the reasoning stabilized the model but after that it was unable to perform in agentic scenarios (it basically tell you it will do something and never does it). It isn't naive to think that the issues may be related, just taking different shapes.

I am providing already quite a big bundle of testing and evidence but I am also keen on providing more if needed.

### Environment

Please replace this section with exact command output from the attached files.

* llama.cpp / llama-server version: `<paste llama-server --version>`
* git commit: `<paste git rev-parse HEAD>`
* OS: `<paste /etc/os-release + uname -a>`
* GPU: AMD Radeon RX590 / Polaris10 / RADV
* Mesa / Vulkan driver: `<paste vulkaninfo --summary relevant lines>`
* Kernel: `<paste uname -a>`
* CPU/RAM: Xeon E5-2630L v4, 32 GB RAM
* Backend: Vulkan
* Model: `Qwen3.5-9B-UD-Q5_K_XL.gguf`
* Server command used for baseline:

```bash
/home/flori/llama.cpp/build/bin/llama-server \
  --host 0.0.0.0 \
  --port 8080 \
  --alias Build-comfort_Qwen3.5-9B-UD-Q5_K_XL \
  --model /home/flori/models/Qwen3.5-9B-UD-Q5_K_XL.gguf \
  --ctx-size 65536 \
  --n-gpu-layers 99 \
  --threads 10 \
  --parallel 1 \
  --batch-size 256 \
  --ubatch-size 32 \
  --reasoning off \
  --reasoning-budget 0 \
  --cache-ram 0 \
  --log-verbosity 3
```

### Reproduction shape

The issue reproduces using repeated identical `stream=true` chat completion requests against a warm `llama-server` process.

The requests use:

* OpenAI-compatible `/v1/chat/completions`
* `stream=true`
* tools enabled
* `top_p=0.9`
* `max_tokens=64`
* same prompt repeated many times
* one slot: `--parallel 1`

The bad outputs appear after many successful warm requests, not immediately on model load.

### Observed result

In one controlled run:

```text
baseline:      100 runs, 5 bad
no_kv_offload: 100 runs, 13 bad
```

Baseline bad cluster:

```text
baseline rep=53 cq=64 tq=0
baseline rep=54 cq=64 tq=0
baseline rep=55 cq=64 tq=0
baseline rep=56 cq=64 tq=0
baseline rep=57 cq=62 tq=0
```

Representative bad baseline output from `baseline_rep57`:

```text
finish_reason: stop
content_len: 62
tool_args_len: 0
content_q_run: 62
tool_q_run: 0
content_head: ??????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????
curl_rc: 0
```

The SSE response is structurally valid, with no JSON parse errors, and the request finishes successfully.

### `--no-kv-offload` behaviour

I also tested the same workload with:

```bash
--no-kv-offload
```

The flag is accepted by this build:

```text
-kvo, --kv-offload, -nkvo, --no-kv-offload
```

This did not eliminate corruption. It produced more bad outputs by the question-mark metric:

```text
no_kv_offload rep=15 cq=62
no_kv_offload rep=16 cq=64
no_kv_offload rep=17 cq=64
no_kv_offload rep=18 cq=31
no_kv_offload rep=66 cq=51
no_kv_offload rep=67 cq=31
no_kv_offload rep=72 cq=64
no_kv_offload rep=73 cq=64
no_kv_offload rep=74 cq=64
no_kv_offload rep=75 cq=64
no_kv_offload rep=76 cq=64
no_kv_offload rep=77 cq=64
no_kv_offload rep=78 cq=31
```

However, `--no-kv-offload` also changed output behaviour substantially:

* baseline: 95/100 responses produced the expected tool call
* no_kv_offload: 0/100 responses produced the expected tool call
* many non-`?` outputs were also semantically incoherent

Example from `no_kv_offload_rep98`:

```text
content_head: ,(

 for say. and
, and? time.. ": of.

 of
 don and
```

So I do not consider `--no-kv-offload` a clean fix/control for this workload, but it is evidence that the symptom is not narrowly fixed by disabling KV offload.

### Other observations

* The failure is bursty/clustered rather than uniformly random.
* `stream=false` was previously clean in a smaller layer-narrowing test: 40/40 direct non-stream runs clean.
* Streaming and warm slot/cache/checkpoint reuse may be contributing factors.
* Disabling context checkpoints with `--ctx-checkpoints 0` caused full prompt reprocessing every request and was too slow for a full comparison.
* A true CPU-only build/control is being tested separately because the full captured prompt is very slow on CPU.

### Expected result

Repeated identical warm streaming requests should either:

* produce valid coherent responses/tool calls consistently, or
* fail explicitly with a server/runtime error if the backend cannot support this model/configuration safely.

They should not intermittently produce structurally valid SSE responses containing repeated `?` or incoherent token streams.

### Attachments

Attached evidence bundle contains:

* `SUMMARY.txt`
* `results.csv`
* `BAD_RUNS.txt`
* `baseline_server.log`
* `no_kv_offload_server.log`
* server warning files
* representative `response.sse`, `classification.txt`, and `timing.txt` for:

  * `baseline_rep53`
  * `baseline_rep57`
  * `no_kv_offload_rep75`
  * `no_kv_offload_rep98`
* system info:

  * `llama_server_version.txt`

items.body: ## Overview This PR adds **ggml-hexagon-jz**, an independent alternative backend for Qualcomm Hexagon NPU on Android, which can coexist with the existing official `ggml-hexagon` implementation. JZ's ggml-hexagon is built on two fundamental architectural choices that originated from the upstream PR #12326(pls refer to [JZ ggml-hexagon vs Qualcomm ggml-hexagon: Architecture Analysis](https://github.com/zhouwg/ggml-hexagon/blob/self-build-jz/docs/backend/jz-ggml-hexagon/ion-mempool-vs-perbuffer-analysis-20260713.md)). This design differs fundamentally from [Qualcomm's official implementation](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/tree/master/ggml/src/ggml-hexagon), which relies on dspqueue and multiple independent per-buffer ION shared buffers. Both backends build on the Hexagon kernel implementations originally provided by Qualcomm's engineers; JZ maintains an independent copy in kernels/ to avoid being affected by upstream cache-maintenance refactors (Pls refer to c220b84ae ggml-hexagon: maintain separate kernels again). Benchmark results on Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 and Snapdragon 8 Elite (8 Gen 4) show that TG performance surpasses QCOM on GQA models (1.1x-1.9x) and PP+TG both surpass on deep GQA stacks (gemma4). Pls refer to [discussion #71](https://github.com/zhouwg/ggml-hexagon/discussions/71). ## How to port to WoA (Windows on ARM) devices powered by Qualcomm desktop SoCs Qualcomm engineers would need to implement several cache coherence functions inside [ggml-hexagon-jz.cpp#L1017-L1129](https://github.com/zhouwg/ggml-hexagon/blob/newpr_to_upstream/ggml/src/ggml-hexagon/ggml-hexagon-jz.cpp#L1017-L1129) to support the WoA platform. ## Build Selection Mechanism - Two backends are isolated in source directories and controlled by independent build flags. - Existing official `GGML_HEXAGON` build option remains untouched for backward compatibility. - New flag `GGML_HEXAGON_JZ` enables the JZ's ggml-hexagon backend. - Zero breaking changes: When the GGML_HEXAGON_JZ flag is not enabled, the official Hexagon backend can be compiled and run normally ## How to perform PP & TG benchmark comparisons between Qualcomm's ggml-hexagon and JZ's ggml-hexagon For fair performance comparison, the same running params (`-ngl 99 -t 6 -n 256 --ctx-size 8192 --ubatch-size 64 --poll 1000 --no-warmup --load-mode none -fa on --jinja -st`), the same prompt, the same LLM model file, and the same 8Elite phone are used in both inference tests. We can run automated AB tests on Snapdragon 8 Elite following the recommended steps below: 1. download codes ``` git clone https://github.com/zhouwg/ggml-hexagon cd ggml-hexagon git checkout newpr_to_upstream ``` 2. build Qualcomm's ggml-hexagon backend ``` ./scripts/build-run-ggmlhexagon-android.sh build_qcom ``` 3. build JZ's ggml-hexagon backend ``` ./scripts/build-run-ggmlhexagon-android.sh build ``` 4. run automated AB test ``` ./scripts/build-run-ggmlhexagon-android.sh run_abtest 2>&1 | tee log_abtest_$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S).txt ``` 5. Analyze logs and generate a performance comparison table from `log_abtest_$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S).txt` We can run non-automated AB tests on Snapdragon 8 Elite following the recommended steps below: 1. download codes ``` git clone https://github.com/zhouwg/ggml-hexagon cd ggml-hexagon git checkout newpr_to_upstream ``` 2. build Qualcomm's ggml-hexagon backend ``` ./scripts/build-run-ggmlhexagon-android.sh build_qcom ``` 3. build JZ's ggml-hexagon backend ``` ./scripts/build-run-ggmlhexagon-android.sh build ``` 4. run llama-cli or llama-bench with Qualcomm ggml-hexagon ``` ./scripts/build-run-ggmlhexagon-android.sh update_qcom_libs ./scripts/build-run-ggmlhexagon-android.sh run_llamacli ./scripts/build-run-ggmlhexagon-android.sh run_llamabench ``` 5. run llama-cli or llama-bench with JZ ggml-hexagon ``` ./scripts/build-run-ggmlhexagon-android.sh update_jz_libs ./scripts/build-run-ggmlhexagon-android.sh run_llamacli ./scripts/build-run-ggmlhexagon-android.sh run_llamabench ``` ## Test results Snapdragon 8 Elite(aka 8Gen4), Vendor: OnePlus PP&TG in JZ's ggml-hexagon: PP&TG in Qualcomm's ggml-hexagon ## Requirements - I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md) - AI usage disclosure: YES - used AI assistance for implementation help and review. I reviewed every changed line, tested locally, and take full responsibility for this PR.

items.body:
## Overview

Kind of a big overhaul of the Hexagon backend to enable support for mulit-NPU devices, and to make it fully asynchronous: async graph-compute, async events, async tensor-copy, cross-device fences -- the whole enchilada!

The PR also includes everything required to properly support and enable multi-NPU tensor-split mode (ie integration with the meta backend) on devices like the [IQ9](https://www.qualcomm.com/internet-of-things/products/iq9-series) and [IQ10](https://www.qualcomm.com/internet-of-things/products/iq10-series) series. 
Tested on the [IQ9 EVK](https://www.qualcomm.com/developer/hardware/qualcomm-iq-9075-evaluation-kit-evk).
See examples below.

The asynchronous implementation ended up requiring many other updates besides just making `graph_compute` and `cpy_tensor_async' not block. To make it fully usable we need to use non-host buffers by default (ie to force async copies and repack), which in turn requires support for more types in `SET/GET_ROWS`, etc. The CPY op needed to be optimized to not slow things down, and to support fused FENCE op to allow for truly async copies.
Hence this PR includes all those updates.  

The multi-NPU support requires new device naming scheme. The original naming `HTP0,...HTP4` is still supported and is enabled if the environment variable `GGML_HEXAGON_NDEV` is defined.  The new scheme is `HTP0:0, HTP1:0` where the first number is physical NPU id and the second number is the virtual id of the session. 

To simplify the migration and support for the devices I included new `./scripts/snapdragon/build.py` and './scripts/snapdragon/run.py`  and update the documenation to cover the new scripts, devices, etc.

## Additional information

Here is an example gemma-4-E4B (q4_0 QAT model) on IQ9 EVK in tensor split mode

```
./scripts/snapdragon/run.py --target ubuntu:maxk@192.168.1.87 --device HTP0:0,HTP1:0 -- llama-completion \
     -m gemma-4-E4B_q4_0-it.gguf -f sample_prompt_1024.txt --jinja -st --split-mode tensor --ctx-size 8192
```

FIXME: add some more info and examples

## Requirements

- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- AI usage disclosure: Yes, Antigravity for a ton of refactoring, testing, debugging and python script updates

## Overview

Removing redundant coopmat1 FA dequantization of KV at prefill.  Coopmat1 currently Dequants 32 times (once per workgroup), Reorganises the F16 KV  to per-head-contiguous in scratch to enable faster memory-bound read by FA.

Closes #25491 

## Additional information
Scratch size grows with KV cache size, the trade off for inflight memory-usage vs token throughput: (~268 MB @128k). 

Patched vs unpatched greedy output (temp 0, seed 1, ~15.5k-token prompt) is byte-identical, no change in results, just speed. 

Unpatched:

items.body:
## Overview The Q4_K/Q5_K scale unpack branches on a runtime value to pick between two layouts. nvcc can't fold that, so it predicates it and then repeats the whole thing for every column of the ncols_dst loop instead of doing it once. Swapping the branch for a mask select fixes it: predicated instructions at ncols_dst=8 go from 226 to 34, and the Q4_K kernel at 16 columns from 2256 to 1648. None of the other quant types have this problem, they already unpack unconditionally (Q3_K does the same 6-bit layout with plain shifts). We see perf gains from batch size >=4 on RTX 5090 and >=5 on RTX 4090 (more details in the Performance drop down), however we do not see a gain with DGX Spark, and in fact a small regression at batch sizes 4-6, which is why the change is gated off there. The most probable reason for this can be that the memory bandwidth on DGX Spark is much lower than that of RTX 4090 or 5090, and this means even with this optimization there is no effective time to save, since in the original code the unpack was already running while the kernel waits on the weight loads and so was not adding to the total time.
Performance

## Benchmarks (RTX 5090, sm_120, CUDA 12.9, driver 620.23) Both builds are from the same commit; the only difference is this patch. Batch size below refers to `ne11`, the number of columns the matmul receives in a single forward pass. It can arise in three ways, which are indistinguishable to the kernel: N concurrent requests against a server started with `-np N`, a draft block of `n_max + 1` tokens on a single slot, or `llama-bench -p N` directly. Two rows per model. `decode` is `llama-bench -p N -n 0 -embd 1 -r 40`, a single forward pass of N tokens with nothing generated, which is the decode step at batch N. `end to end` is llama-server tokens/sec, which also includes prefill, sampling and the draft model, and is therefore always lower. `*` marks a quant type this patch does not modify. ### 1. vs batch size Llama-3.1-8B, no draft model; only `-np` changes. The llama-server figures are total tokens over wall time at 256 tokens per request, temperature 0, across 3 runs alternating between the two builds. The request count is always a multiple of the batch size so that the final wave is not partially filled. | quant | metric | batch 1 | batch 2 | batch 4 | batch 8 | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | **Q4_K_M** | decode | **-0.3%** | **+1.6%** | **+8.9%** | **+14.7%** | | | end to end | +0.4% | +1.1% | +7.4% | +10.8% | | **Q5_K_M** | decode | **+0.4%** | **+2.0%** | **+6.6%** | **+14.2%** | | | end to end | -0.1% | +1.5% | +5.5% | +11.4% | | **Q6_K** * | decode | **-1.2%** | **-1.1%** | **-0.8%** | **-0.9%** | | | end to end | -0.1% | +0.2% | +0.3% | +0.2% | There is no effect at batch 1, which is expected: the unpack can only be amortised once there is more than one column to share it across. ### 2. Other models Batch pinned at 4, no draft model. | model | metric | Q4_K_M | Q5_K_M | Q6_K * | |---|---|---|---|---| | **Llama-3.1-8B** | decode | **+8.9%** | **+6.6%** | **-0.8%** | | | end to end | +7.4% | +5.5% | +0.3% | | **gemma-4-12B** | decode | **+8.2%** | **+6.3%** | **+0.0%** | | | end to end | +6.8% | +6.0% | +0.1% | | **Qwen3.6-27B** | decode | **+6.2%** | **+5.1%** | **+0.3%** | | | end to end | +8.0% | +4.2% | +0.5% | ### 3. Batch from a draft block instead of concurrent requests `--spec-type draft-dflash --spec-draft-n-max 3` on a single slot, so the target verifies 4 tokens in one pass: batch 4 obtained from a draft block rather than from concurrency. The decode rows repeat table 2 because it is the same file at the same batch; the kernel is indifferent to the source of the batch. | model | metric | Q4_K_M | Q5_K_M | Q6_K * | |---|---|---|---|---| | **gemma-4-12B-it** | decode | **+8.2%** | **+6.3%** | **+0.0%** | | | end to end | +6.3% | +6.2% | -0.7% | | **Qwen3.6-27B** | decode | **+6.2%** | **+5.1%** | **+0.3%** | | | end to end | +6.3% | +5.5% | +0.1% | ### 4. Decode over the whole batch range The same llama-bench run on `--pure` single-type models, so that every quantized `mul_mat` is the type in question. The Q4_K_M / Q5_K_M files above are mixed, with output and some attention tensors in Q6_K, which is why they report lower gains. | type | batch 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | **Q4_K** | +1.0% | +3.6% | +6.7% | +13.6% | +17.0% | +19.0% | +17.5% | +17.4% | | **Q5_K** | -0.6% | +2.0% | +1.7% | +9.3% | +10.3% | +16.8% | +15.9% | +17.2% | | **Q6_K** * | +0.3% | +0.4% | -1.0% | -0.5% | -0.8% | -0.4% | -1.6% | -0.6% | | **Q8_0** * | +1.1% | +0.3% | +1.0% | +1.3% | +1.0% | +1.8% | +1.9% | +1.7% | ## Benchmarks (RTX 4090, sm_89, CUDA 12.9, driver 591.86) Both builds are from the same commit; the only difference is this patch. Conventions are as above: `decode` is `llama-bench -p N -n 0 -embd 1 -r 40`, `end to end` is llama-server tokens/sec at 256 tokens per request, temperature 0. `*` marks a quant type this patch does not modify. Clocks were pinned, no interactive session was present on the machine, and the base build was run at both ends of every pass so that the noise floor is measured rather than assumed. Batch size throughout refers to `ne11`, the number of columns the matmul receives in a single forward pass. It can arise in three ways, which are indistinguishable to the kernel: N concurrent requests against a server started with `-np N`, a draft block of `n_max + 1` tokens on a single slot, or `llama-bench -p N` directly. Tables 1, 2 and 4 use the first and third; table 3 uses the second. ### 1. vs batch size Llama-3.1-8B, no draft model. Decode rows use `-p N`; end-to-end rows use `-np N` with the request count kept a multiple of N so that all slots remain occupied. | quant | metric | batch 1 | batch 2 | batch 4 | batch 8 | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | **Q4_K_M** | decode | **+0.0%** |

items.body:
# `tool_choice: "required"` is accepted but not enforced on templates with `supports_preserve_reasoning: true`

### Name and Version

```
build_info: b330-84e908c62
```
Built locally for CUDA 13.0, `-DGGML_CUDA=ON -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=121 -DCMAKE_CUDA_FLAGS="-O2"`.

### Operating systems

Linux (aarch64, NVIDIA GB10 / sm_121)

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

`llama-server`, and the chat/grammar layer under `common/` (`chat-auto-parser-generator.cpp`).

### Command line

```
llama-server -m qwen36-NVFP4-MTP-HQ.gguf --host 0.0.0.0 --port 11435 \
  -c 131072 --jinja -ngl 999 -fa on -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0 --spec-type draft-mtp
```

### Problem description

`llama-server` accepts `"tool_choice": "required"` on `/v1/chat/completions` without error or
warning, and then does not enforce it, on models whose chat template llama.cpp classifies with
`supports_preserve_reasoning: true`.

Instead of being constrained to emit a tool call, the model generates freely until `max_tokens`
is exhausted. The request returns `finish_reason: "length"` with `predicted_n` equal to the full
budget and no `tool_calls`. In the runs I inspected the tail of the output had degenerated into a
repeating emoji sequence, which is consistent with generation being unconstrained rather than
grammar-limited.

The failure is **silent and expensive**: a caller that relies on `required` for structured output
receives ordinary prose, no error, and pays the maximum token cost of the request every time.

Two servers on the same host, same binary, same build string, both `--jinja`, differ only in the
model/template:

| | fast lane | smart lane |
|---|---|---|
| model | Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (NVFP4, MTP) | Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct (Q4_K_M) |
| `supports_tool_calls` | true | true |
| `supports_parallel_tool_calls` | true | true |
| `supports_object_arguments` | true | true |
| **`supports_preserve_reasoning`** | **true** | **false** |
| `tool_choice: "required"` | **ignored** | honoured |

`supports_preserve_reasoning` is the only differing capability in `/props → chat_template_caps`.

**On reproducing this without my exact file:** the GGUF above is a local conversion and is not
something you can download, so please do not treat the filename as the repro target. The trigger
appears to be the *chat template* — specifically whichever templates llama.cpp classifies
`supports_preserve_reasoning: true`, i.e. a `<think>`-style reasoning template. Any model whose
`/props → chat_template_caps` reports that flag together with `supports_tool_calls: true` should
show it. `repro.sh` prints both flags up front so it is obvious at a glance whether a given server
is a candidate. I am happy to attach the exact template text if that helps.

### What is NOT the cause (ruled out by measurement)

- **The model.** An identical hand-written GBNF grammar posted to `/completion` forces a perfect
  tool call on both servers, from a prompt with no intent to call anything. Section B of the
  reproducer is this control.
- **Grammar sampling generally.** `root ::= "BANANA"` is honoured on the affected server.
- **Speculative decoding.** The control above succeeds with `--spec-type draft-mtp` active.
- **Reasoning parsing.** Sending `"reasoning_format": "none"` does not change the behaviour.
- **Token budget.** Identical failure at `max_tokens` 500 / 1500 / 3000 / 5000 — all fully
  consumed, `reasoning_content` exactly 801 chars each time.
- **The tool-call syntax.** Both templates emit `<tool_call>…</tool_call>` with `<|im_start|>`.

### Why this looks like a defect rather than unsupported behaviour

`common/chat-auto-parser-generator.cpp` appears to intend enforcement on this path:

```cpp
// ~line 84
bool include_grammar = has_response_format || (has_tools &&
        ((inputs.tool_choice == COMMON_CHAT_TOOL_CHOICE_AUTO && !trigger_marker.empty()) ||
          inputs.tool_choice == COMMON_CHAT_TOOL_CHOICE_REQUIRED));

// ~line 89 — REQUIRED yields a NON-lazy (eager) grammar
data.grammar_lazy = !has_response_format && inputs.tool_choice == COMMON_CHAT_TOOL_CHOICE_AUTO;

// ~line 369 and ~line 500 — for REQUIRED the tool calls are NOT made optional
if (!require_calls) { tool_calls = p.optional(tool_calls); }
```

So a grammar is built, marked eager, and tool calls are non-optional — yet generation is
evidently unconstrained. I have not isolated the specific line where enforcement is lost; that
likely needs a debug build dumping the emitted GBNF for the two templates.

### Steps to Reproduce

Full script at the bottom of this issue. `./repro.sh <host:port>` exits **1** when the bug reproduces and **0**
when `required` is honoured — it was verified to discriminate between the two servers above.

```bash
curl -s http://HOST:PORT/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
  "model":"local",
  "messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Hello, how are you today?"}],
  "tools":[{"type":"function","function":{"name":"get_disk_free",
    "parameters":{"type":"object","properties":{"host":{"type":"string"}},"required":["host"]}}}],
  "tool_choice":"required","max_tokens":2000,"temperature":0}'
```

Expected: a `tool_calls` response. Actual on an affected template: `finish_reason: "length"`,
`predicted_n` == `max_tokens`, no `tool_calls`.

### Relevant log output

```
finish_reason : length
predicted_n   : 2000
tool_calls    : NONE
content tail  : '🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️…'

# control, same server, hand-written grammar via /completion:
'<tool_call>{"name": "get_disk_free", "arguments": {"host": "beta"}}</tool_call>'
```


### Possibly related open issues

- **#26781** — *"enable_thinking forced true in jinja/caps.cpp capability probe leaks into
  non-DeepSeek templates"*. Same model family (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B), same subsystem, and a very
  similar end state: budget consumed inside `reasoning_content`, no `tool_calls`, a silent dead
  end for an API consumer. **Differences:** that report needs ~38-41 turns of accumulated co

MTP assistant at Q4_0
MMPROJ at F16

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

ChatGPT wrote this, ChatGPT troubleshot and fixed the issue. I submit this in case it is useful to anyone else:
------------

I found what appears to be a regression affecting large models on an AMD Radeon 680M iGPU using Vulkan/RADV.

System
AMD Radeon 680M integrated GPU
amdgpu kernel driver
RADV Vulkan
32 GB physical RAM (~27 GiB usable by Linux)
Kernel reports:
4096 MiB VRAM
13918 MiB GTT
Linux Mint
Kernel 7.0.0-28-generic
Model/configuration

Gemma 4 26B A4B QAT Q4_0 with multimodal projector and MTP speculative decoding:

Main model: ~14 GB
mmproj F16: ~1.2 GB
MTP draft model: ~241 MB
Context: 50000
Parallel slots: 1
GPU layers: auto
Draft GPU layers: auto
Flash attention: auto
Regression

b10353 works reliably with this configuration.

By b10470 the same configuration started failing. I also reproduced it with b10488 (9d77fa172).

The failure is:

radv/amdgpu: Not enough memory for command submission.
ggml_vulkan: device lost on Vulkan0
vk::Queue::submit: ErrorDeviceLost

The kernel reports at the same time:

amdgpu_vm_validate() failed.
Not enough memory for command submission!

Sometimes the model fails while loading after a clean boot. In another test it loaded successfully and completed the first request, then failed during the second request.

Smaller models continue to work normally with the newer builds.

Workaround / important finding

While troubleshooting this with ChatGPT, we noticed that PR #26081 changed the default model-loading behavior for iGPUs between my known-good and known-bad versions.

I tested the newer llama.cpp build with only this additional option:

--load-mode mmap

This completely fixes the problem.

Gemma 4 26B + mmproj + MTP now loads and runs successfully on the newer build when --load-mode mmap is specified.

So on this Radeon 680M/RADV system:

b10353 default behavior                -> works

newer build, --load-mode auto/default  -> Vulkan device loss / command submission OOM

same newer build, --load-mode mmap     -> works

This makes PR #26081 / the new iGPU auto loading path look like a possible regression, although I have not done a git bisect and therefore cannot say that PR #26081 is definitely the cause.

Possibly unrelated warning

The log also contains:

Gemma4Assistant requires ctx_other to be set
failed to measure draft model memory: failed to create llama_context from model

However, this warning was already present in b10353 and in several earlier working builds, so I don't think that warning itself is responsible for this regression.

Additional information

I previously tried:

--no-cache-idle-slots
--fit-target 6144

Neither fixed the problem.

After a Vulkan device loss, subsequent model loads often fail until reboot, but I have also seen the original failure after a clean boot, so stale GPU state does not appear to be the root cause.

I don't personally need an immediate fix because --load-mode mmap is a good workaround for me. I'm reporting this because the clean good/bad behavior may be useful for debugging the new iGPU loading path.

Related change: #26081

Linux (Pop!_OS 24.04 LTS, kernel 7.0.11-76070011-generic





### Operating systems

### Hardware

- CPU: AMD Ryzen 7 1700
- GPU: Intel Arc Pro B70 (Battlemage, BMG G31), 32GB VRAM
- Vulkan device reported: `Vulkan0 : Intel(R) Graphics (BMG G31)`

### Models

Qwen3.6-27B-Q4_K_M (dense, not the MoE variant)



### Problem description & steps to reproduce

### Problem description & steps to reproduce
Crash occurred during a long multi-turn agentic conversation (~32k tokens of accumulated context) driven by a custom agent client making repeated chat-completion requests. The crash happened on a request that matched a previously cached prompt at very high but not exact similarity:

```
found better prompt with f_keep = 0.996, sim = 0.995
```

This triggered context-checkpoint restoration, which hit an out-of-bounds tensor write and aborted the process (SIGABRT, core dump). `Restart=on-failure` under systemd recovered the service automatically about a minute later, but the in-flight client request failed.

### First Bad Commit

Unknown — first observed on build b9754.

### Relevant log output

llama-server -m Qwen3.6-27B-Q4_K_M.gguf \
  --device Vulkan0 -ngl 999 --ctx-size 65536 --jinja \

items.body:
## Summary

Two findings from production benchmarks of `-ctk q4_0 -ctv q4_0`:

1. **q4_0 KV cache is completely lossless on hybrid models** (Qwen3.5) -- BLEU 1.000 across 10 test configurations at 4x compression
2. **For standard models** (Llama, Mistral), per-head entropy-adaptive bit allocation improves quality by +8% BLEU at the same compression ratio

Feature request: per-head KV cache type support to enable adaptive allocation.

## Finding 1: Lossless q4_0 on Hybrid Models

A/B benchmarks on RTX 3060 12GB, Qwen3.5-9B, 3-run averages:

| Test | f16 gen/s | q4_0 gen/s | Speed Diff |
|------|-----------|------------|------------|
| Short (2-turn) | 48.2 | 47.0 | -2.4% |
| Medium (8-turn) | 47.0 | 45.8 | -2.6% |
| Long (20+ turn) | 45.9 | 45.8 | -0.1% |

Quality: **BLEU 1.000** (n=50 completions). Token-level identical output between f16 and q4_0 KV cache.

The 33K-token conversation test ran at 36.5 tok/s on q4_0 -- f16 would OOM on the same 12GB GPU.

## Why Hybrid Models Tolerate q4_0

Qwen3.5 uses only **8 of 32 layers** for full attention with KV cache. The other 24 layers use linear attention (Gated Delta Net) with no KV cache. Similarly, Gemma 4 uses **10 of 60 layers** for global attention.

The linear/sliding attention layers act as error correction -- quantization noise in the few attention layers is absorbed by the surrounding layers. Standard models (Llama, Mistral) have no such correction because all layers use full attention.

## Finding 2: Entropy-Adaptive Allocation for Standard Models

For standard architectures where q4_0 does degrade quality, per-head bit allocation based on attention entropy recovers most of the loss:

```
b_h = b_avg + 0.25 * (H_avg - H_2(h))
```

Where `H_2(h)` is the Renyi entropy of head h's attention distribution.

Results on GPT-2 (all at 4x compression):

| Config | BLEU | Token Match | PPL Ratio |
|--------|------|-------------|-----------|
| Uniform 4-bit | 0.531 | 51.3% | 1.101 |
| Adaptive 4-bit | 0.548 | 53.8% | 1.089 |
| Skip 3 sinks + adaptive | 0.574 | 60.0% | 1.062 |

The key insight: the bottom 2% of heads by entropy ("sink heads") contribute disproportionately to quantization error. Skipping quantization on just 3 out of 144 heads provides more benefit than optimal bit redistribution across all others.

## Feature Request: Per-Head KV Cache Types

Currently `-ctk` and `-ctv` apply uniformly to all layers and heads. Per-head allocation would enable:

- **Sink heads** (lowest entropy, ~2% of heads): keep at f16 or q8_0
- **Standard heads**: q4_0 as today
- **High-entropy heads** (diffuse attention): could go to q3_0 or lower

This maintains the same average compression ratio but shifts bits to where they matter most. The implementation would need:

1. A calibration pass to compute per-head entropy (or accept a pre-computed entropy map)
2. Per-head type selection in the KV cache allocation
3. Appropriate dequantization dispatch per head during attention

The entropy computation is a one-time cost per model architecture (not per session). The per-head map could be distributed alongside GGUF files or computed on first load.

## Production Deployment Data

The full 12x compression stack (q4_0 KV + application-level context eviction) is running in production on RTX 3060:

- 128K context window (vs 32K with f16 KV)
- 45-48 tok/s generation speed
- Infinite conversation length via automatic eviction
- Zero model or llama.cpp source changes required

## References

- Discussion #20969 (TurboQuant for llama.cpp)
- Paper: https://github.com/SCJedi/entropy-adaptive-kv-cache/tree/main/paper
- GPT-2 entropy experiments: https://github.com/SCJedi/entropy-adaptive-kv-cache
- Production benchmarks + deployment guide: https://github.com/SCJedi/BitNet/tree/bitnet-tools

## Overview

**cuda: fuse MoE weighted expert reduction**

Fuses the MoE expert-combine tail on the CUDA backend into one reduction kernel, removing the intermediate tensor traffic between its stages.

After `GGML_OP_MUL_MAT_ID`, the combine is a per-expert scale/weight multiply plus an ordered left-to-right `VIEW`+`ADD` chain that sums the `k = n_expert_used` experts. Those are logical nodes: the backend already fuses consecutive MULs/ADDs, so for the common top-k = 8 case it runs as **two physical `k_bin_bcast` kernels** (fused two-MUL + fused seven-ADD) with the full weighted-expert tensor `[n_embd, k, n_tokens]` written out and read back between them. This PR replaces that with **one kernel** that reads each expert row once and writes the `[n_embd, n_tokens]` result once:

```
dst[t,c] = sum_e ((experts[t,e,c] * expert_scale[t,e]) * weight[t,e])
```

The sum keeps the original left-to-right order. **The primary benefit is reduced global-memory traffic** (the eliminated intermediate tensor)

**Matching** is purely structural (op / shape / stride / view offset / add-chain / closure / aliasing) — never the quant or model. Two shapes: short (`experts * router_weight`) and long (`(experts * expert_scale) * router_weight`). The long form appears whenever a per-expert broadcast scale is applied before the router weight (e.g. the NVFP4 `scale_2` output scale, but the same graph slot can carry other scales); the matcher keys only on that second MUL's presence.

**Kernels:** unrolled templates for `k = 2..8`, one runtime-`k` kernel for `k = 9..15`, a `float4` path when `n_embd % 4 == 0` and aligned (scalar fallback), and an optional per-expert scale via a template flag. The `k <= 15` cap is `ggml_can_fuse_subgraph`'s 31-node limit on the long form (`2*k + 1 <= 31`); larger `n_expert_used` falls back.

**Correctness:** full-model WikiText-2 perplexity is unchanged (**5.8857 ± 0.03661**, on vs off) and `test-backend-ops` passes; the reduction keeps the original left-to-right order. Guards: `weights`/`expert_scale` are copied to scratch when they overlap `dst` (read while writing `dst`); fusion is skipped when `experts` overlaps `dst`; view offsets/strides and the add-chain are validated before fusing.

**Fallback / kill switch:** any unsupported top-k or failed structural/layout/closure/alias check leaves the graph unchanged and runs the per-op path. Enabled by default; `GGML_CUDA_MOE_WEIGHTED_REDUCTION=0` forces the reference path.

## Additional information


**Performance** — prefill `t/s`, default-ON vs `=0`, same binary, mean-vs-mean:

| Hardware | Model | Quant | pp2048 | pp8192 |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|
| RTX 5090 | Qwen3.6-35B-A3B | NVFP4 | +3.6% | +3.6% |
| RTX 5090 | Qwen3.6-35B-A3B | Q4_K_M | +4.1% | +3.9% |
| RTX 5090 | Gemma-4-26B-A4B | NVFP4 | +4.3% | +4.3% |
| DGX Spark (GB10) | Qwen3.6-35B-A3B | NVFP4 | +5.4% | +5.4% |
| DGX Spark (GB10) | Gemma-4-26B-A4B | Q4_K_M | +7.1% | +6.2% |

**Testing** (both modes, same binary): `test-backend-ops` **13,178/13,178** pass; CTest **42/42** pass; CPU-vs-CUDA compared; WikiText-2 PPL identical **5.8857 ± 0.03661**; `llama-cli` output unchanged. CUDA backend only; no changes to weights or numerics.

## Overview

**Co-authors:** @jxia4intel, @sliu39

**PR 2/3** of the Intel Xe optimization series — see https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/24408 (mega PR, draft) for the full feature set.

**Target platforms:** Xe-LPG Plus, Xe2, Xe3

This PR adds Intel Xe-specific flash attention optimization kernels for both ARLH iGPU (Xe1, UMA, coopmat1) and Xe2/Xe3. Dependency: builds on top of https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/24404 (Xe-LPG Plus coopmat1 enable). Independent of https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/24407 (GEMM+CW).

### Flash Attention (Intel Xe)

- New Vulkan shaders: single-phase prefill (`flash_attn_hdim64/96/128`) and two-phase split prefill/decode variants
- Pipelines keyed by `(head_dim, gqa_ratio)` for runtime dispatch across various GQA ratios without combinatorial pipeline proliferation
- Supports non-power-of-two GQA ratios via subgroup splitting (`qk_groups`)
- Intel Xe1 (integrated GPU, UMA, cooperative matrix) and Xe2 paths with separate warptile tuning
- Two-phase decode splits softmax reduction across subgroups; shared QK state copy (`fa_copy_qstate`) between prefill phases

### Name and Version

```
version: 10107 (c0bc8591e)
built with GNU 13.3.0 for Linux x86_64
```

Also reproduced after rebuilding with `-DGGML_CUDA_FA_ALL_QUANTS=ON` added to the CMake configuration (same base commit).

### Operating systems

Linux

### GGML backends

CUDA

### Hardware

2x NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060 Ti (16 GB VRAM each, Blackwell), driver 595.71.05, CUDA 13.2, `CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=89` (Ada Lovelace target, used as a workaround — direct Blackwell arch build was not attempted/needed for this report).

### Models

Reproduced on **two independently produced GGUF quantizations** of Gemma 4 31B, sourced from different origins (one traced back to a direct conversion of Google's original safetensors via a third-party "uncensored/heretic" fine-tune, the other from Unsloth's official quantization):

* `gemma-4-31B-it-qat-q4_0-unquantized-uncensored-heretic.Q4_K_M` (mradermacher-hosted repack)
* `gemma-4-31B-it-qat-UD.Q4_K_XL` (Unsloth)

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

`llama-server` reliably enters an infinite generation loop of the `<unused49>` token (vocabulary ID **62** in this model's tokenizer) after the model has been loaded and left idle (no requests sent) for an extended period — typically several hours up to overnight (\~19 hours in the most recent controlled test). Once triggered, **every subsequent request** on the affected slot produces only `<unused49>` repeated until `n_predict`/max tokens is reached, or forever if unbounded.

Steps:

1. Start `llama-server` with a Gemma 4 31B GGUF (either quant source above).
2. Send one initial warm-up request — this succeeds normally.
3. **Leave the server idle with no further requests for several hours (reproduced most reliably after \~19h).**
4. Send a new request. Prompt processing is abnormally slow (see log below, \~2.4 tok/s vs. the \~600-700 tok/s seen on the same hardware/model shortly after a fresh restart), and generation either produces only `<unused49>` or the request has to be cancelled.
5. Restarting `llama-server` (recomputing KV cache from scratch) immediately resolves the issue — until the next long idle period.

### Key isolating observations from this investigation

* **Not correlated with cumulative token usage or conversation length.** Reproduced with a single short warm-up request followed by pure idle time — no long conversation or heavy prompt history involved.
* **Not specific to one GGUF quant source.** Reproduced on both an Unsloth quant and an independently-produced quant (different conversion pipeline, different uploader), ruling out a single quantizer's conversion bug as the sole cause.
* **Not resolved by fixing missing `tokenizer.ggml.eot_token_id` metadata.** One of the two GGUFs tested was missing this field entirely (confirmed via `gguf-py`); the other (Unsloth) had it set to ID 106. Directly verified via `gguf-py` that `tokens[106] == '<turn|>'` (the correct Gemma-4 end-of-turn token) on both GGUFs before patching. Patching the missing field in with `gguf_new_metadata.py --special-token-by-id eot 106` reduced/delayed but did not eliminate the issue.
* **Not resolved by changing KV cache quantization.** Tested both `-ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0` (symmetric) and `-ctk q8_0 -ctv f16` (asymmetric, after rebuilding with `-DGGML_CUDA_FA_ALL_QUANTS=ON` to avoid the known CPU-fallback/hang issue with asymmetric K/V types — see #20866, #24485). Both configurations eventually reproduced the `<unused49>` loop after sufficient idle time.
* **No corresponding kernel/driver-level errors.** `dmesg` around the time of the failure shows no Xid errors, no ECC errors, no OOM killer activity, and no GPU reset. Persistence mode was confirmed enabled. This suggests the fault is not a GPU/driver-level recovery issue but something in the server process's own state (CUDA context, KV cache bookkeeping, or similar) degrading over idle time.
* `-np 1` (single slot, no `--parallel` specified) in all tests, so the same KV cache slot is reused across all requests via LRU/LCP-similarity selection (`selected slot by LRU, t_last = ...`).

### Related issues that appear connected

* \#23677 — grammar sampler crash on `<unused49>` (ID 62) for Gemma 4, confirming this is a recognized special/reserved token that the codebase already has trouble handling in at least one other code path.
* \#24311 — Gemma 4 12B QAT outputs `<unused49>` continuously on Vulkan when GPU-offloading (CPU-only offload reportedly avoids it).
* \#21516 — separate report of Gemma 4 emitting a different reserved token (ID 14) in an infinite loop on Vulkan.
* \#21321 — separate report of `<unused24>` looping.
* unsloth/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-GGUF HF discussion — multiple independent users report the same `<unused49>` loop after "extended thinking" or long-running sessions, with one user noting the issue also reproduces on non-Unsloth quants (bartowski, ggml, lmstudio) at higher bit-depths but not lower ones, and another explicitly noting restart-fixes-it-temporarily behavior identical to what's described here.

## Summary

Across the two quant sources tested and two different KV cache quantization configurations, the one consistent reproducing factor is **elapsed idle time with the model loaded**, not token throughput, not a specific quantizer, and not (as far as `dmesg` shows) a GPU/driver fault. Since the model weights themselves are static once loaded, a bug in the model file itself seems unlikely to fully explain a fault that only appears after hours of idle time with no requests processed — though this can't be ruled out with certainty. The more likely explanation is some runtime state (KV cache bookkeeping, CUDA context, slot/LRU timestamp handling, or similar) degrading over idle time, with Gemma 4's vocabulary/architecture determining which specific token (62 / `<unused49>` in most reports) the output collapses into once that state is corrupted. ## Overview

Implements adaptive mtp with a new option `--spec-type draft-mtp-adaptive`

Suggested configuration to use is: `--spec-type draft-mtp-adaptive --spec-draft-n-max 12`

The algorithm is a counting based state machine with a climb counter and a weighted drop-pressure accumulator. The depth climbs one step after a number consecutive verifies that accepted every drafted token; any miss adds (N - acceptance) to the drop pressure and the depth drops one step once it exceeds a certain amount. High depths fall quickly (a total miss adds N), low depths hold, and at the floor no pressure accumulates at all.  The specific climb difficulty and drop pressure values were empirically determined over a wide range of tests.

`--spec-draft-n-max` bounds the upper adaptive range and both the floor and the cold-start depth default to 3.  The default floor of 3 may be adjusted  with `--spec-draft-n-min-adpative`, although in testing 3 seems to be the best value to choose here.

As higher depths are reached the barrier to climb higher is reduced.  This allows for predictive runs to quickly ascend after they've "proven" themselves.

## Testing and Performance Results

Model: Qwen3.8-27B Q8_0 on 2x Radeon AI PRO R9700 (gfx1201, ROCm).
Configs: plain `draft-mtp` with `--spec-draft-n-max 2` and `3`, and `draft-mtp-adaptive`
with `--spec-draft-n-max 12` (controller starts at the configured `--spec-draft-n-min-adaptive`
floor of 2 or 3 and adjusts on its own). Temperature 0.6, top-k 20, top-p 0.95, min-p 0.001,
8 threads, ctx 8192, 2 seeds per cell.

Tasks (realistic output lengths):
- prose / hard prose: "write a 1000-word essay ...", capped at 1600 tokens (the model
  generated the full 1600 in every run)
- coding: a mid-file C++ benchmark program (merge sort vs heap sort vs std::sort) to
  complete, ~750-800 tokens of generated continuation



### Throughput

### Demonstration of content replay speedups

It's difficult to fully capture and show the moments where the model is recalling content from memory, or regenerating code where predictions really spike.

Fixes input layer CPU offload on iGPU/UMA systems, mirroring the existing output layer policy.

closes #25700

## Overview

The `tok_embd` (input) layer is always assigned to the CPU backend (`pimpl->dev_input = { cpu_dev, &pimpl->cpu_buft_list }`) regardless of `-ngl` setting, even when full GPU offload (`-ngl 99`) is requested. On integrated GPU (iGPU) and unified memory (UMA) architectures such as AMD Strix Halo (gfx1151), this forces `GET_ROWS(tok_embd, inp_tokens)` onto the CPU backend at the start of every forward pass.

This causes ~20 cross-backend synchronization barriers per token on the ROCm/HIP backend because the HIP path uses synchronous `cudaStreamSynchronize` calls per input tensor copy (`ggml_backend_cuda_buffer_set_tensor`), rather than an async GPU-to-GPU route. On UMA hardware where CPU and GPU share the same physical DDR5 memory, the input buffer should simply be assigned to the GPU device with zero-copy, exactly as the output layer (`dev_output`) already does via `get_layer_buft_list(n_layer_all)`.

The fix mirrors the existing output-layer policy: when `act_gpu_layers >= n_layer_all` (full GPU offload requested), `dev_input` is assigned via `get_layer_buft_list(0)` instead of being hardcoded to CPU. Partial offload remains unchanged.

## Additional information

**Root cause:** In `src/llama-model.cpp`, the `dev_input` assignment hardcodes the CPU backend:

```cpp
// there is very little benefit to offloading the input layer, so always keep it on the CPU
pimpl->dev_input = { cpu_dev, &pimpl->cpu_buft_list };
```

Meanwhile, `dev_output` already uses `get_layer_buft_list(n_layer_all)` which follows `-ngl`. On iGPU/UMA systems, this means every token generation forces `tok_embd` to run `GET_ROWS` on the CPU backend, triggering ~20 cross-backend sync points per token on ROCm (8 `cudaStreamSynchronize` calls per input tensor across 10 input tensors, as identified in issue discussion).

The HIP backend does not benefit from async H2D copies the way Vulkan does (which uses `copy_from_host=true`), so the synchronous fallback path on HIP pays the full cross-backend sync cost on every forward pass. This is why Vulkan performs comparably to ROCm on discrete GPUs but diverges significantly on UMA/iGPU hardware where zero-copy assignment is viable.

**Why this condition is safe:**
- `act_gpu_layers = std::min(n_gpu_layers, n_layer_all + 1)` (line 1358)
- When the user requests `-ngl 99` or `-ngl 0` (full offload auto), `act_gpu_layers >= n_layer_all` evaluates true, and the input layer is offloaded to GPU device 0 via `get_layer_buft_list(0)` — the same path as all other layers.
- When partial offload is requested (e.g., `-ngl 20`), `act_gpu_layers < n_layer_all`, the condition is false, and the input layer stays on CPU — identical to current behavior, preserving memory savings for offloaded models.
- Discrete GPUs (dGPU) with full offload: the input layer is now on GPU like the rest, eliminating unnecessary CPU-GPU round-trips. Performance impact on dGPU is expected to be neutral-to-positive since `GET_ROWS` runs entirely on-device.
- The `get_layer_buft_list(0)` call is valid even when `i_gpu_start == 0` (full offload case), since `il=0` falls in the GPU range and returns the first GPU device's buffer list.

## Performance data

The performance measurements below are from existing issue reporters verified on the same AMD Strix Halo (gfx1151) hardware referenced in issue #25700. They were collected by other contributors (Vasili-Sk, cflury4784) and are not fabricated.

### Vasili-Sk — Patch Decomposition Report (Q8_0 + Q6_K, ROCm on gfx1151)

**Test rig:** AMD Strix Halo (gfx1151), upstream master @ `e8f19cc0a`, ROCm 7.1, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Q8_0 (35.19 GiB) and Q6_K (27.19 GiB)

**Flags:** `-p 16384 -n 1024 -ngl 99 -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0 -fa 1 -b 4096 -ub 2048 -r 3 --mmap 0 --no-host 1 --poll 0`

| R4 (hipDeviceScheduleBlockingSync for gfx1151) | reverted | 1125.96 | 48.65 | 955.40 | 55.68 | -0.02% | -0.11% | +1.39% | +0.14% |

## Summary

Under parallel mixed load (`-np 4 --kv-unified`), `llama-server` on an **integrated HIP GPU** (Strix Halo / gfx1151, 128 GB UMA) returns **complete responses that verbatim belong to a different, earlier request**. A large-prompt request receives, as its entire response, the literal answer text of a short request from an earlier round. We also observed a **chimeric** response fusing tokens of two different requests' expected outputs.

**Bisected to a single commit: c7d87229 "ggml-cuda : restore prop.integrated on HIP builds" (#24233).**

| build | result (validated responses, nonce-checked) |
|---|---|
| 505b1ed1 (parent window start) | clean — 0 violations / 168 |
| 5839ba35 (= parent of c7d87229) | clean — 0 / 36 |
| **c7d87229** | **cross-request replays: 3 hard / 36** |
| e8f19cc0 (window end) | cross-request replays: 7 hard + 1 chimera / 96 |

The same harness against **CPU builds** of both window endpoints shows no build-dependent difference (model-compliance noise only) — consistent with the culprit being the HIP integrated-memory path. This presumably explains why it went unnoticed: discrete GPUs are unaffected; it needs an **integrated** AMD GPU (`prop.integrated == 1`), multiple slots and concurrent mixed traffic.

## Environment

- AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395 (Strix Halo), gfx1151, 128 GB unified memory, ROCm 7.14, Ubuntu 24.04
- Build: `cmake -DGGML_HIP=ON -DAMDGPU_TARGETS=gfx1151 -DGPU_TARGETS=gfx1151 -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=/opt/rocm/llvm/bin/clang -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=/opt/rocm/llvm/bin/clang++` (Release)
- Server: `llama-server -m <model> -ngl 999 -c 65536 -np 4 --kv-unified --jinja --chat-template-kwargs '{"enable_thinking":false}'`
- Model: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B MoE (Q4-class quant). First hit this in production behind LocalAI (same symptom after its vendored-llama.cpp bump crossed this commit); reproducing on vanilla `llama-server` rules the wrapper out.

## Reproduction

Load pattern per round (~30 s, script below): (B) short "repeat exactly this code: <nonce>" request → (C) large-prompt (~10k tokens) request whose system prompt requires echoing a per-request nonce in the first line → (D) burst of 4 concurrent short nonce requests (2 streamed / 2 plain). Every response is validated to contain its **own** nonce and no nonce of an **earlier** request.

On affected builds the round-N large-prompt request receives a literal foreign nonce as its complete response, typically from a round-(N−1) burst request. Verbatim from run logs at e8f19cc0:

```
R4/C got='pd-20260722-115649-3-d1'      (expected: reply echoing pc-...-4-c + a summary)
R5/C got='pd-20260722-115649-4-d2'
R6/C got='pd-20260722-115649-1-d1'
R7/C got='pd-20260722-115649-6-d1'
R8/C got='pd-20260722-115649-7-d1'
R3/C got='<!-- run:pc-20260722-115649-2-d0 -->'   <-- chimera: pc-...-2 stem fused with a -d0 burst suffix
```

In production we additionally observed: a poisoned slot re-serving its stored answer to unrelated requests **20+ minutes later** (the victim's `usage` then reports the foreign request's token counts), and occasional degeneration into repeated single characters (`/////...`).

<details><summary>repro-crossover.py (needs httpx)</summary>

```python

Each round: (B) short "repeat exactly: <nonce>" request, (C) large-prompt

(D) burst of 4 concurrent short nonce requests (2 streamed / 2 plain).

- [x] I am running the latest code. Mention the version if possible as well.

### Feature Description

Improve prefill throughput by removing redundant coopmat1 FA dequantization of KV at prefill (like coopmat2's  decode-callback and ROCm's WMMA). 

### Motivation

items.body:
## Overview

ggml_vk_get_cpy_pipeline only routed to the tiled shared-memory transpose shader when dim1 was the innermost dimension, i.e. ggml_transpose (a 0<->1 swap). A 0<->2 swap -- ggml_cont(ggml_permute(x, 2, 1, 0, 3)) -- fell back to the generic per-element strided copy, whose source reads stride by ne0*ne1 elements: one cache line per lane.

DeepSeek-V4's lightning indexer performs exactly that permute on a [n_kv, n_tokens, n_head] tensor. On Vulkan/RADV gfx1151 it ran at ~7-20 GB/s of a ~200 GB/s part and accounted for 43% of total prefill time.

Add copy_transpose_02.comp, mirroring copy_transpose.comp but tiling over dst dims (0, 2) with dims 1 and 3 as the batch, so reads walk src dim2 and writes walk dst dim0 -- both contiguous. The selection condition additionally requires a non-contiguous source and a contiguous destination so it cannot take cases the contiguous-copy shader already handles.

test-backend-ops only exercised ggml_transpose for CONT, so the strided path was untested. Add test_cont_permute covering (2,1,0,3), (1,2,0,3) and (0,2,1,3) over f32/f16 at tile-aligned, tile-unaligned and large shapes. The large shapes are in the eval set rather than only in perf because perf mode does not verify results.

Measured on gfx1151, ne=[n_kv,64,64,1], perm=(2,1,0,3), f32:

| n_kv | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| 1024 | 9.08 GB/s | 579.85 GB/s |
| 1280 | 20.03 GB/s | 153.71 GB/s |
| 2048 | 7.11 GB/s | 91.68 GB/s |
| 2304 | 16.24 GB/s | 86.49 GB/s |

The ~2.2x penalty previously seen at power-of-two n_kv (destination-stride aliasing) is gone. End to end, DeepSeek-V4-Flash IQ3_XXS prefill on a 9k-token prompt goes from 56.33 t/s to 103.74 t/s (+84%).

Note: at n_tokens=512 a single slow-path dispatch takes ~273 ms and looping it in perf mode can trip the GPU watchdog, so the perf cases use n_tokens=64.
