"""Repro: llama-server cross-request response mix-up under -np 4 --kv-unified.

Each round: (B) short "repeat exactly: <nonce>" request, (C) large-prompt
(~10k tokens) request whose system prompt requires echoing a per-request nonce,
(D) burst of 4 concurrent short nonce requests (2 streamed / 2 plain).
Every response must contain its OWN nonce and no nonce of an EARLIER request.

Usage: python3 repro-crossover.py --url http://127.0.0.1:8080 [--rounds 8]
Requires: pip install httpx
"""

items.body: This PR adds a new `--numa mirror` option which mirrors model weights to each Numa node on the system, and uses a thread-local var in the OMP threadpool to select the correct mirror copy local to the thread at runtime, to eliminate cross-socket traffic. Build instructions: ``` apt-get update apt-get install -y libnuma-dev libgomp1 cmake -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DCMAKE_C_FLAGS="-march=native" -DCMAKE_CXX_FLAGS="-march=native" -DGGML_OPENMP=ON cmake --build build --parallel ``` To test: ```bash # No mirroring: ./build/bin/llama-bench -m ~/models/Qwen3-30B-A3B-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf # Numa mirroring of model weights to every node: ./build/bin/llama-bench -m ~/models/Qwen3-30B-A3B-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf --numa mirror ``` Test system is a two-socket Xeon 6238R Cascade Lake, with 768GB of DDR4-2933 (6 channels per socket). Without `--numa mirror`: ``` developer@81ec6c6e6af6:/workspaces/llama-cpp-dbsanfte-dev$ ./build/bin/llama-bench -m ./.devcontainer/Qwen3-32B-Q6_K.gguf | model | size | params | backend | threads | test | t/s | | ------------------------------ | ---------: | ---------: | ---------- | ------: | --------------: | -------------------: | | qwen3 32B Q6_K | 25.03 GiB | 32.76 B | CPU | 56 | pp512 | 20.99 ± 0.01 | | qwen3 32B Q6_K | 25.03 GiB | 32.76 B | CPU | 56 | tg128 | 1.91 ± 0.00 | build: c665d3c9 (6468) ``` With `--numa mirror`: ``` developer@81ec6c6e6af6:/workspaces/llama-cpp-dbsanfte-dev$ ./build/bin/llama-bench -m . /.devcontainer/Qwen3-32B-Q6_K.gguf --numa mirror | model | size | params | backend | threads | test | t/s | | ------------------------------ | ---------: | ---------: | ---------- | ------: | --------------: | -------------------: | | qwen3 32B Q6_K | 25.03 GiB | 32.76 B | CPU | 56 | pp512 | 21.36 ± 0.11 | | qwen3 32B Q6_K | 25.03 GiB | 32.76 B | CPU | 56 | tg128 | 2.70 ± 0.00 | build: c665d3c9 (6468) ``` Intel PCM tool during mirror inference showing both sockets using local mem: There's still a bit of cross-socket traffic (5%) because only model weights are mirrored, not tensors created at inference time. I'll play with that, maybe mirroring those aggressively will help too, or maybe not. Right now anything created at inference time just gets set to live on Node 0.

This PR adds support for lightning attention based models: MiniMax-Text-01 and MiniMax-M1. They are old models - released over a year ago, basically fossils.

Fixes #11290.

### Feature Description

Add support for GLM 5.2, which makes use of sparse attention acceleration by skipping top-k index calculation for some layers

### Motivation

GLM 5.2 is currently the top ranked open weights model.

### Possible Implementation

The main change since 5.1 seems to be the sparse sparse attention, specifically the `index_skip_topk_offset: 3` and `index_topk_freq: 4` which signal that the sparse attention is only recalculated every 4 layers after the first 3, while in GLM 5.1 it was calculated every layer. A `indexer_types: [...]` is provided, but seems to just codify the offset+freq.

(I would figure this is being worked on, but I couldn't find any discussion, PR, or issue so I figured I would make one. If no one is actually looking into it, I could give it a shot at some point today.)

### Git commit

b10252 (2026-08-03). **Already fixed at HEAD by 6fed9f6f (#27071)** (global `n_merge <= 0` reject). Filing for the record: the pre-fix behavior is a divide-by-zero reachable from an untrusted mmproj in shipping downstream builds (LM Studio backend 2.28.2 = b10252).

### Operating system

Windows (0xC0000094) and Linux (SIGFPE), x86_64, CPU backend.

### Steps to reproduce the bug

1. Craft a Step3VL mmproj with `clip.vision.projector.scale_factor = 0` (KEY_PROJ_SCALE_FACTOR, optional read defaulting to 4). The global n_merge validation in b10252 (`clip.cpp:1884`) only rejects `< 0 || >= 65536` — **0 passes**. Generator: `python3 gen_mmproj_step3.py s30.gguf 0 256`.
2. Load it (loads and warms up cleanly — warmup_image_size path doesn't divide here), then send any image (128×128 grayscale works).
3. `mtmd_tokenize` → `split_batch_to_chunk` → `clip_n_output_tokens` (b10252 `clip.cpp:3618`):

```cpp
case PROJECTOR_TYPE_STEP3VL:
    int x_patch = img->nx() / (params.patch_size * params.n_merge);  // /0
```

Windows VEH (LM Studio 2.28.2 mtmd.dll): `[VEH] exception 0xC0000094 ... module=mtmd.dll rva=9A22C` during tokenize. Control with scale_factor=4: tokenize + encode all return 0.

Related: same-root-cause unchecked n_merge divisions exist in hunyuanvl (`clip.cpp:3736`, `hunyuanvl.cpp:36`) and minimax_m3, but in b10252 those are intercepted earlier by preprocessor/graph asserts — Step3VL is the only clean path to the native SIGFPE.

### Expected behavior

Reject `n_merge <= 0` at load (as 6fed9f6f does). Downstream builds on pre-6fed9f6f commits crash on a single image message after loading a malicious mmproj.

### Other

Generator `gen_mmproj_step3.py` available on request.

items.body:
## Router per-model config

This PR implements INI-based per-model configuration for llama-server router mode, as discussed in #17850.

### Summary

Advanced users can define custom configurations using an .ini file. Each model can have its own preset with custom parameters while inheriting router defaults for unspecified options.

### Motivation

Multi-model inference servers for small/medium teams need declarative configuration with zero operational friction. Operators should be able to set global defaults via router CLI and override specific parameters per model in a simple text file.

### Key Features

1. INI-based presets - Define model-specific configurations in a simple .ini file
2. Three independent model sources - Cached models (LLAMA_CACHE), local GGUF files (--models-dir), and custom-path models (--models-preset via paths defined in INI file)
3. Flexible argument formats - Accepts long args (ctx-size), short args (c), and env vars (LLAMA_ARG_CTX_SIZE) as INI keys
4. Inheritance system - Preset args are merged with router base args before spawning child processes
5. Custom model paths - Define models with absolute paths directly in presets without filesystem scanning

### Usage

```sh
llama-server --models-preset ./presets.ini
```

The router can combine multiple sources:

```sh
llama-server --models-dir ./local-models --models-preset ./custom-configs.ini -ngl 999 -fa
```

### INI Format

Section names define model identifiers. Keys correspond to CLI arguments without leading dashes.

Supported key formats:
- Long form: n-gpu-layer = 123
- Short form: c = 4096
- Env var: LLAMA_ARG_CACHE_RAM = 0

All three formats are equivalent and can be mixed in the same file.

Example presets.ini:

```ini
version = 1

; Preset for cached HuggingFace model
[ggml-org/gemma-3-27b-it-GGUF:Q6_K]
chat-template = chatml
ngl = 123
jinja = on
ctx-size = 131072

; Custom local model with absolute path
[my-custom-model]
m = /absolute/path/to/model.gguf
mmproj = /absolute/path/to/mmproj.gguf
ctx-size = 65536
temp = 0.7
top-p = 0.8

; MoE model with specific settings
[MoE-Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking]
m = /models/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-Q6_K.gguf
n-cpu-moe = 30
temp = 0.6
top-p = 0.95
ctx-size = 32768
```

### How Models Are Loaded

The router discovers models from three sources:

1. Cached models - Scanned from LLAMA_CACHE (typically ~/.cache/llama.cpp)
2. Local directory - Scanned from --models-dir (non-recursive, direct children only)
3. Preset definitions - Custom models defined in --models-preset with explicit paths

Model names from presets can match cached or local models to apply custom configurations, or define entirely new models with custom paths.

### Argument Inheritance

When spawning a child process for a model, arguments are merged in this order:

1. Start with preset args from INI (model-specific settings)
2. Add router base args for any missing keys (global defaults from router CLI)
3. Force control args (port, host, alias - always overridden by router)

Priority order (highest to lowest):
- Control args (port, host, alias, model path) - managed by router, cannot be overridden
- Router base args (inherited from router CLI) - fill in missing preset keys
- Preset args (from INI) - model-specific overrides

Control args automatically managed by router:
- --port, --host, --alias
- --api-key
- --model, --mmproj, --hf-repo
- --models-dir, --models-max, --models-preset

If a preset contains control args, they are removed with a warning.

### Changes

New files:
- common/preset.cpp - INI parser using PEG grammar and preset management
- common/preset.h - Preset structures and API

Modified files:
- common/arg.cpp/h - Added common_params_parse() for map output, is_truthy/is_falsey/is_autoy utilities
- common/common.h - Added models_preset parameter
- common/CMakeLists.txt - Added preset.cpp/h to build
- tools/server/server-models.cpp/h - Integrated preset system with model loading and spawning
- tools/server/README.md - Added preset documentation and examples

### Technical Details

INI parsing:
- Uses existing PEG parser from common/peg-parser.h (grammar by @aldehir)
- Line-oriented parsing handles comments, blank lines, and standard INI sections
- Whitespace and inline comments properly handled

Argument mapping:
- Three key formats (long, short, env) all map to same common_arg via lookup table
- Deduplication handled automatically (short -c and long --ctx-size are the same arg)

Child process spawning:
- Child servers listen on 127.0.0.1 (not inherited hostname) to avoid conflicts when router runs on 0.0.0.0
- Arguments passed as CLI args (not environment variables)
- Router port exported as LLAMA_SERVER_ROUTER_PORT env var for child processes

### Use Case Example

Development team runs inference server with multiple models:

```sh
llama-server --port 8082 -ngl 999 -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0 -fa on --mlock -np 4 -kvu --jinja --models-preset config.ini

# You can combine --models-preset with :
# --models-max N         for router server, maximum number of models to load simultaneously
# --models-dir PATH      directory containing models for the router server (default: disabled)
```

The presets.ini file defines per-model overrides:

```ini
; Minimal setup
[MyModel]
m = /path/to/model.gguf ; or relative path from current working directory

; For this model we want precise sampling parameters and more context
[MoE-Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct]
m = /path/to/unsloth/Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct-GGUF/Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct-Q6_K.gguf
temp = 0.7
top-p = 0.8
top-k = 20
ctx-size = 131072

; Disable flash attention for this model
[Problematic-model]
m = /path/to/problematic-Q8_0.gguf
fa = off

; Large MoE models don't fit in VRAM, so we use n-cpu-moe = 18
[MoE-Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct]
m = /path/to/unsloth/Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct-GGUF/Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct-Q4_K_M.gguf
n-cpu-moe = 18
ctx-size = 32768
```

Global defaults (-ngl 999 -fa -ctk q8_0 etc.) apply to all models, but each preset can override

items.body:
Hybrid KDA (linear) + MLA (full) attention as in Kimi-Linear-48B, plus five things that architecture does not have:

  1. cross-layer residual attention  (attn_res_block_size)
  2. latent MoE                      (routed experts run at n_expert_latent)
  3. situ activation                 (replaces SwiGLU everywhere)
  4. MLA output gate                 (sigmoid gate before o_proj)
  5. full-rank KDA gate              (single ssm_g instead of ssm_g_a/ssm_g_b)

Reuses DeepSeek4's HC_PRE for the cross-layer residual weighted sum. Supports repack for the MXFP4 weights in conversion.

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

I am seeing extremely poor token generation performance with all Gemma 4 variants compared to Qwen3.6 on the same hardware.

Prompt processing works normally, but token generation is much slower than expected.

I tested multiple (at least 4-6) Gemma variants (Q6_K, Q4_K_XL, with and without MTP), different context sizes, GPU layer configurations, Flash Attention, and Programmatic Dependent Launch (PDL). The overall behavior remains the same.

Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-UD-Q6_K and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-UD-Q8_K_XL.gguf performs normally on the same system.

I would like to know whether this behavior is expected on Blackwell GPUs or whether it could indicate a CUDA backend or Gemma-specific performance issue.

approximately 6 tokens/sec
CPU ~95–100%

significantly higher generation speed

## Overview

With CCCL >= 3.2, top-k processes multi-row inputs with one sequential DeviceTopK dispatch per row. This is ok for a few rows and is even optimal for single row or large ncols cases, but for batch workloads it serializes thousands of dispatches per graph. More specifically MiniMax M3's block selection calls top-k with HD * n_tokens rows, causing a massive prompt processing regression (1250 - 77 t/s on 3 * RTX 6000s  https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/26297#issuecomment-5146180851 vs https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/26297#issuecomment-5146982417. ) for anyone on CUDA toolkit >= 13.2 or with the official release binaries.

<!-- Describe what this PR does and why. Be concise but complete -->

## Additional information

This PR keeps the per row DeviceTopK path for nrows <= 16, and routes larger row counts to the existing batched argsort + copy path. (behaviour for CCCL < 3.2 is unchanged). Also routes stream capture to the argsort path, which has explicit capture handling, since DeviceTopK's support is not verified. I can drop that if it is known safe.

Long term the proper fix is DeviceSegmentedTopK when CCCL implements it.

items.body:
## Overview

<!-- Describe what this PR does and why. Be concise but complete -->
Adds support for MiniMax-M3, a 60-layer / 128-expert MoE (3 dense + 57 MoE layers) using MiniMax Sparse Attention (MSA): a GQA block-sparse attention where a lightweight per-GQA-group indexer scores the visible causal context, max-pools the scores into 128-token key blocks, and selects the top-16 blocks (the query's local block is always force-included). The main attention then runs only over the selected blocks (16*128 = 2048 KV per query), independent of context length, so decode attention cost stops scaling with context.

Implements the architecture from the MSA paper (arXiv:2606.13392v2) and follows the transformers reference (modular_minimax_m3_vl) for the indexer construction, selection semantics, and RoPE. MTP heads are not present in the released weights. Vision support is a separate PR (#25113).

Note that MSA is not an optional speed optimization, as the model is trained with sparse attention, so block selection is part of the model's semantics. Running dense attention is an out-of-distribution approximation that degrades output quality. The dense path exists only as a fallback for configurations that can't run MSA.

## Additional information

<!-- You can provide more details and link related discussions here. Delete this section if not applicable -->

### Implementation
Batch and decode implement the same block-scoring and selection semantics, block scores bs = maxpool_128(idx_q*idx_k^T + causal mask) plus a host-provided local-force bias (large positive bias on each query's local block), ranked together for top-k. Selection is per GQA group (4 indexer heads, one per group, shared across the group's 16 query heads).

Within each stream, the four GQA groups are mapped onto the FA mask's ne[3] broadcast dimension and executed in one grouped flash-attention call.

- Batch (n_tokens_per_stream > 1, ie. prefill): a small CPU op turns block scores into a block-level 0/-inf mask, then the token-level expansion and combination with the causal mask happens on the GPU, and masked FA runs over the full cache views.

- Decode (1 token per stream): batched top_k on the GPU, index arithmetic expands block ids to flat (token, kv-head) row ids, one ggml_get_rows each gathers the selected K/V/mask, and FA runs over just the 2048 gathered tokens. 

Multi-stream (--parallel N) is supported whenever the KV cache is per-sequence (so kv_unified is false). In that configuration each stream's slots are then position-aligned, which MSA's slot-anchored block selection requires. 

The indexer also needs its own per-layer key cache. It is allocated F32 on the same backend buffer as the main K/V cache. Context-shift is not supported, since shifting would desynchronize the index cache.

### Requirements and fallbacks

- Flash attention required. Both batch and decode call ggml_flash_attn_ext directly and assume the non-transposed V layout that llama.cpp only provides with FA on. FA off uses dense build_attn (no sparsity) with a one-time warning that output quality may be degraded. 

- Unified KV cache with multiple sequences (--kv-unified + -np > 1) would silently break block anchoring so it also falls back to dense with a one-time warning. 

### Limitations

- Block selection is anchored to absolute KV slots. Erasing a prefix or middle of a sequence's history (llama_memory_seq_rm of a partial range) breaks selection silently. Removing whole sequences, trimming the suffix and reusing server slots is fine.
 
- Main KV cache: F16/BF16 are tested. Quantized KV-cache types are not yet validated.

### Quantization

Quants should keep the indexer projections (index_{q,k}_proj) at high precision(F32 ideally) since they drive block selection, so quant error there changes which blocks are read (a discrete retrieval loss), unlike a value projection. The cost is ~1 GB and these are some of the highest-value tensors in the model.

### Conversion

GGUFs must be converted with this branch and must keep the indexer tensors, weights with the indexers stripped will not work. 

### Performance

My tested config is expert-offload  bound.  MSA decode is essentially flat with context (7.7 tok/s at 5k -> 7.67 at 62k), prefill is roughly ~420-480 tok/s at 62k with -b and -ub 2048. Compute buffer at -ub 2048 / 62k ctx is ~4.6 GiB.

### How to test

As mentioned GGUFs converted with this PR are necessary, other's will fail to load. You can either convert one yourself, or you can use [this](https://huggingface.co/Serpen/Minimax-M3-MSA-GGUF/tree/main/Q4_K_M) Q4KM one (graciously provided by @AesSedai). 

CUDA build assumed (`-DGGML_CUDA=ON`), but in theory other backends with flash_attn_ext support for head-dim 128 should work (dense fallback otherwise), ROCm/HIP, Vulkan, Metal untested, reports welcome.

- Feed a ~4k and a ~30k+ prompt and generate. Decode throughput should stay roughly flat with context (fixed 2048-KV budget).

- Multi-stream: llama-server --parallel 2 (or 4) with concurrent requests of different prompt lengths.

### Credits

The initial MiniMax-M3 scaffolding was based on work by @danielhanchen. The sparse-attention indexer, the unified batch/decode MSA graphs, the KV-cache index handling, FA gating, and multi-stream support in this PR are new work.

## Requirements

<!-- IMPORTANT: Please do NOT delete this section, otherwise your PR may be rejected -->

- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)

items.body:
## Overview

Enable the CUB code paths on HIP by using hipCUB (the CUB-compatible API that ships with rocPRIM), so AMD builds stop falling back to the slow/CPU paths for device-wide primitives.

Today `GGML_CUDA_USE_CUB` is only defined for CUDA (`CUDART_VERSION >= 11070`), so on HIP:

* `argsort` / `top_k` with `ncols > 1024` exceed the single-block bitonic path and fall back to the **CPU backend**. For DeepSeek-Sparse-Attention models (DeepSeek-V4, DeepSeek-3.2, GLM-DSA, MiniMax-M3) the per-token indexer `top_k` runs over the whole context, so this fallback is hit on **every token**, with cost growing as context grows.
* `sum`, `mean`, `cumsum` and `ssm_scan` use their inefficient fallbacks. `ggml/src/ggml-cuda/sum.cu` already notes this:

  > `// For AMD there is rocPRIM which could be used as a drop-in replacement via hipcub but this would require...`

## Implementation

`common.cuh` enables the existing CUB paths when hipCUB is available:

```c
#elif defined(GGML_USE_HIP) && !defined(GGML_HIP_NO_HIPCUB) && __has_include(<hipcub/hipcub.hpp>)
#    define GGML_CUDA_USE_CUB
#    define GGML_HIP_USE_HIPCUB
```

* **Feature-detected**, so ROCm installs without `hipcub-dev` keep building exactly as before.
* **Opt-out** via `-DGGML_HIP_NO_HIPCUB`.
* Call sites are unchanged — each translation unit does `namespace cub = hipcub;` and pulls in the specific symbols it uses, rather than dumping the namespace globally.
* `vendors/hip.h` gains the `cudaStreamIsCapturing` / `cudaStreamCaptureStatus` mappings the CUB paths need.

8 files changed, 53 insertions(+), 7 deletions(-).

## Correctness

`test-backend-ops test` passes on the ROCm backend for every affected op: `ARGSORT`, `TOP_K`, `SUM`, `MEAN`, `CUMSUM`, `SSM_SCAN`.

## Performance

Hardware: Radeon 8060S iGPU (**gfx1151**, Strix Halo), 128 GB unified memory, ROCm 7.2.4, Debian.

Both arms built from the same commit, differing only by this patch. `llama-bench -p 0 -n 64 -d <depth> -fa 1 -mmp 0`, ROCm backend.

**DeepSeek-V4-Flash** (284B-A13B, IQ2_XXS, KV `q4_0`, `-b/-ub 2048`), tg t/s:

| depth | master | this PR | delta |
|------:|-------:|--------:|------:|
| 0      | 12.60 ± 1.15 | 12.65 ± 0.09 | +0.4% |
| 8192   | 10.54 ± 0.40 | 11.95 ± 0.79 | **+13%** |
| 32768  |  8.27 ± 0.17 | 11.36 ± 0.35 | **+37%** |
| 65536  |  7.54 ± 0.14 |  9.81 ± 0.21 | **+30%** |
| 131072 |  6.40 ± 0.08 |  8.02 ± 0.15 | **+25%** |

Depth 0 is the natural control: with no context there is no indexer `top_k` work and the two builds are identical. The gain appears as soon as context exists and stays ≥25% out to 128K — consistent with removing a fallback whose cost scales with depth.

Models that do **not** use these ops are unaffected, as expected:

| model | class | tg @32K master → this PR |
|---|---|---|
| Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Q4_K_M | MoE (routing uses the fused `topk-moe` path, ≤256 cols) | 47.72 → 46.62 |
| Gemma-4-31B Q4_K_XL | dense | 8.40 → 8.46 |

Those two are within run-to-run noise (arms were run sequentially, so the second arm sees slightly warmer hardware).

## Requirements

- [x] I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)

## Overview

Follow up to #24908, addressing https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/24908#issuecomment-5130176748 and https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/26338#issuecomment-5134746310. Everything the original MSA pr added to `llama_kv_cache` has been reverted. MSA is now implemented inside a new `llama_kv_cache_msa` which mirrors `llama_kv_cache_dsa`, with two `llama_kv_cache` instances, one for K/V and one for the indexer keys as a plain K cache(allocates an unused V cache), kept in sync.  I believe a separate class is cleaner than extending dsa's, since the base caches and graph inputs differ.

Initially MSA block selection was anchored to cache cell indices, which was only correct for append only streams. This PR also moves the block selection into position space.

The only addition to `llama_kv_cache` is a read only get_cells() accesor, used to fill the MSA position converter maps.

None of the changes produced any quality regression up to the 70k ctx I tested. I experienced a minor prefill speed regression, which is most likely the cost of the position ->  cell translation. Decode speed remains unchanged.

## Overview

[GigaChat-3.5-432B-A28B](https://huggingface.co/ai-sage/GigaChat3.5-432B-A28B-GGUF) is a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language model with 432B total parameters and 28B active parameters. Built on a DeepSeek-V3-style backbone (MLA attention + DeepSeek MoE), it employs a hybrid attention architecture in which most layers use a Qwen3-Next Gated-Delta-Net (GDN) linear-attention block while a periodic subset retains full MLA attention. The architecture further incorporates gated RMSNorm with a low-rank gating bottleneck arranged as a four-norm sandwich (pre/post attention, pre/post MLP), gated attention applied before the output projection, and learnable MLA query/key scaling factors (alpha_q / alpha_kv). It utilizes 2-layer Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) for accelerated inference via speculative decoding.

## Overview

This PR fixes the error of webgpu ci error for minimax-m3 introduced by https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/24908.

minimax-m3 graph calls `ggml_tensor * bmx = ggml_repeat_4d(ctx0, ...);` followed by `ggml_add_inplace(ctx0, bmx, ...)`, but existing webgpu backend doesn't have F16 repeat, so it crashes with `Bus error`, because the GPU ADD op ends up with an inplace destination on CPU buffer. So it fixes the error by adding F16 repeat support.

## Additional information

The root cause seems to be in ggml scheduler, so I'll investigate it and follow up on it in separate PR.

### Name and Version

version: 0.1.0-dev (build 10438, commit 9d57ce456)
built with GNU 14.2.0 for Linux x86_64

Also reproduced on master (b94041a), built for macOS arm64.

### Operating systems

Linux

### GGML backends

CUDA

### Hardware

NVIDIA RTX PRO 4000 Blackwell SFF (SM120)
Apple M3 Max

### Models

https://huggingface.co/RedHatAI/Muse-Glimmer-30B-NVFP4, converted with `convert_hf_to_gguf.py --outtype q8_0`

The converted GGUF: https://huggingface.co/gabrielcosi/Muse-Glimmer-30B-NVFP4-GGUF


### Problem description & steps to reproduce

A compressed-tensors NVFP4 Muse Glimmer checkpoint converts to a GGUF that does not load. Past the load error, the model runs but returns the same token for every prompt.

K-quant conversions of the same model work. Only the NVFP4 path is affected.

Three things go wrong.

**1. The QK-norm tensors are missing.** [`_generate_nvfp4_tensors`](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/b94041a/conversion/base.py#L800-L802) removes quantized tensors from `model_tensors`, so `modify_tensors` never sees them. Muse Glimmer carries no QK-norm weights of its own, so [`MuseGlimmerModel.modify_tensors`](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/b94041a/conversion/muse_glimmer.py#L65) synthesizes `attn_q_norm` and `attn_k_norm` there. It keys on `self_attn.q_proj.weight`, which is quantized and already removed. The tensors are never written and the load fails.

**2. Q and K keep the transformers layout.** The same bypass skips [`_unpermute_for_rope`](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/b94041a/conversion/muse_glimmer.py#L58-L61) on `q_proj` and `k_proj`.

**3. Most NVFP4 scales are ignored.** [`build_lora_mm`](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/b94041a/src/llama-graph.cpp#L1493) applies the per-tensor scale only when the caller passes it. The muse-glimmer graph passes it for `wo` ([L142](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/b94041a/src/models/muse-glimmer.cpp#L142)) and `output` ([L190](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/b94041a/src/models/muse-glimmer.cpp#L190)) only. `attn_gate` ([L107](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/b94041a/src/models/muse-glimmer.cpp#L107)) and the three FFN projections ([L163-L168](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/b94041a/src/models/muse-glimmer.cpp#L163-L168)) pass `NULL`, so those weights run unscaled. The scales are around 4e-5. `qwen3.cpp` passes all three FFN scales.

Steps to reproduce items 1 and 2:

1. Download `RedHatAI/Muse-Glimmer-30B-NVFP4`.
2. Run `python convert_hf_to_gguf.py <dir> --outtype q8_0`. This needs `transformers>=5`, because the model ships `tokenizer_class: TokenizersBackend`.
3. Run `llama-server -m <gguf>`. The load fails with the error below.

To see item 3 on a stock build, download the GGUF linked above. I converted it with items 1 and 2 fixed ([9ec0ea1](https://github.com/gabrielcosi/llama.cpp/commit/9ec0ea187ea86390cf6a480ea6db156894850c18)), so it loads on an unpatched build. Every prompt then returns one repeated token.

### First Bad Commit

_No response_

### Relevant log output

<details>
<summary>Logs</summary>
<!-- Copy-pasted short logs go into the "console" area here -->

```console
check_tensor_dims: tensor 'blk.0.attn_q_norm.weight' not found
llama_model_load_from_file_impl: failed to load model
common_init_: failed to load model 'muse-nvfp4.gguf'

# Running the linked GGUF, with `--temp 0`:

CUDA:  "The capital of France is" -> "22222222222222222222"
CUDA:  "1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6,"        -> "22222222222222222222"
CPU:   "The capital of France is" -> "33333333333333333333"
CPU:   "1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6,"        -> "33333333333333333333"

```
</details>

## Overview

<!-- Describe what this PR does and why. Be concise but complete -->

Enables Muse-Glimmer for OpenVINO backend.

- Added New Op Support: GGML_UNARY_OP_SIGMOID, GGML_OP_ARGMAX
- Decline bf16 `GET_ROWS` on GPU
- Classify sliding-window vs full-attention layers from the per-layer KV cache extent.
- Accuracy improvement: Keep the RoPE angle in f32 under the f16 inference hint.
- Honour `GGML_TENSOR_FLAG_OUTPUT` in `compute_model_outputs()`, which previously used only
  use-count analysis and so dropped tensors that the host reads back.
- Refresh the decoder IO when the cgraph instance changes, and invalidate a cached graph when its
  output set changes.
- Keep the token dimension dynamic for a 2-D activation graph input, plus three dynamic-dim
  propagation gaps (shape-preserving `VIEW`, `CONCAT`, `SSM_CONV`/`GATED_DELTA_NET`).
- Tolerate graph inputs and outputs with no backing storage instead of constructing an `ov::Tensor`
  over a null pointer.
- `GGML_OPENVINO_REDUCE_COMPILE_MEM`: stream requantization in row chunks instead of
  materializing one full F32 array.
- `GGML_OPENVINO_REQUANT_KQUANT`: optionaly choose a 4-bit requant target
  (`q4_sym128`/`q4_asym64`[`_all`]/`native`) instead of inflating Q6_K/Q5_K to Q8_0.
- `GGML_OPENVINO_RELEASE_WEIGHTS` — drop host weight pages after the GPU plugin has its own copy.
  Single model per process; two guards abort loudly rather than read dropped pages.
- `GGML_OPENVINO_SPILL_DIR` — back the repacked weight buffer with an unlinked file so the pages
  are reclaimable.

## Requirements

<!-- IMPORTANT: Please do NOT delete this section, otherwise your PR may be rejected -->

items.body:
### Summary

`--spec-type draft-dflash` works well at low concurrency, but under concurrent slots the **draft model's predictions get corrupted**, draft acceptance collapses, and throughput goes into reverse (slower than no speculation). We traced this on an AMD gfx1151 APU across two ROCm versions and pinned down that the corruption **scales with the number of concurrently-drafting sequences, not with batch token count, server slot count, or draft length alone**:

| server `-np` | active requests | `--spec-draft-n-max` | noise-block batch | per-slot draft acceptance | aggregate throughput |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | 4 | 15 | 64 tok | **0.51 – 0.66** (healthy) | healthy |
| **16** | **4** | 15 | 64 tok | **0.51 – 0.66** (bit-identical to the row above, same seed) | healthy |
| 8 | 8 | 15 | 128 tok | 0.11 – 0.46 (degraded) | degraded |
| 16 | 16 | 7 | 128 tok | 0.22 – 0.74 (bimodal) | bad |
| 16 | 16 | 15 | 256 tok | **0.06 – 0.49** (bimodal; sustained load collapses to **0.0018**) | ~17–21 tok/s vs **37 tok/s** no-spec baseline |
| 16 | 16 | **1** | 32 tok | **0.83 – 0.92** | **~80 tok/s (2.2× the no-spec baseline)** |

Key observations that localize the defect:

1. **Per-slot corruption is established during prefill and persists for the request's lifetime.** 16 *identical* requests (same prompt, seed, temperature) produce an ~8× spread in acceptance across slots, visible from the very first speculative tick. The draft model's top-1 confidence is bimodal per slot: median 0.25 on "broken" slots vs 0.92–0.98 on "healthy" ones.
2. **It is not the server's slot configuration** — a `-np 16` server with only 4 in-flight requests produces bit-identical results to a `-np 4` server.
3. **It is not the drafter's intrinsic quality** — with `--spec-draft-n-max 1` the same 16-way load accepts 83–92 % of drafts and beats the no-spec baseline by 2.2×.
4. **It is not a ROCm-version regression** — identical pathology on ROCm 7.2.1 and 7.14.0 (we cannot test CUDA here; see "ask" at the end).

### Git commit

- Verified at `0b1bad14ff204627636aeb1de22ddcd5acb859d4` (2026-08-11).
- **Still reproduces on current master `0177dcc7300bad8914bb838baabce87899812491` (2026-08-15, freshly built)**: 16 identical concurrent requests → the same bimodal per-slot acceptance (0.05–0.50, broken slots waste 500–977 drafts per 160-token request); the 4-concurrent control on the same server recovers (0.19–0.61). The numbers below are from the pinned build.

Build: `-DGGML_HIP=ON -DAMDGPU_TARGETS=gfx1151 -DROCM_PATH=…` (Release, GCC 13.3, `GGML_HIP_GRAPHS=ON` default).

Hardware/runtime: AMD Ryzen AI MAX+ 395 / Radeon 8060S iGPU (gfx1151, 96 GB unified), kernel 6.17, ROCm 7.14.0 (side-by-side 7.2.1 with identical results).

Models: Muse-Glimmer-30B target (Q4_K "kquant" GGUF, ~17 GB, all layers on GPU) + the matching DFlash draft GGUF (`general.architecture = dflash`, 5 layers, `block_size=16`, 5 extracted target layers). Any supported dense target + DFlash pair should reproduce the concurrency dependence.

### Command line

```bash
llama-server -m muse-glimmer-30B-kquant-17gb.gguf -ngl 999 \
  -np 16 -c 131072 --jinja \
  -md dflash-kquant.gguf -ngld 99 \
  --spec-type draft-dflash --spec-draft-n-max 15 \
  --temp 1.0 --top-p 0.95 --top-k 64 --seed 42 \
  --port 8080 > server.log 2>&1
```

Reproduce (the server log is the instrument — `/metrics` spec counters stay 0 on these builds):

```bash
# 16 identical concurrent streaming requests
seq 16 | xargs -P16 -I{} curl -sN http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Explain in detail why the sky is blue."}],
       "max_tokens":160,"temperature":1.0,"top_p":0.95,"top_k":64,"seed":42}' >/dev/null

grep 'draft acceptance' server.log
```

Controls (each on a fresh server):

- `-P4` instead of `-P16` (same `-np 16` server) → acceptance recovers to ~0.5–0.66.
- `--spec-draft-n-max 1` with `-P16` → acceptance 0.83–0.92, ~2.2× no-spec throughput.
- `-np 4` server, `-P4` → bit-identical to the `-np 16`/`-P4` run (same seed).

### Problem description & logs

Expected: draft acceptance roughly constant w.r.t. concurrency (speculative decoding is lossless; batching drafts from many sequences should not change per-sequence predictions), and DFlash at `-np 16` to at least not be slower than no speculation.

Actual (16 identical concurrent requests, fresh server, `0b1bad1`):

```
slot print_timing: id  1 | draft acceptance = 0.05333 (    4 accepted /    75 generated), mean len =  1.80
slot print_timing: id  7 | draft acceptance = 0.25424 (   45 accepted /   177 generated), mean len =  3.50
slot print_timing: id 10 | draft acceptance = 0.49074 (   53 accepted /   108 generated), mean len =  6.89
slot print_timing: id 12 | draft acceptance = 0.19048 (   44 accepted /   231 generated), mean len =  3.44

```

Under sustained long-generation load this collapses completely — a 16×512, 5-rep run on ROCm 7.2.1 was aborted after 5 h 16 min with **3,270,000 drafted / 6,060 accepted (0.18 %)**.

Secondary symptoms at `-np 16` (measured on the same runs):

- Prompt processing with DFlash injection runs at ~57 ms/token (~17.5 tok/s) vs ~23 ms/token (~43 tok/s) without DFlash at the same `-np` — the per-sequence sequential `llama_encode` + inject `llama_decode` in `process()` is paid once per sequence per batch.
- Steady-state speculative tick is 1.15–1.5 s; `draft()` alone averages 133 ms per call (256-token noise block); per-token time grows ~3× over a 320-token request (207 → 570 ms/token), i.e. it decays as generations lengthen.
- The HIP backend logs `CUDA graph warmup reset` 1–2× per tick (54–194 per run) as batch composition chang

### Name and Version

version: b10349 (62bf73d25, includes the #26841 merge)
Built from source (CUDA, `CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=86;120`) in a local Docker image.
Hardware: RTX 3090 + RTX 5060 Ti.

### Operating systems

Linux (Docker container on a Windows host)

### GGML backends

CUDA

### Models

- **Target (FAILS):** [meta-models/Muse-Glimmer-30B-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/meta-models/Muse-Glimmer-30B-GGUF) → `muse-glimmer-30B-kquant-dynamic.gguf`
- **Draft:** same repo → `dflash-kquant.gguf`
- **Target (WORKS):** [unsloth/Muse-Glimmer-30B-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/unsloth/Muse-Glimmer-30B-GGUF) with the exact same drafter

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Binding the DFlash drafter (`--spec-type draft-dflash`) crashes at load time when the **target** GGUF encodes `muse-glimmer.attention.sliding_window_pattern` as an **array**, which is how the model creator's own official GGUF (`meta-models/Muse-Glimmer-30B-GGUF`) encodes it:

```
llama-server -m muse-glimmer-30B-kquant-dynamic.gguf \
    -md dflash-kquant.gguf --spec-type draft-dflash -fa on --jinja
```

crashes with:

```
vector::_M_range_check: __n (which is 1) >= this->size() (which is 1)
```

The exact same drafter file binds and runs fine when the target is the unsloth conversion of the same model, whose `muse-glimmer.attention.sliding_window_pattern` is encoded as a **scalar** (`UINT32 = 4`).

Both target GGUFs load and generate fine **without** the drafter — `src/models/muse-glimmer.cpp` accepts both encodings (scalar period → `set_swa_pattern()`, array → per-layer `is_swa_impl`). The crash only happens on the DFlash bind path, which inherits the target's config and apparently only handles the scalar form. Note the irony: the model creator's official GGUF is the one that cannot bind the official drafter shipped in the same repo, while a third-party conversion can.

**Validated workaround:** copying the target GGUF with gguf-py `copy_with_new_metadata`, rewriting `muse-glimmer.attention.sliding_window_pattern` to scalar `UINT32 = 4`. With that single metadata change the drafter binds and runs (~137 t/s on the RTX 3090).

**Suggested fix:** when the DFlash path inherits the target's config, accept both encodings of `<arch>.attention.sliding_window_pattern`, mirroring what `src/models/muse-glimmer.cpp` already does at target load. Possibly related: the scalar overload `llama_model_loader::get_key_or_arr(enum llm_kv, uint32_t &, bool)` in `src/llama-model-loader.cpp` returns `false` (non-required) or throws when the key is an array, so any call site expecting a scalar silently takes the wrong branch on array-encoded GGUFs.

### First Bad Commit

Not bisected — observed on b10349 (62bf73d25). Possibly present since the DFlash path landed.

### Relevant log output

```
vector::_M_range_check: __n (which is 1) >= this->size() (which is 1)
```

items.body:
`common_speculative_init_result` computes the draft model path, logs it, and then passes the **target** model path to `llama_model_load_from_file`:

```cpp
model_path = params.speculative.draft.mparams.path;
LOG_INF("%s: loading draft model '%s'\n", __func__, model_path.c_str());

llama_model * model_dft = llama_model_load_from_file(params.model.path.c_str(), mparams);
```

So with `-md <draft.gguf> --spec-type draft-dflash` (or any draft-based spec type routed through this init), the target model is silently loaded a second time as the "draft". Depending on available memory this either:

- fails draft context creation and **silently disables speculative decoding** (generation proceeds at baseline speed with no indication beyond a fitting-time warning), or
- doubles the target model's memory footprint.

The log line above makes it look like the correct file was loaded, which makes the no-op hard to notice — we only caught it because with/without `-md` benchmarked identically.

## Fix

Load the draft path that was computed on the line above (one line).

## Validation

Muse-Glimmer-30B-UD-Q3_K_XL + `dflash-kquant.gguf` (unsloth GGUFs), Apple M5 24 GB, Metal backend, `llama-server --spec-type draft-dflash --spec-draft-n-max 15`:

| | draft_n / draft_accepted | generation |
|---|---|---|
| before | absent (spec silently off); t/s identical with and without `-md` | 3.5–5 t/s |
| after | e.g. 2067 / 461 (chat, 22%) up to 735 / 548 (code continuation, 75%) | up to 19.5 t/s on high-acceptance workloads |

Acceptance-rate range is workload-dependent as expected for a block drafter; the point of the table is that draft stats exist at all and the speedup appears only after the fix.

## Describe the bug

A significant performance regression occurs between builds b10356 and b10359/b10360/b10369 on RTX 5080 (Blackwell, compute capability 12.0). The regression affects both prompt processing and generation speed, and appears to worsen with each new build.

## Environment

- **GPU:** NVIDIA RTX 5080 (16GB, Blackwell, compute capability 12.0)
- **Driver:** 610.62, CUDA 13.3
- **OS:** Windows 11 x64
- **Model:** Muse-Glimmer-30B-UD-IQ2_M.gguf (11.4 GB, IQ2_M quantization, `muse-glimmer` architecture)
- **Draft model:** dflash-kquant.gguf (DFlash speculative decoding)

## Full build comparison (4 builds tested)

| Build | Prompt processing | Generation (peak) | Generation (avg) | DFlash mean len |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **b10356** (best) | 1029-1271 tok/s ✅ | 62 tok/s | ~53 tok/s | 2.3-3.5 |
| b10359 | 834 tok/s ❌ (−34%) | 37 tok/s ❌ (−40%) | ~32 tok/s | 2.2-3.0 |
| b10360 | 740-914 tok/s ❌ (−30%) | 83 tok/s ✅ (+34%) | ~68 tok/s | 2.4-3.7 |
| **b10369** (worst) | 413-534 tok/s ❌❌ (−60%) | 49 tok/s ❌ | ~38 tok/s | 2.2-3.5 |

**Key finding:** The regression is getting **worse with each build**. b10369 is the worst of all four — prompt processing dropped to 413 tok/s on the first task (vs 1029 on b10356), a **−60% regression**.

## Reproduction

```bash
llama-server \
  -m Muse-Glimmer-30B-UD-IQ2_M.gguf \
  -ngl all -c 60000 -np 1 \
  -fa on --kv-unified \
  --cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0 \
  --batch-size 2048 --ubatch-size 2048 \
  --spec-type draft-dflash \
  --spec-draft-model dflash-kquant.gguf \
  --spec-draft-p-min 0.2 --spec-draft-n-max 3 \
  --jinja --no-ui
```

All builds are official prebuilt `llama-bXXXX-bin-win-cuda-13.3-x64.zip` (Clang 20.1.8).

## Sample timings

### b10356 (best — baseline)

```
prompt eval time = 5387 ms / 6195 tokens → 1149 tok/s
eval time = 6655 ms / 365 tokens → 54.8 tok/s
draft acceptance = 0.694, mean len = 3.08
```

### b10359 (regression — both metrics slower)

```
prompt eval time = 38292 ms / 31965 tokens → 834 tok/s  (−27%)
eval time = 2109 ms / 78 tokens → 36.9 tok/s  (−33%)
draft acceptance = 0.693 (identical → regression is NOT in speculative decoding)
```

### b10360 (mixed — generation improved, prefill worse)

```
prompt eval time = 1599 ms / 1385 tokens → 865 tok/s  (−25%)
eval time = 14026 ms / 1166 tokens → 83.1 tok/s  (+51%)
draft acceptance = 0.879, mean len = 3.63
```

### b10369 (worst — severe prefill regression)

```
prompt eval time = 14999 ms / 6198 tokens → 413 tok/s  (−64% vs b10356)
eval time = 2068 ms / 86 tokens → 41.6 tok/s  (−24%)
draft acceptance = 0.667, mean len = 3.00
```

Later tasks in same session:
```
prompt eval time = 22368 ms / 11953 tokens → 534 tok/s  (still degraded)
eval time = 23841 ms / 792 tokens → 33.2 tok/s
draft acceptance = 0.440, mean len = 2.29
```

## Analysis

Two separate regressions identified:

### 1. Prefill/prompt processing regression (affects b10359, b10360, b10369 — getting worse)

Prompt processing speed has degraded progressively:
- b10356: ~1200 tok/s
- b10359: ~834 tok/s (−30%)
- b10360: ~830 tok/s (−30%)
- b10369: **~470 tok/s (−60%)** ← severe

This suggests a **compounding issue** in the prefill kernels for Blackwell (sm_120). Each build makes it slightly worse.

### 2. DFlash mean acceptance length is low on stock builds

DFlash mean acceptance length is consistently 2.2-3.7 across all official builds. Community members report that **custom Blackwell-optimized builds** achieve mean acceptance lengths of 6-8 (peak 14.4), which would roughly **double or triple** the generation speed.

This suggests the stock CUDA kernels for Blackwell are not optimized for the DFlash verification path, limiting speculative decoding efficiency.

## Impact

For agentic workloads with large prompts (20-60k tokens common in code review and agent loops):
- b10356 is the only usable build (~1200 tok/s prefill)
- b10369 is nearly unusable (413 tok/s on first task — a 60k token prompt would take 145s just for prefill)

**Workaround:** Reverting to b10356 restores acceptable performance, but this is not sustainable as newer builds contain important bugfixes and model architecture support.

## Additional context

- The regression appears specific to **Blackwell (sm_120)** — consistent across multiple sessions and workloads
- Both batch_size (2048) and ubatch_size (2048) are used
- The model uses GQA (32 query heads / 8 KV heads, 16:1 ratio)
- Related issue: #26873 (mmproj loading causes persistent performance degradation on Muse Glimmer)
- The `muse-glimmer` architecture support was added in PR #26841 (merged between b10344 and b10356)

## Overview

Muse Glimmer sometimes answers the user and calls a tool in a single turn:

    <user answer><|eom|><|start|>assistant to=<tool><|message|><atem:function_calls>...

items.title: Muse Glimmer: fix detection of tool calls after EOM

items.body:
Two server-side tool-calling bugs, found while exercising the Muse Glimmer chat handler against a multi-turn agentic benchmark. The first is generic and affects every model; the second is specific to the Muse Glimmer parser.

## 1. Named `tool_choice` was silently downgraded to `"auto"`

`tool_choice` may be a string (`"auto"` / `"none"` / `"required"`) or, to force one specific function, an object:

```json
"tool_choice": {"type": "function", "function": {"name": "get_weather"}}
```

`json_value()` only understands the string form. Given the object it logs a type warning and returns the default `"auto"`, so the request is served as if no choice had been made — nothing surfaces to the caller.

That is not cosmetic for templates whose grammar is lazy under `"auto"`. The Muse Glimmer handler only arms its grammar once this trigger matches:

```
<|start|>assistant( to=(?!self<|message|>)(?!user<|message|>)[^<]*?<|message|>)
```

Asked to call a tool with empty arguments, the model writes the call *without* the `<|start|>assistant` header and never leaves the analysis channel:

```
to=skill<|message|><atem:function_calls>
<atem:invoke name="skill"></atem:invoke>
</atem:function_calls>
```

The trigger never fires, the grammar never arms, and the call stays buried in `reasoning_content` — `finish_reason: "stop"`, no `tool_calls`. Deterministic at temperature 0. `tool_choice: "required"` was unaffected because that path builds a non-lazy grammar.

**Fix:** parse the object form, narrow `tools` to the named function and map it to `"required"`. The grammar is then non-lazy and admits only that call, which is the OpenAI semantics and needs no per-template changes. Malformed `tool_choice` now returns 400 instead of silently behaving as `"auto"`.

## 2. A trailing tool call was swallowed into `message.content`

The Muse Glimmer parser read assistant content with `until("<|eot|>")`. The model routinely answers the user *and* calls a tool in one generation, and there is no `<|eot|>` before the call — so content ran to the end of the generation and absorbed the tool markup, which was then delivered to the user as chat text.

On a multi-turn agentic run this leaked raw tool markup into the visible reply on 43 turns across 19 of 113 tasks (~17% of tasks affected).

**Fix:** make content stop at `<|eom|>` / `<atem:function_calls>`, make the `to=<tool><|message|>` header optional, and allow content-then-tool-call with both delimiters optional.

## Testing

Against the Muse Glimmer 30B bf16 weights:

| case | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| named `tool_choice`, empty args | `finish_reason: stop`, no `tool_calls` | `tool_calls: skill {}` |
| named `tool_choice`, with args | ok | unchanged |
| named `tool_choice`, no-parameter tool | ok | unchanged |
| `tool_choice: "required"` (2 cases) | ok | unchanged |
| 5 malformed `tool_choice` inputs | silently treated as `"auto"` | 400 with a specific message |

Re-running the 19 tasks that leaked tool markup: 19/19 leaking → 0/19, and 43 leaked turns → 0 of 425.

On RTX 5090 (Blackwell, compute 12.0), this returns 4294967297 (0x100000001) : what?!... 3. CUDA_SET_SHARED_MEMORY_LIMIT passes smpbo to cudaFuncSetAttribute(..., int) a 32-bit parameter 4. 0x100000001 truncated to int = 1 5. GPU now thinks max dynamic shared memory is 1 byte 6. Softmax kernel requests 1152 bytes -->> cudaErrorInvalidValue -->> crash Fix appears to resolve my issue on my setup

items.body:
## Overview

<!-- Describe what this PR does and why. Be concise but complete -->

IQ quants are particularly slow on CPU at large batch sizes (what you'd see for imatrix and perplexity)

Part of this comes from the fact that during a 512-token batch, every weight in the model is decoded 512 times from the associated lookup table

This change introduces a GEMM panel, `block_iqp_x8`, which is 8 weight rows x 256 columns:

```
struct block_iqp_x8 {
    float   dfac[8];               // per row: the float part of the scale (d * 2^-k)
    int32_t bias[8];               // per row: unsigned-activation correction
    int8_t  iscales[16 * 8];       // per (sub-block, row): the integer part of the scale
    int8_t  qs[256 * 8];           // the decoded weights, interleaved
};
```

Now, instead of decoding each weight 512 times at batch 512, we decode 8 rows at a time into a cache-sized `int8` tile and run integer GEMM over it.

For dense models, this is a huge increase, up to 10x

For MoE it's more modest, more like 2x, but still quite good

PPL shifts a tiny bit, only ~0.24%, aka margin of error

<details>
<summary>Design details from Claude</summary>

Four design details make it work:

1. Interleaving 8 rows. qs[sb*128 + g*32 + row*4 + k] holds column sb*16 + g*4 + k. So one 32-byte load pulls 4 consecutive columns for each of 8 rows — exactly the operand shape _mm256_dpbusd_epi32 wants against a broadcast int32 of 4 activations. Eight output rows advance per instruction.

2. Sub-blocks of 16, not 32. iq2_xs/iq2_s take a group of 32 weights' scale from two nibbles, one per half. One scale per 32 couldn't represent them exactly, so 16 is used uniformly for all eight types → one kernel.

3. Split scale = float × integer (this is commit 4f7e113af). Every supported type's sub-block scale factors as (d · 2⁻ᵏ) · small_int — e.g. iq2_xs is d·(0.5+ls)·0.25 = (d/8)·(2ls+1). So dfac holds the float, iscales the integer. The kernel then applies sub-block scales in integer (mullo_epi32), accumulates the whole 256-weight super-block exactly in int32, and touches float exactly once per (row, super-block). That's 16 float roundings → 1. A float64 reference harness measured the result as 12–22% more accurate than upstream vec_dot (the previous float-scale version had been 2.6× less accurate).

4. The bias trick. VNNI's dpbusd needs unsigned × signed, but both operands here are signed. Instead of fixing that with _mm256_sign_epi8 per operand, activations are fed as y ^ 0x80 (i.e. y + 128), and the resulting spurious 128·Σw term — a per-row, per-super-block constant — is precomputed into bias at decode time and subtracted with one int32 op. Non-VNNI AVX2 builds fall back to the sign trick with bias disabled, because the maddubs int16 accumulator would overflow with unsigned operands.

</details>

## Additional information

<!-- You can provide more details and link related discussions here. Delete this section if not applicable -->

On dense models, this only kicks in when batch >= 32 columns, less than that was found to have lower performance

for MoE, it instead gates per-expert, and only works when needs to see 16 tokens to route through the new panel, otherwise old performance is better.

Can be disabled with `GGML_NO_IQ_PANEL=1`

Confirmed with tests that setting `GGML_NO_IQ_PANEL=1` returns original performance and PPL completely, as well as when using a lower batch size (`-ub 16`). At `-ub 16`, there is still an ~80% speed up in performance on dense

## Benchmark numbers

I ran PPL against master and this PR to get speed and numbers on `--chunks 50` for Qwen3.6-27B and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on EPYC 9654 using 24 threads

Created pure `IQ1_S`, `IQ1_M`, `IQ2_XXS`, `IQ2_XS`, `IQ2_S`, `IQ3_XXS`, `IQ3_S`, `IQ4_XS`, and `IQ4_NL`. Made pure to make sure each tensor type is fully exercised.

items.body:
## Overview
This PR is to fix a bug in MoE scatter. 

- MoE prompt processing on the OpenCL backend is not reproducible run-to-run: the same binary on the same prompt returns one of several outputs. 
- Measured on granite-3.0-3b-a800m-Q4_K_M (Adreno X2-90, greedy, llama-simple -n 64, 3 prompts × 5 runs each), every prompt produced 2–3 distinct outputs across 5 runs.

### Root cause
- `kernel_moe_scatter` assigns each token its slot within its expert via `atomic_inc(&slot_counter[expert])`, so the token→slot packing depends on which work-item wins the atomic and varies every run. 
- The ragged MoE prefill GEMM is sensitive to that packing order; the non-ragged path happens to be immune.

### Fix
- This PR replaces the atomic slot grab with a deterministic rank: a token's slot is its position in flat (token, k) order among the tokens routed to the same expert — a fixed function of the routing input. 
- One workgroup per expert walks the routing list in blocks of 64 with a workgroup scan and a running carry. 
- Default on; GGML_OPENCL_MOE_STABLE_SCATTER=0 restores the previous behavior.
- 2 files, backend-only (ggml-opencl.cpp + kernels/moe_sort_by_expert.cl).

<!-- Describe what this PR does and why. Be concise but complete -->

## Additional information

<!-- You can provide more details and link related discussions here. Delete this section if not applicable -->
### Determinism verification
- With the fix: 5/5 identical runs on every prompt, and the output matches an O(N·topK) reference implementation exactly.
- Six MoE models on the X2-90, 3 runs each, all single-output and coherent: gpt-oss-20b-MXFP4, Qwen3-30B-A3B-Q4_K_M, Qwen3-unsloth-30B-A3B-Q4_0, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-MXFP4_MOE, and granite-3.0-3b in Q4_K_M and MXFP4_MOE. 
- gpt-oss also 3/3 on the Adreno 840.

### Cost
Prefill only — the scatter runs on the GEMM path, decode never calls it: pp512 −0.63% on granite-3.0-3b (40 experts), −0.15% on Qwen3-30B-A3B (128 experts).
### Scope
- This fixes run-to-run reproducibility. 
- The ragged and non-ragged paths still produce different roundings of equal quality (MUL_MAT_ID max err 2.68e-05 vs 2.79e-05 against the CPU reference); 
- A host comment claiming the ragged path is byte-identical is corrected as part of this change. That difference is a rounding choice, not a wrong answer.
### Testing
test-backend-ops -o MUL_MAT_ID: Adreno X2-90, 383 OK / 0 FAIL.
The Adreno 840 declines all MUL_MAT_ID cases at these shapes in test-backend-ops; its evidence is the real-model determinism runs above.

items.body:
## Summary

On Intel Arc Pro B70 (Battlemage G31, 32 GB, 608 GB/s), token-generation
speed collapses with context depth far beyond what KV-cache bandwidth can
explain. The excess cost is a near-constant **~21-25 ns per KV position per
full-attention layer per token**, and it is invariant across:

- **backend**: Vulkan (Mesa 26.1.6 ANV) and SYCL (oneAPI 2025.3, L0 V2) pay the same tax;
- **model/geometry**: hybrid Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (2 KV heads × hs256), Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B (4 × hs128), Gemma 4 26B-A4B / 12B (8 × hs512) — KV row width 1 KiB vs 8 KiB makes no difference;
- **build**: b8183 and b10235 behave identically at depth;
- **quantization**: Q2_K vs Q4_K_M identical depth deltas.

Byte-independence rules out DRAM bandwidth. The signature fits
memory-latency-bound attention matvecs: too few outstanding loads to cover
GDDR6 latency. Supporting evidence: GPU holds max clock at its power cap
while useful traffic is a fraction of peak; running 4 concurrent streams
scales aggregate throughput ~2.4× (parallel streams supply the MLP a single
stream lacks); the same llama.cpp code on an AMD Strix Halo iGPU with less
than half the bandwidth holds the sibling model flat to 65k
(https://lilting.ch/en/articles/qwen35-ctx-kv-cache-vulkan-optimization).

## Environment

- GPU: Intel Arc Pro B70 32 GB (PCI 8086:e223), PCIe passthrough to a Linux VM (6 vCPU, 16 GB RAM). d0 results match published bare-metal numbers, and all depth effects are on-card, so virtualization is not a factor.
- Host driver: xe, kernel 6.17; Vulkan: Mesa 26.1.6 (kisak), KHR_coopmat active; SYCL: oneAPI 2025.3 image, compute runtime 26.18.
- llama.cpp b10235 (also tested b8183), Vulkan and SYCL builds, `-ngl 999 -ub 512 -fa 0 -n 256 -p 0 -r 1 -d <depth>`.

## Data (tg256, t/s)

| model | backend | d0 | d32k | d65k | d127k |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Q4_K_M (hybrid, 10 attn layers) | Vulkan | 70.7 | 58.4 | 32.2 | 20.7 |
| Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Q2_K | Vulkan | 72.0 | 60.2 | 33.4 | 21.2 |
| Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Q2_K | SYCL | 81.5 | 52.9 | 38.5 | 22.8 |
| Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B Q4 (48 attn layers) | Vulkan b10235 | 87.1 | 37.6 | ~11-13 | |
| Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B Q4 | Vulkan b8183 | 103.7 | 35.8 | | |
| Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B Q4 | SYCL | 105.9 | 20.5 | 11.2 | |
| Gemma 4 26B-A4B Q4 | Vulkan | 69.2 | 57.8 | 30.9 | |
| Gemma 4 12B Q4 | Vulkan | 48.4 | 31.7 (d32k) | 22.5 | |
| Gemma 4 12B Q4 | SYCL | 51.8 | 34.8 (d32k) | 25.3 | |

Per-token excess over each model's own d0 baseline, divided by
(n_kv × full-attention layers), lands at 21-25 ns for every row above
(Gemma global-layer counts estimated from sliding_window_pattern).

Physics reference: Qwen3.6's KV is only 20 KiB/token (10 attn layers × 2 KV
heads × 256 × 2 × f16; 30 of 40 layers are DeltaNet with fixed state), i.e.
2.6 GB at 127k — ~5 ms/token at realistic bandwidth. Measured excess: ~33 ms.

## Control: same card, same model, different kernels — no depth tax

Intel's own stack (intel/llm-scaler-vllm 0.21.0-b2, vLLM v0.21.1 XPU, same
B70, same Qwen3.6-35B-A3B as GPTQ-Int4) decodes **flat to 127k**:

| depth | llama.cpp Vulkan b10235 (Q4_K_M) | vLLM XPU (GPTQ-Int4) |
|---|---|---|
| ~0 | 70.7 | 18.8-22.4 |
| 32k | 58.4 | 22.6 |
| 65k | 32.2 | 18.3-22.5 |
| 127k | 20.7 | 16.2-21.8 |

vLLM XPU's baseline is ~3.5× lower (eager GPTQ-MoE kernels), but its depth
cost is ~zero — demonstrating the Xe2 hardware itself can serve 127k
context with no per-position penalty. The tax measured above is specific to
ggml's decode-attention kernels.

## Additional findings from the same investigation

1. **Silent CPU fallback** (gdb-verified): with fa off, when the prefill
   score tensor (n_kv × n_ubatch × n_heads × 4B) exceeds free VRAM, the
   scheduler reroutes the matmul to the CPU backend with no warning —
   ~100× slowdown that presents as a hang. A log line when an op planned
   for GPU falls back would save users days. Likely the mechanism behind
   #18808's "almost stops".
2. **`-ctk q8_0` with fa off** also silently falls back to CPU on Vulkan.
3. **SYCL cannot load models whose weight buffer exceeds ~16.5 GiB**
   (`ggml_backend_sycl_buffer_type_alloc_buffer: can't allocate ... on
   device`, 29 GiB free): the SYCL backend allocates weights as one buffer
   and get_max_size does not reflect the device's real single-allocation
   ceiling; the Vulkan backend chunks. Qwen3.6-35B Q4_K_M (19.6 GiB)
   cannot run on SYCL on a 32 GB card. UR_L0_ENABLE_RELAXED_ALLOCATION_LIMITS,
   NEOReadDebugKeys/AllowUnrestrictedSize, legacy L0 adapter: no effect.
4. **b8183 → b10235 regressed MoE decode d0 ~19% on Vulkan**
   (Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B: 103.7 → 87.1 tg256).
5. fa=on is uniformly slower than fa=off on Xe2 for tg at every depth
   (Qwen3.6: 68.5/32.1/20.8/12.5 vs 70.7/58.4/32.2/20.7), q8_0 KV does not
   close the gap.

## Ask

The per-position constant suggests the decode-path attention matvec kernels
(both backends) issue too few concurrent loads on Intel to hide memory
latency at large n_kv. Happy to run diagnostics/patches on this hardware —
single-owner box, can bisect or profile on request.

items.body:
## Overview

Draft SM120 CUTLASS MoE prefill path, disabled by default. It currently supports:

- GPT-OSS MXFP4 with fused W13
- Qwen3.6-35B-A3B NVFP4

It repacks expert weights, reuses one routing schedule and input quantization per layer, then runs grouped W13/W2 with CUDA epilogues. Unsupported cases fall back to the existing CUDA path.

This branch also contains earlier CUDA and Attention experiments and is not intended to merge as one patch. Useful pieces can be split out separately.

## Additional information

Measured on one RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition with batch 8192, 25 CPU threads and FlashAttention.

### GPT-OSS-120B MXFP4 prefill

| Path | Best ubatch | pp8192 |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Existing llama.cpp | 2048 | 11,738.58 tok/s |
| Strict native CUDA | 8192 | 17,708 tok/s |
| Optimized CUTLASS | 8192 | 25,713.80 tok/s |
| Same-machine vLLM | 8192 | 36,819 tok/s |

CUTLASS is 2.19x faster than current llama.cpp and reaches 69.8% of same-machine vLLM.

### Qwen3.6-35B-A3B NVFP4 prefill

| Prompt | Native eager | CUTLASS eager | Speedup |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 512 | 9,819.79 tok/s | 12,998.69 tok/s | 1.324x |
| 2048 | 11,362.81 tok/s | 15,309.67 tok/s | 1.347x |
| 8192 | 10,065.18 tok/s | 13,548.77 tok/s | 1.346x |

CUDA Graphs reach 13,551.11 tok/s at pp8192, close to eager CUTLASS.

| Component | Native | CUTLASS |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Steady CUDA kernel time | 1,291.861 ms | 863.054 ms |
| MoE GEMM | 282.364 ms | 63.213 ms |
| Expert scheduling | 61.069 ms | 1.108 ms |
| Activation quantization | 45.941 ms | 27.656 ms |
| Attention | 76.195 ms | 75.589 ms |

The first CUTLASS use adds a 74.715 ms weight transform, excluded above.

### Decode

| Path | Decode |
| --- | ---: |
| Native MMVQ | 201.868 tok/s |
| CUTLASS | 170.207 tok/s |

Nsys reports 5.882 ms/token for MMVQ and 6.634 ms/token for CUTLASS. All 36 expert layers used CUTLASS, so MMVQ remains better for single-token decode.

```text
supported SM120 W4A4 prefill -> CUTLASS
single-token decode          -> MMVQ
everything else              -> existing llama.cpp path
```

Correctness passed 6/6 Qwen eager cases, 6/6 CUDA Graph cases, and all six GPT decode cases. Full-model Qwen logits validation is still pending.

Enable with `GGML_CUDA_CUTLASS_MOE=ON`. Current CUTLASS revision: `b46b16d003484063bca4ed365e44095c4c6ed633`.

- [Full results](https://github.com/leonardHONG/llama.cpp/blob/feat/blackwell-moe-prefill-experiments/scripts/blackwell-moe-prefill/RESULTS.md)
- [Build and experiment commands](https://github.com/leonardHONG/llama.cpp/blob/feat/blackwell-moe-prefill-experiments/scripts/blackwell-moe-prefill/README.md)
- [GPT-OSS decode notes](https://github.com/leonardHONG/llama.cpp/blob/feat/blackwell-moe-prefill-experiments/scripts/blackwell-moe-prefill/gpt_oss_mxfp4_decode.md)
- [Qwen NVFP4 prefill notes](https://github.com/leonardHONG/llama.cpp/blob/feat/blackwell-moe-prefill-experiments/scripts/blackwell-moe-prefill/qwen_nvfp4_prefill.md)



## CUTLASS integration

CUTLASS does not provide a single runtime API like cuBLAS. The kernel shape, layout, data types, and GPU architecture are fixed at compile time.

For this path, CUTLASS only provides the SM120 block-scaled W4A4 GEMM.

| Part | Where it is handled |
| --- | --- |
| SM120 W4A4 GEMM | CUTLASS |
| GGUF weight conversion | llama.cpp repack code |
| Activation quantization | llama.cpp CUDA code |
| Kernel selection and fallback | llama.cpp CUDA backend |
| MoE token grouping | llama.cpp CUDA code |
| SwiGLU and expert reduction | llama.cpp CUDA code |

GGUF stores quantized values and block scales together. CUTLASS expects separate value and scale tensors in its own layout, so the GGUF weights cannot be passed to the kernel directly. They are repacked on first use and cached.

For dense models the flow is basically:

```
GGUF weight -> repack -> activation quantization -> CUTLASS GEMM -> output scale
```

Dense and MoE use the same repack/cache code and the same GEMM launcher.

## MoE-specific work

For MoE, each token selects several experts and each expert receives a different number of rows. CUTLASS runs the grouped W13 and W2 GEMMs, but it does not build the groups.

I group the routed rows by expert and reuse that grouping for W13 and W2:

```
routing
  -> group rows by expert
  -> expand and quantize
  -> CUTLASS grouped W13
  -> scale, bias, SwiGLU, and A2 quantization
  -> CUTLASS grouped W2
  -> scale, bias, routing weight, and expert reduction
```

The W13 post-processing produces the quantized input for W2. The W2 post-processing combines the selected expert outputs back into one row per token. These two stages and the expert scheduling are the parts that remain MoE-specific.

These are custom CUDA kernels rather than CUTLASS epilogues. They fuse the scale, bias, activation, or routing reduction so another intermediate tensor is not materialized between stages.

Once the tensors are in the layout CUTLASS expects, the actual GEMM launch is fairly small. Most of the code is the glue around it: repacking GGUF weights, quantizing activations, caching converted weights, choosing the kernel, and handling graph and fallback cases.


## Requirements

-  I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)
-  AI usage disclosure: Yes, paired with Codex

items.body:
Fixes input layer CPU offload on iGPU/UMA systems, mirroring the existing output layer policy.

closes #25700

## Overview

The `tok_embd` (input) layer is always assigned to the CPU backend (`pimpl->dev_input = { cpu_dev, &pimpl->cpu_buft_list }`) regardless of `-ngl` setting, even when full GPU offload (`-ngl 99`) is requested. On integrated GPU (iGPU) and unified memory (UMA) architectures such as AMD Strix Halo (gfx1151), this forces `GET_ROWS(tok_embd, inp_tokens)` onto the CPU backend at the start of every forward pass.

This causes ~20 cross-backend synchronization barriers per token on the ROCm/HIP backend because the HIP path uses synchronous `cudaStreamSynchronize` calls per input tensor copy (`ggml_backend_cuda_buffer_set_tensor`), rather than an async GPU-to-GPU route. On UMA hardware where CPU and GPU share the same physical DDR5 memory, the input buffer should simply be assigned to the GPU device with zero-copy, exactly as the output layer (`dev_output`) already does via `get_layer_buft_list(n_layer_all)`.

The fix mirrors the existing output-layer policy: when `act_gpu_layers >= n_layer_all` (full GPU offload requested), `dev_input` is assigned via `get_layer_buft_list(0)` instead of being hardcoded to CPU. Partial offload remains unchanged.

## Additional information

**Root cause:** In `src/llama-model.cpp`, the `dev_input` assignment hardcodes the CPU backend:

```cpp
// there is very little benefit to offloading the input layer, so always keep it on the CPU
pimpl->dev_input = { cpu_dev, &pimpl->cpu_buft_list };
```

Meanwhile, `dev_output` already uses `get_layer_buft_list(n_layer_all)` which follows `-ngl`. On iGPU/UMA systems, this means every token generation forces `tok_embd` to run `GET_ROWS` on the CPU backend, triggering ~20 cross-backend sync points per token on ROCm (8 `cudaStreamSynchronize` calls per input tensor across 10 input tensors, as identified in issue discussion).

The HIP backend does not benefit from async H2D copies the way Vulkan does (which uses `copy_from_host=true`), so the synchronous fallback path on HIP pays the full cross-backend sync cost on every forward pass. This is why Vulkan performs comparably to ROCm on discrete GPUs but diverges significantly on UMA/iGPU hardware where zero-copy assignment is viable.

**Why this condition is safe:**
- `act_gpu_layers = std::min(n_gpu_layers, n_layer_all + 1)` (line 1358)
- When the user requests `-ngl 99` or `-ngl 0` (full offload auto), `act_gpu_layers >= n_layer_all` evaluates true, and the input layer is offloaded to GPU device 0 via `get_layer_buft_list(0)` — the same path as all other layers.
- When partial offload is requested (e.g., `-ngl 20`), `act_gpu_layers < n_layer_all`, the condition is false, and the input layer stays on CPU — identical to current behavior, preserving memory savings for offloaded models.
- Discrete GPUs (dGPU) with full offload: the input layer is now on GPU like the rest, eliminating unnecessary CPU-GPU round-trips. Performance impact on dGPU is expected to be neutral-to-positive since `GET_ROWS` runs entirely on-device.
- The `get_layer_buft_list(0)` call is valid even when `i_gpu_start == 0` (full offload case), since `il=0` falls in the GPU range and returns the first GPU device's buffer list.

## Performance data

The performance measurements below are from existing issue reporters verified on the same AMD Strix Halo (gfx1151) hardware referenced in issue #25700. They were collected by other contributors (Vasili-Sk, cflury4784) and are not fabricated.

### Vasili-Sk — Patch Decomposition Report (Q8_0 + Q6_K, ROCm on gfx1151)

**Flags:** `-p 16384 -n 1024 -ngl 99 -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0 -fa 1 -b 4096 -ub 2048 -r 3 --mmap 0 --no-host 1 --poll 0`

| R4 (hipDeviceScheduleBlockingSync for gfx1151) | reverted | 1125.96 | 48.65 | 955.40 | 55.68 | -0.02% | -0.11% | +1.39% | +0.14% |

items.body:
### Summary

The failure is not a single isolated bad completion. It appears in clusters during repeated warm `stream=true` chat completion requests. The most reproducible symptom is an assistant response consisting almost entirely of repeated `?` characters, while the HTTP/SSE stream remains structurally valid and `curl` exits successfully.

I am on 9682 (558e221b7).

This looks possibly related to #20610 and #21888, but my case is not identical:

* Linux + Mesa RADV
* AMD RX590 / Polaris10
* `llama-server`
* streaming chat completions
* warm repeated requests
* clustered failures after many successful requests
* Qwen3.5 model
* `--no-kv-offload` does not eliminate the issue, but changes the output regime significantly

I have seen some very promising results with the hardware when the responses are healthy, the generation is fast, the GPUs are great value and you can fit so many models on it. If we could solve this issue, that would make AI accessible to a whole generation of cards.

Note that in this ticket, I refer and test a lot Qwen but I had a similar experience with Gemma4 producing '<unused49>' tokens. Disabling the reasoning stabilized the model but after that it was unable to perform in agentic scenarios (it basically tell you it will do something and never does it). It isn't naive to think that the issues may be related, just taking different shapes.

I am providing already quite a big bundle of testing and evidence but I am also keen on providing more if needed.

### Environment

Please replace this section with exact command output from the attached files.

* llama.cpp / llama-server version: `<paste llama-server --version>`
* git commit: `<paste git rev-parse HEAD>`
* OS: `<paste /etc/os-release + uname -a>`
* GPU: AMD Radeon RX590 / Polaris10 / RADV
* Mesa / Vulkan driver: `<paste vulkaninfo --summary relevant lines>`
* Kernel: `<paste uname -a>`
* CPU/RAM: Xeon E5-2630L v4, 32 GB RAM
* Backend: Vulkan
* Model: `Qwen3.5-9B-UD-Q5_K_XL.gguf`
* Server command used for baseline:

```bash
/home/flori/llama.cpp/build/bin/llama-server \
  --host 0.0.0.0 \
  --port 8080 \
  --alias Build-comfort_Qwen3.5-9B-UD-Q5_K_XL \
  --model /home/flori/models/Qwen3.5-9B-UD-Q5_K_XL.gguf \
  --ctx-size 65536 \
  --n-gpu-layers 99 \
  --threads 10 \
  --parallel 1 \
  --batch-size 256 \
  --ubatch-size 32 \
  --reasoning off \
  --reasoning-budget 0 \
  --cache-ram 0 \
  --log-verbosity 3
```

### Reproduction shape

The issue reproduces using repeated identical `stream=true` chat completion requests against a warm `llama-server` process.

The requests use:

* OpenAI-compatible `/v1/chat/completions`
* `stream=true`
* tools enabled
* `top_p=0.9`
* `max_tokens=64`
* same prompt repeated many times
* one slot: `--parallel 1`

The bad outputs appear after many successful warm requests, not immediately on model load.

### Observed result

In one controlled run:

```text
baseline:      100 runs, 5 bad
no_kv_offload: 100 runs, 13 bad
```

Baseline bad cluster:

```text
baseline rep=53 cq=64 tq=0
baseline rep=54 cq=64 tq=0
baseline rep=55 cq=64 tq=0
baseline rep=56 cq=64 tq=0
baseline rep=57 cq=62 tq=0
```

Representative bad baseline output from `baseline_rep57`:

```text
finish_reason: stop
content_len: 62
tool_args_len: 0
content_q_run: 62
tool_q_run: 0
content_head: ??????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????
curl_rc: 0
```

The SSE response is structurally valid, with no JSON parse errors, and the request finishes successfully.

### `--no-kv-offload` behaviour

I also tested the same workload with:

```bash
--no-kv-offload
```

The flag is accepted by this build:

```text
-kvo, --kv-offload, -nkvo, --no-kv-offload
```

This did not eliminate corruption. It produced more bad outputs by the question-mark metric:

```text
no_kv_offload rep=15 cq=62
no_kv_offload rep=16 cq=64
no_kv_offload rep=17 cq=64
no_kv_offload rep=18 cq=31
no_kv_offload rep=66 cq=51
no_kv_offload rep=67 cq=31
no_kv_offload rep=72 cq=64
no_kv_offload rep=73 cq=64
no_kv_offload rep=74 cq=64
no_kv_offload rep=75 cq=64
no_kv_offload rep=76 cq=64
no_kv_offload rep=77 cq=64
no_kv_offload rep=78 cq=31
```

However, `--no-kv-offload` also changed output behaviour substantially:

* baseline: 95/100 responses produced the expected tool call
* no_kv_offload: 0/100 responses produced the expected tool call
* many non-`?` outputs were also semantically incoherent

Example from `no_kv_offload_rep98`:

```text
content_head: ,(

 for say. and
, and? time.. ": of.

 of
 don and
```

So I do not consider `--no-kv-offload` a clean fix/control for this workload, but it is evidence that the symptom is not narrowly fixed by disabling KV offload.

### Other observations

* The failure is bursty/clustered rather than uniformly random.
* `stream=false` was previously clean in a smaller layer-narrowing test: 40/40 direct non-stream runs clean.
* Streaming and warm slot/cache/checkpoint reuse may be contributing factors.
* Disabling context checkpoints with `--ctx-checkpoints 0` caused full prompt reprocessing every request and was too slow for a full comparison.
* A true CPU-only build/control is being tested separately because the full captured prompt is very slow on CPU.

### Expected result

Repeated identical warm streaming requests should either:

* produce valid coherent responses/tool calls consistently, or
* fail explicitly with a server/runtime error if the backend cannot support this model/configuration safely.

They should not intermittently produce structurally valid SSE responses containing repeated `?` or incoherent token streams.

### Attachments

Attached evidence bundle contains:

* `SUMMARY.txt`
* `results.csv`
* `BAD_RUNS.txt`
* `baseline_server.log`
* `no_kv_offload_server.log`
* server warning files
* representative `response.sse`, `classification.txt`, and `timing.txt` for:

  * `baseline_rep53`
  * `baseline_rep57`
  * `no_kv_offload_rep75`
  * `no_kv_offload_rep98`
* system info:

  * `llama_server_version.txt`

## Overview

Dequantize quantized KV caches (Q4_0, Q4_1, Q5_0, Q5_1, Q8_0) to contiguous F16 and run the existing F16 flash-attention kernels (including the pad and mask-block kernels) for `FLASH_ATTN_EXT` on Metal.

- New small dequant kernel (full 16-element block chunks via `dequantize_*_t4x4`), dispatched separately for K and V into per-op scratch
- When V is a view of K (MLA models), the redundant V dequant is skipped: the dequantized V is a view of the dequantized K, and the pad/attention kernels read it with K's strides
- `test-backend-ops`: new quantized-KV FA cases, including the MLA shape (576/512, V is a view of K)
